fit: common-sage extract chemistry and antiproliferative experiment
assessment: The author abstract confirms sage-derived extracts and chemical and cancer cell endpoints. P33 references this same report. It provides no culinary dose or Parkinson symptom comparison.

fit: inhaled common sage distillate and acute labor pain
assessment: Unblinded groups of 52 had mean pain 2.46 with common sage distillate and 3.17 with water at 30 minutes, and 4.00 versus 3.98 at 60 minutes. Overall three-group p values were .001 and .10, respectively. IRCT138811192515N1 identifies the same trial.

fit: oral sage extract and a premenstrual symptom composite
assessment: The author abstract describes a favorable broad symptom comparison. Separate pain results require the original tables. A 2017 companion is potentially overlapping.

fit: oral sage leaf extract and evoked pain after peripheral nerve injury
assessment: Six mice per group; mechanical withdrawal thresholds favored oral extract over injured controls on days 7, 14 and 21. The paper also reports reduced cold and heat hypersensitivity. This measures evoked pain in a peripheral mouse injury rather than Parkinson pain severity.

fit: oral dry sage extract and the joint and muscular discomfort item
assessment: Table 2 reports a lower item score versus placebo after treatment in postmenopausal participants (p<.001), with inconsistent numerical reporting. No culinary exposure or Parkinson cohort.

fit: Pooled pain events after common-sage extract plus Spanish-sage oil
assessment: Nine pain or injury events are pooled across randomized groups. The article does not give arm-specific pain counts or severity. The capsule combines species and contains no fresh culinary leaves.

fit: oral fresh-sage-tip extract and the joint and muscular discomfort item
assessment: The placebo-controlled study reports a favorable single-item change among 48 per-protocol participants (p<.05). The item effect size and intention-to-treat comparison are unreported. Extract and menopause limit transfer to the frozen Parkinson comparison.

fit: Abdominal pain after reported excessive intake of common-sage plant material
assessment: The single case recorded abdominal pain of 6/10. Actual amount, freshness and preparation were unspecified. Coexisting symptoms, medication history and subsequent treatments leave causation uncertain.

fit: common sage leaf extract spray and clinical throat pain
assessment: Two-hour pain AUC favored the 15% spray versus a matched 0.3% spray (p = .0021) in 164 phase-two participants. The local route and acute throat pain do not resolve fresh dietary leaf or Parkinson pain.

fit: sage rinse and surgical pain with an active analgesic comparator
assessment: Moderate or severe pediatric postoperative pain was less frequent with benzydamine than sage at four time points. Both arms received NSAIDs. The study supplies no estimate versus an inactive control.

fit: sage tea mouth rinse with sparse oral pain reporting
assessment: The randomized advanced-cancer trial recorded baseline mouth and swallowing pain. The authors omitted both items from their comparisons because few participants reported them. Sage rinse results for dry mouth give no pain effect.

fit: single-dose oral common sage extract and qualitative mouse tail-prick response
assessment: The Results report delayed tail-prick response at 180 minutes after 1,000 and 3,000 mg/kg hydroethanolic leaf extract. Vocalization, tactile irritability and Straub tail also occurred at those doses. This was a safety observation in ICR mice with no numerical pain effect, fresh-leaf exposure or Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: topical sage cream and subjective pediatric spasticity pain
assessment: Three of six older participants reported less pain during the four-week subjective follow-up. There is no concurrent comparator for those reports. Topical extract and pediatric spasticity differ from consuming fresh sage for Parkinson pain.

fit: oral grapeseed oil cookie and registered grip strength
assessment: Registered secondary correlation analysis included grip strength. The published results report biomarkers without grip, dexterity or Parkinson outcomes. Oil pressing was unspecified.

fit: oral grapeseed oil cookie and registered grip strength
assessment: The single-arm pilot plans grip-strength correlations with cardiolipin in healthy adults. No posted results. Grip strength differs from dexterity and no Parkinson cohort is enrolled.

fit: hydroalcoholic grape seed extract and forepaw measures in Parkinson-model rats
assessment: Forepaw stride length increased (p < .05) and grid-descent latency fell (p < .01). The extract, rodent measures and model leave clinical hand dexterity after cold-pressed oil unresolved.

fit: grapeseed oil wristband and hand motor tests
assessment: The patent reports 12% higher finger tapping speed, 15% higher precision speed and 14% higher steadiness after four weeks in its grapeseed wristband group. Study size was small, dispersion was unreported and exposure was topical in healthy men.

fit: curry leaf extract and timed motor tasks in rotenone mice
assessment: The publisher figure shows shorter beam and pole times after leaf extract given before rotenone exposure. Approximate times were 7 versus 108 seconds for beam traversal and 10 versus 13 seconds for pole descent. Ground leaf and clinical bradykinesia were untested.

fit: oral aqueous curry leaf extract and movement initiation in rats
assessment: The paraquat-exposed extract groups initiated movement faster and showed shorter bar-test immobility. No ground leaf or clinical bradykinesia outcome was tested.

fit: curry leaf fractions and haloperidol catalepsy in mice
assessment: The fractions prolonged bar-test catalepsy and reduced apomorphine-associated movement. The extracts and tests differ from the paraquat study and from clinical bradykinesia after ground leaf.

fit: methanol curry leaf extract and drug-induced catalepsy
assessment: At 120 minutes bar-test immobility averaged 110.0 seconds with the highest extract level versus 256.7 seconds with haloperidol alone. The 113.0-second extract value is from 150 minutes. The lead author's 2021 fractions produced an opposite signal under another protocol. Neither tests ground leaf or clinical bradykinesia.

fit: curry leaf coingredients and IBS rather than motor outcomes
assessment: The official species-targeted registry hit links to one crossover with a composite bowel symptom result. It provides no bradykinesia estimate.

fit: curry leaves in a Parkinson diet menu with composite motor score
assessment: The menu lists curry leaves and UPDRS III includes bradykinesia. The pilot gives no isolated curry leaf arm, verified ground preparation or separate bradykinesia estimate.

fit: basil odor identification in Parkinson’s
assessment: Participants with Parkinson’s misidentified the basil item 74.3% of the time. Exposure was an odor identification stimulus with no basil ingestion or pre/post olfactory treatment comparison.

fit: memory-care almond comparator and combined neuropsychiatric symptoms
assessment: The recovered model estimates total NPI at 7.97 for almond oil and 8.68 for lavender, difference .71 (p = .0022). Visual hallucinations were not reported separately and almond oil was topical and diffused.

fit: odor cards with aroma constituents found in tea
assessment: Median odor identification was 7 versus 10 in older versus younger healthy participants. Mandarin and rose cards share constituents with tea; the study administered no green tea.

fit: odor-card scores by cognitive group
assessment: Of 115 day-service users, the 36 with cognitive decline scored lower than the normal and MCI groups. No green-tea intervention or intake-by-olfaction contrast was tested.

fit: observational tea analysis or prediabetes egg program
assessment: An observational member reports current green tea drinking and odds of cognitive impairment. No Parkinson population, fatigue outcome or olfactory endpoint is supplied.

fit: registered perioperative odor enrichment
assessment: Multiscent inhalation versus sham includes green-tea scent and olfactory outcomes. The recruiting registry has no results. It contains no culinary intake or Parkinson contrast.

fit: separate two-year extract experiment and olfactory histopathology
assessment: Male mouse nerve atrophy and epithelial fibrosis increased across tested extract doses. This refers to the separate two-year cohort and does not count the program's linked short-term report twice. No smell function result.

fit: caffeinated beverage history and UPSIT in Parkinson relatives
assessment: Adjusted identification scores were 2.6 points higher (95% CI 0.5 to 4.5) for two to three cups of caffeinated drinks daily versus below one. Participants were relatives, and neither tea type nor exposure assignment was isolated.

fit: pre-existing smell status and concentration selected in a sensory study
assessment: Participants were grouped by existing olfaction. Older smell-impaired participants added more green tea powder than young normosmic controls, a possible reverse path from olfaction to exposure, without a measured post-tea smell change.

fit: concentrated tea extract and olfactory histopathology
assessment: The fourteen-week mouse experiment found more olfactory epithelial and nerve atrophy after concentrated gavage. No odor performance or effect of ordinary brewed tea in Parkinson disease was measured.

fit: caffeinated espresso and standardized testing in acquired hyposmia
assessment: The 76-participant study found no clear acute smell function difference after caffeinated or decaffeinated espresso. It used a different beverage and different causes of olfactory loss.

fit: bottled oolong and acute retronasal ratings
assessment: Peak rated aroma rose from 3.71 to 4.13 after the second sip of the same oolong. This compares successive ratings of the beverage itself and provides no clinical impairment or Parkinson estimate.

fit: caffeinated coffee and separate smell test components in healthy adults
assessment: No clear difference on threshold, discrimination or identification was reported in 49 normosmic participants. No tea or Parkinson cohort was tested.

fit: isolated caffeine and threshold plus identification outcomes
assessment: No clear overall threshold effect. Identification changes averaged −1.13 and +0.03 (condition p=.06). An eight-person exploratory nonconsumer subgroup gave differing threshold and identification patterns.

fit: green-tea history and nonmotor symptom status in two PRKN Parkinson cases
assessment: Table 1 lists never versus quit in the green tea row and absent olfactory dysfunction in both. Brew, timing, symptom change and an exposure effect are unreported.

fit: intranasal white tea extract and functional odor tests in stressed mice
assessment: Buried-food retrieval and the other odor tests favored intranasal white tea extract relative to stressed controls. Figure 3 involves a different tea, route and model from brewed green tea and Parkinson disease.

fit: green-tea scent in active training comparators
assessment: Frequency comparison included green-tea scent in the five-odor second stage for both groups. Olfactory sensitivity favored standard over more frequent training, without a tea-only response or ingestion.

fit: multiscent training and postinfectious parosmia
assessment: Nine-month TDI was 27.9 versus 14.0 in self-selected groups. TDI had already risen to 21.4 before the green-tea scent phase. No tea-only or oral comparison was made.

fit: genetically proxied tea intake and baseline smell impairment
assessment: Lower odds of hyposmia in nominal analysis. The result did not pass the multiple-testing threshold.

fit: green tea as a familiarity label
assessment: The questionnaire gave green-tea odor a familiarity score of 66. The final test did not include green tea, and the different test scores result from changing stimuli and answer choices.

fit: tea exposure and separate olfactory phenotype in a GBA1 family survey
assessment: The study compared tea exposure against Parkinson status and hyposmia by group in 59 nonmanifesting GBA1 carriers, 62 controls and 107 GBA1-Parkinson cases. Available author text gives no tea-by-hyposmia comparison or brewed preparation. Full tables remain open.

fit: tea and hyposmia tested as separate cfDNA methylation correlates
assessment: The abstract describes 20 Parkinson participants and nine controls. It reports separate phenotypic associations with methylation without a tea-to-hyposmia estimate or beverage preparation. Possible participant overlap with a different clinical report is unverified.

fit: tea sachet odors in a memory training trial
assessment: The TDI post-training contrast was +0.27 points (p=.871). Two follow-up estimates conflict in the published narrative and table. Tea type and an ingestion effect remain unverified.

fit: isolated EGCG plus lifestyle and exploratory UPSIT
assessment: Supplementary Table 6 reports +0.1 points (95% CI −1.3 to 1.5, p=.853) at 12 months. The participants had subjective cognitive decline, and both arms received lifestyle intervention. The study used isolated EGCG capsules rather than brewed green tea.

fit: standardized extract alone or in a mixture in cultured dopaminergic cells
assessment: The cell experiment measured survival and oxidative or inflammatory markers. It uses an extract in culture and mentions human hyposmia only as clinical background.

fit: habitual Japanese green tea beverages and binary hyposmia in Parkinson's
assessment: Tables 1 and 2 report cross-sectional binary hyposmia by frequency (p=.854) and reported daily volume (p=.519). No smell severity or standardized brew was studied. The 2025 poster shares ethics approval 220137 and provides no separate smell outcome.

fit: habitual black or herbal tea and odor identification
assessment: The CHRIS supplement defines tea as black tea and herbal tea. Hyposmia OR was 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96) and ordinal identification OR 1.07 (1.02 to 1.12). This general-population cross-sectional study gives no green-tea or Parkinson-specific estimate.

fit: coconut odor recognition and standing lightheadedness
assessment: Gaining recognition of coconut odor was associated with higher MDS-UPDRS item 1.12 scores (B = 1.147, nominal p = .003). The study used odor strips and no coconut oil intake.

fit: Parkinson-related rat histology after leaf extract
assessment: Injected leaf hexane fraction preserved TH-positive neurons in the 6-OHDA experiment. The overlapping journal report contains no identified stride measure.

fit: essential oil and nonspecific mouse motor impairment
assessment: The seizure-model report describes motor impairment and sedation under essential oil. It does not quantify stride length.

fit: registered sunflower oil comparator in major depression
assessment: The official 2010 record plans 2 g/day of sunflower oil and Hamilton scale change after eight weeks. Its historical status is not yet recruiting and there are no posted results, actual enrollments or refining grade.

fit: sunflower oil on a lapel and residential-care NPI depression
assessment: NPI depression changes were −1.0 with sunflower oil and −2.8 with essential oils pooled (p=.15). The oil was on a lapel and one Parkinson diagnosis was a per-protocol violation. No Parkinson subgroup or oral refined exposure was tested.

fit: sunflower capsules and geriatric depression ratings in mild cognitive impairment
assessment: The overall Geriatric Depression Scale treatment test gave p=.95. An APOE ε4 interaction favored DHA/EPA (p=.04). The sunflower comparator included matched orange oil and vitamin E. No refining grade, oil-free group or Parkinson cohort was reported.

fit: sunflower oil plus positive suggestion and BDI-II
assessment: In adults awaiting psychotherapy, BDI-II changes were −3.30 with the combined oil and positive suggestion versus −0.05 with standard waiting (p<.001). There was no oil-plus-neutral-instruction arm or Parkinson cohort.

fit: Parkinson depression trial with corn oil comparator
assessment: The author abstract reports Hamilton response in 75% on DHA plus EPA versus 25% on corn oil. Arm means and exact analyzed denominators remain unavailable. No sunflower oil was assigned.

fit: sunflower oil comparator and depression in NAFLD
assessment: The 12-week trial reported depression improvement in the sesame arm relative to the sunflower comparator during a hypocaloric diet. The same-cohort companion identifies both oils as refined and odorless. Arm-specific sunflower values remain unavailable in the mood abstract.

fit: Parkinson blood fatty-acid measures and depression item
assessment: Cross-sectional preprint reports adjusted blood DHA association with lower depression item severity, with no clear adjusted linoleic-acid affective association. Blood fatty-acid levels do not identify intake or refining of sunflower oil.

fit: ingested sunflower oil comparator and standardized depression ratings
assessment: The 73-person trial reported no clear within-arm BDI-II change and greater HAMD-7 decline with olive oil (p=.001). The official registry matches the exposure and planned sample but does not list the mood scales. There was no Parkinson cohort, confirmed sunflower refining grade or oil-free arm.

fit: sunflower and fish oil comparator in adults with major depression
assessment: The mixed comparator contained 2% fish oil. In 432 randomized participants, adjusted overall group differences were inconclusive on IDS-SR30 (p=.088) and MADRS (p=.053). No Parkinson group, oil-free control or refining grade was available.

fit: oral sunflower and fish-oil comparator with standardized depression ratings
assessment: The author Methods identify sunflower oil with 0.2% fish oil. The full-sample adjusted HAM-D difference for EPA versus comparator was −1.5 (95% CI −3.7 to 0.7). Both arms improved. The population had psychological distress and the study did not isolate a refined sunflower effect.

fit: sunflower oil emulsion active comparison with pediatric depression scores
assessment: Sunflower CDI means were 24.9 at baseline and 22.2 at 12 weeks, with paired change −2.9 and Friedman p=.233. Unadjusted between-oil change p=.064 at week 12. No oil-free control, grade confirmation or Parkinson participants. Pilot and laboratory papers share the study registry.

fit: sunflower food frequency and composite Parkinson symptom burden
assessment: The poster reports +2 total PRO-PD points per intake frequency category (95% CI −10 to 13, p=.787). The cross-sectional exposure did not specify an oil grade. It gives no individual depressive symptoms estimate.

fit: oral high-oleic sunflower oil comparator and three depression-related scales
assessment: At 26 weeks the sunflower CES-D mean change was −0.4 versus −0.2 and +0.2 under two fish-oil doses, with overall p = .87. Neither refining grade nor an oil-free comparator was verified. This population did not have Parkinson depression.

fit: sunflower oil comparator and depression ratings after prostatectomy
assessment: HADS depression was 3.2 at baseline and 2.3 at 12 months in the sunflower group. There was no clear treatment-by-time interaction for this measure. The trial used high-oleic capsules, reported no oil grade and had no no-oil group or Parkinson cohort.

fit: high-oleic sunflower comparator with planned depression ratings in prostate cancer
assessment: The recurrence protocol plans HADS-D and PHQ-9 up to month 12; no outcomes are posted. It is distinct from the presurgery protocol, with person-level overlap unverified. The oil grade and a Parkinson group are unspecified.

fit: sunflower comparator with binary depression item in multiple sclerosis
assessment: The multiple sclerosis protocol plans sunflower oil and DHA with and without exercise, with a binary depression item. The registration dates conflict and outcomes remain unposted.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: T1:PO.44 assigns sunflower oil in yogurt for a serum lipid comparison. The grade and separately measured Parkinson outcomes are absent.

fit: depressive and distress outcomes with sunflower comparator
assessment: No clear whole-cohort benefit over the sunflower comparator. The overall group and Cochrane's smaller subgroup are the same trial family.

fit: clinical depression and sunflower/fish-oil comparator
assessment: The IDS-SR contrast slightly favored EPA/DHA over the sunflower/fish-oil comparator and crossed zero. Parkinson depression, pressing grade and oil-only effect remain unresolved.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: Included depression families use sunflower oil with a small fish-oil admixture. The Australian registration planned a sunflower comparator. Review entries do not provide a separate oil effect or executive comparison.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: PO2.161 lists refined sunflower oil in a mixed adolescent diet survey and gives no oil-specific IQ estimate. PO2.229 includes sunflower oil in a calorie-plus-probiotic menu and measures body composition.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: Reference 79 traces emulsified and nonemulsified sunflower oil in the same rat metabolic study. Endotoxemia and triglycerides do not measure the frozen clinical outcome.

fit: high-oleic sunflower oil in mouse feed and adipose gene expression
assessment: The report evaluates gene expression by age and diet duration. It offers no culinary grade or Parkinson symptom estimate.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: Table 1 and methods identify oral sunflower oil as the naringenin vehicle and as part of the saline control. No oil-only contrast within the Alzheimer's-like impairment model isolates the exposure.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: P169 appears in the complete PMC HTML for the oral record and separately in the printed poster supplement. The original oral PDF omits it. This is a duplicate sunflower capsule exposure family, with no separate oral-section result.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: P169 reports similarly measured sedentary time and steps for resistance-exercise groups with sunflower or fish oil capsules. The oil pressing grade is unspecified, no separate Parkinson outcome, and one comparison family with the duplicated HTML.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: OC5 is the BENEFIC MCI trial with a high-oleic sunflower placebo and active ketogenic MCT comparator. Its final paper identifies refined oil. This is one trial family and no Parkinson group or oil-free control.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: Study groups shared injected tamoxifen in sunflower oil. Gait and nonmotor tests include a buried-food olfaction task and operant sensation seeking, with no separate dietary oil comparison.

fit: sunflower oil original source context
assessment: The progressive dopaminergic-loss model used sunflower oil as a common injected tamoxifen carrier. Forebrain gene-expression outcomes concern subsequent L-DOPA and genotype.

fit: Parkinson depression pilot with mineral oil comparator
assessment: Fish oil versus mineral oil favored MADRS and CGI in completers, with an inconclusive Beck comparison. The original Methods confirm mineral oil, without a sunflower oil group.

fit: sunflower oil with expectancy in two CBT course arms
assessment: The 2020 trial and 2021 follow-up are one study. Oil presented as a remedy plus CBT favored the combined arm. At three months, 74% versus 53% were below the BDI-II cutoff among 82 returning. No group isolates oil from expectancy or therapy practice.

fit: open-label sunflower oil and depression during CBT
assessment: Separate 60-person study. Score changes were −7.93 versus −5.47 (p=.001) at course end. The three-month reduction comparison was inconclusive (p=.052). Oil was coupled with instructions and practice, without Parkinson participants or verified oil grade.

fit: injected sunflower oil control and forced-swim immobility
assessment: Rotenone increased immobility relative to injected sunflower oil vehicle (p=.0059). The study has no independent oil contrast and did not test oral refined sunflower oil or clinical depression.

fit: inhaled sunflower carrier in both groups and a reported HADS depression outcome
assessment: Both groups inhaled sunflower carrier and one added lavender. The published within-lavender depression result has p = .025. No numerical between-arm depression effect, trial oil grade or oral exposure was verified.

fit: oral ethanol seed extract and motor assays in haloperidol mice
assessment: Highest extract group had better cylinder movement and rotarod latency. This is a pharmacological mouse model with no clinical bradykinesia measure.

fit: seed extract and motor assays in rotenone-exposed rats
assessment: The author abstract reports better open-field, narrow-beam and hanging performance. Clinical bradykinesia and culinary ground nutmeg remain unmeasured.

fit: oral nutmeg solvent extracts and general mouse locomotion
assessment: Three oral extracts increased general activity at 500 mg/kg. Higher dichloromethane and delipidated methanol did not show a clear locomotor effect. This is spontaneous movement in healthy mice rather than clinical bradykinesia.

fit: Capsicum fruit fractions and mouse anxiety-like outcomes
assessment: A hexane fraction increased open-arm entries and time in a mouse maze. Muscle relaxation and induced sedation can affect behavior. The experiment provides no smoked paprika or Parkinson exposure.

fit: repeated oral isolated capsaicin and anxiety-like behavior in intact rats
assessment: Open-arm entry and time decreased after oral capsaicin, and the stress corticosterone elevation lasted longer. Parkinson anxiety, smoke preparation and food dose were unavailable.

fit: repeated oral isolated capsaicin after oral sensory denervation
assessment: Center activity and general locomotion increased, while elevated plus-maze outcomes did not clearly differ. Forced-swim immobility p=.0547. Both basal and stress corticosterone increased. The altered sensory model limits transfer.

fit: isolated oral capsaicin and anxiety events in runners
assessment: Supplement anxiety was 5% in both capsaicin and placebo immediately after exercise and 15% versus 10% at 24 hours. Pooled OR 1.43 (95% CI .26–7.74). No smoked paprika or clinical severity comparison.

fit: oral Capsicum pubescens and DASS anxiety
assessment: Different pepper species, inconsistent anxiety table and no valid between-group test. Reported within-group comparisons do not establish an effect.

fit: leaf extract and gastric-emptying mechanism
assessment: An ethanol-loaded rat experiment linked isolated leaf sesquiterpenes to slower gastric emptying. The experiment did not administer levodopa or measure medicine OFF time.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S7.514 and S7.519 use apple tree material in branch testing or grafting. Separate references study fruit ripening optics. None administers baked apple or tests dystonia.

fit: Baked apple in the low-fat menu of a randomized Parkinson diet trial
assessment: The supplement documents preparation and planned servings. Table 2 provides the Part IV aggregate without the painful OFF-state dystonia item or a baked-apple comparison. Individual baked-apple intake is unavailable.

fit: red pepper decoction and mouse pole performance
assessment: Three oral aqueous decoction groups had shorter pole-test times in the MPTP mouse experiment. Freezing episode frequency was outside the study.

fit: Parkinson case with formula and walking trajectory
assessment: Walking improved during combination therapy and daily rehabilitation. The clinical course contains no separate freezing-frequency measurement.

fit: Japanese pepper distillate and motor performance
assessment: An intranasal related-species extract shortened mouse pole descent and prolonged rota-rod latency. The tasks do not count freezing.

fit: oral edible sesame oil versus sunflower and clinical anxiety
assessment: Original abstract concludes lower anxiety with sesame. The p=.011 contrast definition and arm estimates are unavailable. Oil described as refined in matching trial reports. No Parkinson disease, cold press or oil-free arm.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: Sesame oil acts as an injected vehicle in rat corticosteroid or AF64A experiments, with no oral oil comparison.

fit: acute injected sesame oil and rat anxiety-like behavior
assessment: Open-arm activity was lower after injected oil. This route, dose and endpoint are distinct from food intake and clinical anxiety.

fit: sesame aroma and mouse stress behavior
assessment: Oil volatile exposure in a mouse stress paradigm. No dietary oil, clinical anxiety or Parkinson disease.

fit: sesame oil aroma timing and open-arm behavior
assessment: Temporary increase in open-arm exploration after inhalation in mice. No oral food or clinical outcome.

fit: sesame oil carrier shared by both arms and anxiety
assessment: Both solutions contained sesame oil. The measured anxiety contrast compares added cannabinoids and does not isolate oil or report cold pressing.

fit: mint-flavored gum and short walking tests in a Parkinson cohort
assessment: Gait composite improved but 10-meter walking and timed mobility comparisons were null. No brewed spearmint exposure.

fit: brewed spearmint and six-minute walk in knee osteoarthritis
assessment: No significant walking-distance difference. Both groups received spearmint tea and no Parkinson cohort was included.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S1.97 proposes parsley as a possible dietary source of related Rubisco peptides while modelling spinach-derived rubiscolin. No parsley isolate, dose or Parkinson outcome is measured.

fit: parsley root juice and cramps
assessment: Reported cramps decreased from 334 to 206 after root juice in an uncontrolled comparison. Reported percentages do not reconcile to one stated denominator. No dystonia was measured.

fit: high-dose nutmeg misuse and uncontrolled depressive symptoms
assessment: The self-reported temporal relation of recurrent dysphoria and psychosis to deliberate misuse prompted a substance-induced mood diagnosis. Prior bipolar diagnosis, toxicity and uncertain cooking limit transfer.

fit: multi-ingredient food including nutmeg and perimenopausal mood
assessment: The crossover lists mood measured by HADS as a secondary outcome and no posted results. Nutmeg is one of many ingredients. No Parkinson cohort or separate grated nutmeg intervention is specified.

fit: oral nutmeg seed extract and rodent depression-like behavior
assessment: Lower forced-swim immobility was reported, opposite the claim direction on this surrogate. Grated nutmeg and human Parkinson depression remain unmeasured.

fit: oral n-hexane extract and mouse immobility
assessment: Forced-swim and tail-suspension immobility fell with extract and spontaneous movement showed no clear change. Clinical depression was unmeasured.

fit: nutmeg extract and mouse immobility
assessment: Tail-suspension immobility fell without increased locomotion. The experiment used an extract and no patients.

fit: intranasal essential oil and mouse immobility
assessment: Intranasal essential oil lowered immobility in a mouse tail-suspension assay. The route and endpoint differ from the claim.

fit: timed speech in oral safflower crossover in Friedreich ataxia
assessment: Small timed speech improvement during safflower periods was reported. The authors found no significant comparative effect on specific clinical features and report practice gains. The speech endpoint, disease and oil grade limit transfer to Parkinson.

fit: safflower oil comparator and Huntington scale with dysarthria item
assessment: The UHDRS dysarthria score considers whether speech can be understood. The study paper reports only the total motor comparison without item estimates.

fit: USP oil comparator and ALS items with speech
assessment: The full report gives overall ALSFRS-R and ALSAQ-40 changes. ALSFRS-R total declined 4.91 points with safflower oil and 3.00 with RT001. Baseline bulbar onset is separate from post-treatment speech and the paper gives no intelligibility result.

fit: oral safflower comparator with singing acoustics in nonrandom alternating design
assessment: Max SPL fell 1.23 dB on oil with a CI spanning zero. Low-pitch energy range increased descriptively and the comparative test was nominal. Speaking intelligibility and cold-press grade are unresolved.

fit: safflower comparator, phonation threshold pressure and voice effort
assessment: Professional voice users are planned and the sponsor lists no results. The outcome is sustained voice production effort and pressure rather than listener intelligibility.

fit: RCT of oral safflower comparator and singer voice self-ratings
assessment: Singing voice handicap improved across groups. Nominal interaction p=0.046 exceeded the adjusted 0.017 threshold. A listener intelligibility assessment and product processing were absent.

fit: sprouted chickpea composition
assessment: The study measured plant tissue chemistry by spectrophotometry. It did not test roasted chickpeas or dyskinesia.

fit: cinnamon in both diets and daytime sleepiness by diet
assessment: The eight-week ketogenic comparison favored the ketogenic plan by 0.45 points on the daytime sleepiness item. Both plans included cinnamon, and the randomized comparison gives no ground-cinnamon effect.

fit: Human clove-oil gargle trial with severe sore throat including hoarseness
assessment: The published sore-throat result used a composite grade. It provides no isolated hoarseness count or acoustic low-volume assessment in Parkinson disease.

fit: Registered clove-oil lozenge arm and postoperative sore throat
assessment: The registry lists sore throat and pain, without vocal intensity or public results. Route and population differ from the frozen claim.

fit: Human Parkinson multi-odor trial with matched motor scale components
assessment: Figure 6 reports total MDS-UPDRS and Parts I–IV. The report provides no component speech item result or acoustic sound-pressure level, and the eugenol exposure was inhaled.

fit: red onion and cognitive outcomes after a 6-OHDA lesion
assessment: Ethanol extract of dried onion was given orally. A water maze was the behavioral task. The paper does not report Parkinson dystonia.

fit: onion peel and haloperidol-induced imposed-posture maintenance
assessment: The day-seven data table shows shorter holding time in extract arms, with a direction discrepancy in adjacent prose. The test does not measure spontaneous dystonic contractions.

fit: dried-species blend and rotating rod or imposed bar posture
assessment: Highest dose improved rotarod retention, whereas bar catalepsy and pole comparisons were nonsignificant. The blend includes neither chive species and has no dystonia outcome.

fit: commercial onion and garlic powders and reported model coordination
assessment: A conference abstract reports a model motor coordination benefit. It provides no named motor test, group estimates or dystonia measure and has no chive species.

fit: garlic use and familial nonkinesigenic dyskinesia
assessment: Affected family members reported a benefit with garlic, without direct measured exposure or a garlic challenge. The 1997 observation was from the same pedigree. Exposure, condition and endpoint differ from the frozen claim.

fit: onion bulb saponins and ileal smooth muscle
assessment: Isolated guinea-pig ileum spasm was reduced by compounds from red onion bulbs. Tissue, preparation and endpoint differ from fresh common chives and Parkinson dystonia.

fit: randomized-order meals and a composite motor-state continuum
assessment: Nine men received the three equal-calorie breakfasts. The continuum included dystonia, but the reported clinical results combined dyskinesia with restlessness for one arm and did not identify chive intake.

fit: cranial dystonia phenotype and medication state
assessment: Investigators separate blepharospasm from eyelid-opening apraxia and report cases in idiopathic Parkinson’s in OFF and peak-dose states. Diet exposure was not studied.

fit: one Parkinson case with dystonia explicitly reported after a dietary change
assessment: A neurologist reported apparent dystonia resolution after six months on a multi-food diet with sources of fisetin and N-hexacosanol. The primary abstract gives neither chive exposure nor a standardized dystonia rating and describes one patient.

fit: fresh and steamed Chinese chive preparations in vitro
assessment: The tested species is Chinese chive. Volatiles and extract cytotoxicity in rat liver and kidney cells do not address dystonia.

fit: Chinese chive seed fraction and cavernosal smooth muscle
