assessment: Rat offspring receiving interesterified fat were less active in adulthood than offspring receiving soybean oil. Neither the developmental exposure nor locomotor activity isolates human Parkinson walking speed.

fit: soybean oil assigned in a rotenone mouse diet
assessment: Rotenone soybean and perilla groups differed in motor proxies, including rearing at equal diet-fat percentage. Walking speed and the soybean oil lot grade were unverified.

fit: soybean oil in high-fat feed and beam coordination in a multiple system atrophy mouse model
assessment: The high-fat blend contains lard and soybean oil and differs from standard chow. The reported comparison is between genotypes under high-fat feed, with no isolated soybean oil or walking-speed estimate.

fit: soybean oil in an enteral formula given during advanced Parkinson care
assessment: The regulator identifies soybean oil in the combined formula. Oil grade and walking speed were unreported, with medication and formula changes during care.

fit: olive oil coding and diagnosis-level diet patterns
assessment: Olive oil was pooled with green olives, with a separate general vegetable oil code. Oil grade and constipation response were unavailable.

fit: olive oil and coconut oil for bowel symptoms in hospital staff
assessment: Stool outcomes did not clearly differ. The comparison did not specify oil grade, an oil-free arm or a Parkinson subgroup.

fit: whole diet with lactulose and unspecified olive oil
assessment: The cohort showed no isolated effect of olive oil on constipation. Lactulose and multiple foods changed together.

fit: single-arm Parkinson diet pilot with olive oil counseling and graded constipation
assessment: GSRS constipation mean changed from 2.25 to 1.54 in eight participants, p=.04. The original supplement reports oleic acid and fiber, without an oil-specific dose, specified grade or separate treatment contrast.

fit: Mediterranean diet plus standard care and clinical Parkinson constipation
assessment: Figure 1 randomizes 45 and analyzes 36 after nine did not receive their allocation. Median changes −0.5 versus −0.8, p=.600. The diet supplies no separate oil or identified grade, and supplementary nutrient totals give no oil-specific effect.

fit: olive oil advised in both mixed dietary phases and bowel frequency
assessment: Both randomized-order Mediterranean phases encouraged olive oil with grade and independent consumption unspecified in the inspected body. The same-cohort bowel analysis gives between-phase frequency OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.82–1.28) and similar stool form. The comparison supplies no extra-virgin olive oil-specific effect on Parkinson constipation.

fit: six-month modified Mediterranean diet with olive oil and registered constipation
assessment: The protocol includes raw olive oil in multicomponent dietary advice. It gives no isolated oil arm or assigned grade. The official registry has no posted bowel results.

fit: extra-virgin olive oil within a factorial Mediterranean diet trial
assessment: The original schedule verifies GSRS constipation and separate Bristol stool form measurements at baseline and weeks 24, 36 and 48. Oil is a diet recommendation and planned intake records and outcomes have no posted results.

fit: unspecified olive oil alongside other dietary changes
assessment: The contributor reported resolution of constipation after removing wheat, changing breakfast, and adding olive oil. Grade, stool counts and clinical confirmation were unavailable.

fit: extra-virgin olive oil in a multicomponent informal case report
assessment: Reported constipation resolved after a mixture plus probiotics and B12. The 2011 and 2012 posts describe the same person and give no oil-specific effect.

fit: olive oil and incident diagnosis
assessment: The cohort measured incident Parkinson disease. Baseline constipation was used in sensitivity analyses, without estimating an oil effect on constipation.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1106 studies extra-virgin olive phenols in macrophages and P1678 compares parenteral lipid formulations in vitro. A separate gastric study records habitual exposure. No Parkinson anxiety or constipation contrast is supplied.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: T1:PO.26 compares a virgin-olive-rich Mediterranean pattern with conventional low-fat guidance for antioxidant capacity. T2:PO.11 is a metabolic-syndrome dietary score; neither isolates the frozen symptom or preparation.

fit: olive-oil-enriched diet and incretin response in normal rats
assessment: The early GLP-1 increment was higher, and glucose tolerance improved at day 36. Gut tissue GLP-1 content was comparable at day 50. The original congress report and paper are one family. Bowel motility and oil grade were unverified.

fit: olive-oil-enriched diet in a separate streptozotocin rat model
assessment: The rat cohort had greater acute GLP-1 release with oil but lower chronic weight gain, lower intestinal GLP-1 content and no improvement in oral glucose tolerance. The outcome and model do not answer the frozen symptom.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: MS food-intake reporting and a hydroxytyrosol animal study are distinct exposures. Neither assigns matched oil grade and Parkinson outcomes.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: The cognition symposium refers to Mediterranean diet supplemented with olive oil and separate comparison diets. No independently graded cold-pressed or extra-virgin Parkinson constipation or walking result.

fit: olive oil within a supplied 28-day Mediterranean diet
assessment: In 22 men, systolic pressure was lower after the mixed diet. No ingredient-specific comparison or bowel, anxiety or insomnia outcome was reported.

fit: olive-oil comparator capsules for a fish-oil metabolic study
assessment: The olive-oil group was an active dietary comparator, with no oil-free arm and no matched symptom measure.

fit: structured lipid blend including olive oil in a mouse diet
assessment: A modified mixture containing olive oil, soy oil and crambe oil was studied. It cannot identify an isolated olive-oil effect or any of these symptoms.

fit: different olive-oil feed matrices and mouse liver proteome
assessment: Fat dose and matrix differ between the mouse diets. Reported metabolic and hepatic findings do not establish an oil-preparation or clinical symptom direction.

fit: olive oil in a composite dietary score among older coronary patients
assessment: The outcome is reported by Mediterranean dietary score and diabetes status. No grade, oil-specific estimate or Parkinson symptom result was reported.

fit: dietary questionnaire grouped by fat sensitivity
assessment: The original fat-sensitivity and food-frequency poster lists olive oil. Its grade is unspecified and it estimates dietary reports by sensory group without the frozen symptom comparison.

fit: oral unspecified olive oil versus mineral and flaxseed oils in hemodialysis
assessment: Rome III changed 10.3 to 3.2 in the olive-oil group and 10.5 to 4.1 with mineral oil. Group by time p = .15 across arms. The active-comparator result gives no equivalence claim or Parkinson-specific grade contrast.

fit: different olive-oil grades and fecal microbiota in mice
assessment: The author abstract compares extra-virgin and refined olive oil, butter and standard diets using fecal culture and molecular profiling. It supplies no constipation severity or Parkinson outcome.

fit: constipation during a ketogenic program rich in extra-virgin olive oil
assessment: The uncontrolled pediatric epilepsy program reported constipation in 102/389 participants. Many diet components changed and the report has no comparable oil-free or separately assigned oil group.

fit: topical extra-virgin olive oil massage and constipation score
assessment: A randomized nursing-home trial compared oil massage, water massage and usual care. Scores fell most in the oil-massage group. Its administration was topical and no Parkinson-specific result was reported.

fit: matching oil and symptom outside Parkinson disease
assessment: The comparator study found a constipation signal in a population outside Parkinson disease.

fit: cooking oil frequency and adjusted composite diet constipation association
assessment: Supplementary Table 7 gives model-3 OR 0.88 per composite score point (95% CI 0.77–0.98, p=.035). Table 3 relates an oil-frequency item to the composite score. The study gives no grade-specific constipation model.

fit: mixed-diet counseling and days with at least one bowel movement
assessment: The three-month first randomized contrast for days with a bowel movement gave OR 0.85 (95% CI 0.5–1.3). Tables identify distinct p-values for main and longitudinal analyses and correct the preprint abstract timing to three months. The handout recommends unspecified olive oil. No separate intake or grade-specific constipation outcome was reported.

fit: caregiver-reported stool softening with unspecified olive oil
assessment: The caregiver reported softer stool after one week, with persistent initial hard stool and concurrent walking. Oil grade and clinical attribution were unverified.

fit: separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context
assessment: P0635 uses olive-oil-containing intravenous emulsion in hospital nutrition. Route, mixed composition and endpoints differ from oral olive oil in the frozen claim.

fit: rice bran oil as a placebo and aggregate clinical scores
assessment: The trial compares cannabis oil with rice bran oil. The aggregate scale result was inconclusive and no speech intelligibility item estimate or oil grade was published.

fit: oral pumpkin seed oil and depressive-like behavior in chronically stressed rats
assessment: Sucrose preference improved and tail-suspension immobility fell. This model and the oil processing differ from the frozen claim. The 2022 cortical study may overlap and is grouped with this study family.

fit: oral pumpkin seed oil and menopause depression item
assessment: Depression stayed at median zero after oil and rose from zero to one with wheat germ oil. The unadjusted endpoint p was .046. The oil preparation and Parkinson population were untested.

fit: pooled poultry item and total Parkinson symptom score
assessment: Preference for chicken, turkey, or rabbit was inconclusive against total PRO-PD. There was no attention or preparation-specific analysis.

fit: Parkinson reaction and cueing tasks during amino-acid depletion
assessment: Short-interval reaction outcomes improved while delayed recall worsened. Depletion of tryptophan did not test consuming turkey.

fit: plasma alpha-linolenic acid and Parkinson speech items
assessment: Examiner-rated speech had age-adjusted ρ = .014 (p = .936) and sex-adjusted ρ = −.116 (p = .493). Daily-living speech also showed no clear association. The study did not isolate intelligibility or compare oil ingestion.

fit: time-sampled oral processing of cooked black beans
assessment: The abstract gives differences in chewed particle size at 18 and 24 seconds. No clinical swallowing measure is established. Overlap with the earlier 17-person study is unresolved.

fit: boiled beans tolerated after surgery and dysphagia rehabilitation in a Parkinson case
assessment: One stage IV Parkinson patient resumed boiled beans in a right side-lying position ten months after surgery for dysphagia from concurrent Wallenberg syndrome. Bean species and any causal food effect were unreported.

fit: human cooked black-bean oral processing and swallow-readiness task
assessment: Participants expectorated the boluses. Chewing time and particle size provide relevant food-texture context without an observed swallow or Parkinson dysphagia contrast.

fit: black kidney bean protein fibrils and dysphagia-oriented texture tests
assessment: Hydrogel textures reached IDDSI levels 4–5 in material testing. No human swallowing result or boiled whole bean exposure follows from the texture level.

fit: multi-ingredient tonic and subjective weakness
assessment: The uncontrolled study reported weakness changes. Weakness, Parkinson fatigue and an ingredient-specific effect were not separately estimated.

fit: Parkinson sleep reports during broccoli tea with white mustard
assessment: Six of eight symptomatic volunteers reported less broadly defined sleep impairment. The uncontrolled preparation combines broccoli with ground white mustard powder. It does not compare toasted mustard or measure validated insomnia severity.

fit: prepared mustard plus Tabasco and overnight polysomnography
assessment: Within-person sleep efficiency was 0.90 versus 0.94 after mustard plus Tabasco versus a plain meal. Sleep onset was longer numerically with p between .05 and .10. Mustard contribution and toasted seed were not isolated.

fit: isolated eugenol plus levodopa in lesion-model mice
assessment: Levodopa-related abnormal behavior did not improve and striatal dopamine depletion increased. The study supplies no ground allspice clinical comparison.

fit: isolated oral eugenol and levodopa in a lesion rat model
assessment: The author abstract reports improved behavioral outcomes from eugenol alone or in combination. It does not identify dyskinesia scores and does not compare ground allspice.

fit: extra-virgin olive oil comparator with oxybutynin in overactive bladder
assessment: The registered outcome was daily void count. Both groups received oxybutynin and the trial stopped with 31 participants and no posted results. There is no separately estimated oil effect or Parkinson cohort.

fit: lycopene-enriched oil and prostate symptom score
assessment: The composite that includes urgency showed no clear within-arm change, with no separate urgency frequency and no oil-only control.

fit: multi-food dietary pattern and general urinary complaints in Parkinsonism
assessment: In 1205 participants the MIND score was inversely associated with general urinary symptom severity. The Mediterranean score was inconclusive. The outcome is broader than urgency frequency, and neither score isolates extra-virgin olive oil.

fit: olive oil food-frequency item and urinary dysfunction in Parkinson
assessment: The cohort measured olive oil use and MDS-UPDRS urinary dysfunction. The adjusted urinary OR is for total Mediterranean diet adherence; oil grade, independent exposure and urgency frequency are unspecified.

fit: conflicting placebo identity in the saw palmetto urinary trial
assessment: The paper describes olive oil as comparator in a study of IPSS and OABSS totals. The exact linked registration instead specifies polyethylene glycol-400. Actual oil exposure remains unresolved and no separate urgency or frequency result is given.

fit: observational caffeine and bradykinesia progression in idiopathic Parkinson disease
assessment: The original indexed preprint abstract reports faster progression with caffeine exposure. Body access failed. Intake definition, model estimates and confounders remain unverified.

fit: black tea brew and horizontal rat open-field crossings
assessment: Tea-only and water groups showed an inconclusive crossing difference at 12 weeks. The test assesses spontaneous activity and is not a Parkinson bradykinesia measure. Twenty allocated versus ten in the outcome table.

fit: caffeinated black tea and Parkinson daily motor composite
assessment: Exploratory LRRK2 subgroup association not reproduced in idiopathic cohorts. No separate bradykinesia or brew method.

fit: isolated caffeine and examiner-rated bradykinesia in Parkinson disease
assessment: The six-week UPDRS III bradykinesia contrast was −1.70 points (95% interval −3.10 to −0.31). The limb-only interval included zero. The exposure was caffeine capsules and no brewed black-tea contrast was reported.

fit: isolated caffeine and six-month Parkinson composite motor severity
assessment: Total motor difference −0.48 (95% CI −3.21 to 2.25). No isolated examiner-rated bradykinesia comparison or brewed tea.

fit: isolated caffeine and short-term Parkinson total motor responder status
assessment: Three-week 12/15 versus 2/12 improvement on a total motor threshold. Motor baseline imbalance, no component estimate, and tea was restricted.

fit: black tea brew and acute rat hole-board exploration
assessment: Tea increased exploratory crossings after acute administration. Means were nonmonotonic across doses. Healthy rats and an exploration count do not provide a bradykinesia estimate.

fit: cumin extract in Wistar rodent anxiety tasks
assessment: Open-arm measures were reported after extract. The report is inconsistent about the extraction medium and does not involve people or toasted seed.

fit: multi-ingredient cumin formula and anthropometric measures
assessment: LBP4.128 reports anthropometric outcomes from a multi-ingredient cumin-containing formula. It does not isolate culinary cumin, its preparation or the frozen symptom.

fit: Parkinson survey recording cumin use with aggregate nonmotor measures
assessment: Cumin intake was recorded and exploratory nonmotor comparisons were inconclusive after correction. No preparation or cumin-specific anxiety estimate is reported.

fit: macadamia oil comparator beverage and negative-affect outcomes
assessment: The registered oil serves as a comparator and its pressing grade is unverified. The terminated record has no posted results.

fit: oral macadamia oil comparator and mood in military officers
assessment: The elated/depressed POMS subscale did not differ clearly between macadamia oil and krill oil (group p = .2103). There was no oil-free arm or Parkinson cohort.

fit: isolated eugenol and abnormal motor observation in a mouse model
assessment: The official associated project report describes abnormal hind-limb extension after levodopa. The tested constituent treatments did not suppress it. This is not timed gait or ground allspice. The journal body remains unavailable and exact sample identity is unverified.

fit: oral isolated eugenol and rodent motor testing
assessment: The journal abstract reports selected motor observations. The institutional companion describes open-field exploration, rotarod and rotational outcomes. Its methods do not establish clinical walking speed or a ground-allspice effect.

fit: isolated eugenol and schedule-dependent beam comparisons in mice
assessment: The original figure reports shorter crossings with the earlier schedule and longer crossings with the later schedule. The experiment describes a single model-only comparator and different observation times, limiting causal interpretation. It supplies no result for ground-allspice intake and clinical walking speed.

fit: Parkinson diet plans include uncooked spinach-or-kale preparations and assess aggregate MDS-UPDRS measures
assessment: Individual spinach choice and quantity are unknown; speech-specific item changes and listener-rated intelligibility are not reported. Whole-diet and medication changes cannot isolate an effect of raw spinach.

fit: pearl millet cultivar and reaction-time tasks in adolescents
assessment: Response times favored iron-biofortified millet over conventional millet. The tests do not directly assess manual dexterity or Parkinson symptoms.

fit: randomized pearl millet cultivar feeding and accelerometer activity
assessment: Light physical activity favored the iron-biofortified cultivar by 22.3 minutes per day. Hand dexterity, Parkinson disease and millet versus no millet were not tested.

fit: pearl millet substitution and handgrip strength
assessment: Grip strength favored millet substitution in athletes. The test did not assess manual dexterity or a Parkinson subgroup.

fit: black mustard seed extract in drug-exposed rats; activity and catalepsy
assessment: Extract and animal motor tasks do not measure fall frequency after ground mustard in humans with Parkinson disease.

fit: PD self-selected broccoli and white mustard tea; balance observation; no fall count
assessment: Single participant balance rating and mixed uncontrolled exposure cannot establish effect of ground mustard seed on fall frequency; participant overlap across reports is unresolved.

fit: seven inhaled oils including rosemary and laboratory gait measures
assessment: The patent gives rotarod and CatWalk results for a blend. The rosemary contribution, ground preparation and clinical gait speed remain unresolved.

fit: injected rosemary extract and activity in a rotenone mouse model
assessment: Higher activity, rearing and bar performance in the highest group. Ground rosemary intake and walking velocity were unmeasured.

fit: aqueous and hydroalcoholic rosemary leaf extract in antioxidant assays
assessment: Rosemary extract IC50 values differed by assay and extraction conditions. These are chemical endpoints without culinary oral administration, depression or gait observations.

fit: isolated rosmarinic acid and Parkinson-model pole and open-field measures
assessment: Pole descent and open-field motor outcomes favored one or more pre-exposure groups. No ground rosemary or clinical gait.

fit: isolated rosmarinic acid and a hyperlocomotor MPTP model
assessment: Rosmarinic acid reduced the abnormal increase in open-field movement. The model showed no clear deficit in pole or rotarod measures.

fit: bundled seed extract in chlorpromazine motor model
assessment: The combined methanolic almond, peanut and watermelon seed extract favored less block catalepsy and greater activity. It did not test peanut oil, an isolated seed arm or a resting-tremor outcome.

fit: traditional culinary and topical oil uses
assessment: Table 2 records customary cooking and topical uses. Study citation counts measure use reports and cannot establish response or clinical effect.

fit: groundnut oil in human meals, fasting glucose and lipids
assessment: Metformin-treated outpatients consumed dietary oils including groundnut. The reported glucose and lipid outcomes do not record tremor or an acute hypoglycemic movement phenotype.

fit: cold-pressed edible-oil composition and cell-free assay
assessment: Measured fatty acids, tocopherols and phytosterols in specified cold-pressed oil. Availability of measured composition supplies no observed symptom contrast.

fit: traditional peanut-oil massage for infantile paralysis
assessment: The table associates peanut-oil massage with infantile paralysis. This row identifies no direct witness, measured response or comparable oral route.

fit: oral peanut-oil comparison and sarcopenia outcomes
assessment: The ENHANce trial and nested TEMPUS-FUGIT use a peanut-oil omega-3 placebo in older adults with sarcopenia. The protocol and feasibility report address physical function, and the family has no separate Parkinson tremor result.

fit: 1951 review of the 1949 carrier formulation
assessment: Ebin summarizes the same Bird and Meyers comparison. The recovered primary observes a lower tremor amplitude but no frequency or incidence change under the drug treatments. Treat the review as a companion and do not count it independently.

fit: oral dietary oil and same-cohort activity report
assessment: One assigned dietary trial with eight weeks of peanut, olive, safflower oil or no study oil in healthy adults. Its companion paper reports no significant change in general activity, and neither report assessed tremor.

fit: historical Parkinsonian tremor, injected drug and carrier
assessment: At least eight of eleven historical Parkinsonian cases had tremor. Injected drug in oil and wax and oral belladonna lowered amplitude without materially changing incidence or rate. No oil-only exposure. The 1951 Ebin review is the same study family.

fit: early curare suspension, mixed clinical population and indication
assessment: The 200-person clinical series covered several diagnoses. The author describes possible relief of painful rigidity with the injected drug and gives no individual tremor estimate or oil-only comparison.

fit: peanut-oil-based spread and cognitive or mood outcomes
assessment: The main report identifies oil-based control spread in healthy adults and tests cognition, stress and mood. Registration and later companion outcomes belong to the same intervention. No distinct oil-free comparator or tremor endpoint.

fit: shared peanut oil diets and motor proxy assays
assessment: Both diets contained peanut oil. The low rod yielded longer retention under the low-alpha-linolenic acid diet, the high rod and traction comparisons were inconclusive or unchanged, and some learning measures were weaker. No resting-tremor assessment.

fit: oral crude-versus-refined peanut oil allergy safety
assessment: Six of sixty participants with peanut allergy reported reactions after crude oil, including two observable or measurable reactions. None reacted after the refined oil. Outcomes are acute allergy signs, with no identifiable rest-tremor response.

fit: multi-oil diets, locomotion and monoamines
assessment: The peanut-plus-rapeseed blend was the comparison for salmon-palm oil, with several dietary fatty acids changing. The fish-oil blend reduced general activity or changed habituation.

fit: injected carrier with dyskinesia and motor findings
assessment: Three of six animals received the drug dissolved in injected peanut oil. The reported effect is on levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Rest tremor appears in model description without an oil-only contrast.

fit: corn oil as the active comparison in a Parkinson depression trial
assessment: The paper reports UPDRS change at total scale level for the corn-oil and DHA groups, without a separate drooling rating, verified refinement or oil-free comparator.

fit: oral corn oil comparator and unstimulated salivary flow
assessment: The six-month Sjögren trial reports no clear change in unstimulated whole sialometry or group difference in dryness. The study evaluates autoimmune hyposalivation and does not measure Parkinson drooling or report oil grade.

fit: shared oral Parkinson trial carrier and UPDRS part II total
assessment: The treatment table provides an overall part II score. Salivation item changes are unavailable and all arms used corn oil.

fit: topical oxidized corn oil derivative and dry-mouth symptoms
assessment: The randomized 24-person crossover used a topical active comparator derived from oxidized corn oil. Baseline hyposalivation and treatment-period symptom ratings do not estimate dietary corn oil or Parkinson drooling.

fit: oral dietary corn oil and rat salivary flow
assessment: Corn oil was the base diet. After 30 days, cannulated submandibular flow was lower in the retained corn arm than in the chia replacement arm. The experiment measures secretion in healthy rats and does not measure clinical drooling.

fit: curry leaf extract and motor tasks in rotenone mice
assessment: The publisher figure shows shorter beam and pole times and a partial increase in open-field distance after leaf extract. These tests do not measure clinical freezing episodes after cooked curry leaf.

fit: isolated isolongifolene and toxin-model rat behavior
assessment: A separate isolated-compound study assessed open-field and rotarod performance. Neither cooked leaf nor clinical freezing episodes were measured.

fit: curry leaf extract and fly climbing or jumping
assessment: Climbing and jumping favored an extract arm in the fly toxin model. The test does not measure human freezing events or cooked leaf.

fit: intralaryngeal almond oil carrier and hoarseness
assessment: A laryngeal case reports hoarseness resolving after a course including menthol in almond oil and surgery; no oral exposure, cold pressing, Parkinson diagnosis or measured vocal intensity.

fit: Rat leaf extract with contradictory charcoal transit direction
assessment: The authors interpret slower propulsion, while the extracted table shows larger charcoal travel after both extract treatments than the labeled control. The study supplies no separate gastric or Parkinson outcome.

fit: Human mixed decoction and irritable bowel symptoms
assessment: The completed trial used three botanical ingredients and found an inconclusive bowel severity contrast. The registration and article did not measure OFF time or levodopa.

fit: Diabetic rat intestinal transit and colon assay
assessment: Leaf extract was reported to improve small-intestinal charcoal transit and distal colon cholinergic response. The reported measures do not establish gastric emptying or OFF time.

fit: Clinical iron tablet with levodopa drug exposure
assessment: Levodopa and carbidopa AUC fell, and the mean clinical response was inconclusive. The experiment does not contain ground curry leaf or daily OFF time.

fit: Hydroalcoholic leaf extract and rat transit
assessment: The authors report slower transit after a castor-oil challenge in rats. Methods call the extracted powder bark in one sentence and describe leaves elsewhere. The study measured neither levodopa uptake nor Parkinson OFF time.

fit: Measured iron in a ground curry leaf food formulation
assessment: The report gives compositional iron in finished idli, with no medication exposure or OFF measure. Food matrix and pharmaceutical iron are distinct exposures.

fit: Ferrous-sulfate-fortified curry-leaf product in laboratory study
assessment: The formulation adds ferrous sulfate and reports in vitro iron handling. It does not test ordinary ground curry leaf use with levodopa or measure daily OFF time.

fit: Overlapping mouse charcoal transit experiments
assessment: Five arm means and SDs match across the original reports. The full series adds distinct verapamil and atropine comparisons without gastric emptying, levodopa or OFF time.

fit: oat bran in a multi-ingredient meal and mobility measures
assessment: The protocol includes balance and chair stands, and excluded diagnosed neurodegenerative disease. It supplies no Parkinson falls outcome for rolled oats.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S7.478 orally administers oat-stem lignin to irradiated mice and S6.415 studies oat seed germination. Neither is a prepared oat-grain or Parkinson motor comparison.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-14-021 studies oat globulin hydrolysates and P-15-007 applies isolated oat phenolics to keratinocytes. Oat-beverage fermentation is another member. OATS also names a semen phenotype.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: The SYSDIET bundle includes whole grains including oats, and P422 measures dietary fiber in rolled oats. No isolated Parkinson fall result.

fit: fortified oatmeal within a randomized nutrition package and falls
assessment: First-fall HR 0.41 (95% CI 0.19–0.86) for the program versus usual care. Oatmeal was part of a bundle with supplements, calcium-vitamin D and diet counseling. No isolated rolled-oat or Parkinson estimate.

fit: cayenne frequency and combined anxiety and depression scores
assessment: The cohort gives a cayenne frequency item and no adjusted anxiety-specific result. Preparation is unspecified.

fit: oral related pepper extract and DASS anxiety in students
assessment: The anxiety table has inconsistent visit totals and no valid between-arm change estimate. Distinct Capsicum pubescens extract, not ground cayenne or Parkinson.

fit: oral cinnamon capsules and blood pressure in type 2 diabetes
assessment: Blood pressure fell with capsules relative to placebo. Symptomatic lightheadedness on standing was unmeasured.

fit: ground cinnamon capsule and repeated post-meal supine blood pressure
assessment: Nine participants had inconclusive systolic and diastolic pressure contrasts. The protocol used supine measurements and supplied no orthostatic or Parkinson outcome.

fit: dried cinnamon powder capsules and ambulatory blood pressure in hypertension
assessment: Day-90 24-hour pressure comparisons were inconclusive. No standing challenge or Parkinson symptom score.

fit: cinnamon use and cardiovascular nonmotor domain in a Parkinson survey
assessment: The corrected exploratory comparisons found no clear clinical differences. Cinnamon-specific coefficients and the lightheadedness item are not reported.

fit: ground cassia beverage and acute blood pressure in middle-aged adults
assessment: Reported pressure contrasts were inconclusive across the post-beverage times. No standing lightheadedness result was measured.

fit: black soybean seed coat extract and drowsiness during a task
assessment: Contemporaneous author summary and likely same-study patent report lower task-day VAS at two time points in healthy adults. The baseline change comparison is inconclusive. Journal full text and trial identity remain open. Exposure is Glycine max extract.

fit: randomized whole diet and daytime dysfunction in diabetes
assessment: Adjusted PSQI daytime dysfunction difference −0.41 (95% CI −1.00 to 0.18, p=.163). The diet analysis pools bean intake and measures neither black bean preparation nor Parkinson daytime sleepiness.

fit: verified boiled black common bean meals in healthy adults
assessment: Registered crossover, dissertation and journal report describe one trial with vascular and metabolic measures. Sleepiness was outside the reported endpoints.

fit: Parkinson diet scores and daytime sleepiness with pooled bean intake
assessment: Table 2 reports lower self-rated sleepiness per point of MIND score (−1.91), with a similar association for the Mediterranean diet. Supplemental Table S4 analyzes the pooled bean category against total symptom burden. The survey does not estimate black bean intake, preparation, or change in daytime sleepiness.

fit: three arm soybean extract comparison and sleepiness on waking
assessment: The earliest verified patent source reports no statistically significant between-arm sleep factor differences, with 65 evaluable. It uses Glycine max extract and a waking-time measure in healthy adults. The different 2025 study design cannot establish participant independence.

fit: black soybean seed coat extract and sleepiness on rising
assessment: In 64 healthy adults randomized to extract or placebo, immediate-on-waking OSA-MA scores favored extract at weeks eight and twelve. Extract species, population and outcome differ from the frozen claim.

fit: topical piperine rinse and composite of pronunciation difficulty and worsened taste
assessment: Uncontrolled burning-mouth series reported a two-item composite improvement from 1.8 to 1.0. It did not measure intelligibility or isolate the pronunciation item. No PD cohort or ground-pepper exposure.

fit: dark chocolate and acute state anxiety in healthy adults
assessment: The detailed measurements did not establish a clear acute difference after dark chocolate. The healthy population and acute follow-up limit interpretation.

fit: solid dark chocolate and measured postbiopsy anxiety
assessment: Randomized non-Parkinson trial reported postbiopsy anxiety scores 34.31 versus 38.89 with a group-by-time p = .01. No matched snack and masking limitations leave expectancy unresolved.

fit: plain dark chocolate and self-reported anxiety in nursing students
assessment: Open-label comparison favored chocolate on both anxiety scales after three days. It has no matched snack, no blinding and no Parkinson population.

fit: brewed cocoa with caffeine and anxiety during a task
assessment: The published anxiety interaction favored caffeinated cocoa against caffeine alone. Cocoa versus placebo did not have a detectable mood interaction. The drink and mental challenge differ from ordinary dark chocolate and Parkinson anxiety.

fit: limited dark chocolate within Mediterranean advice and Parkinson anxiety
assessment: The protocol restricts dark chocolate to at most one weekly serving. The trial assigns counseling plus standard care and reports HAM-A group-by-week p=.745. It cannot estimate a culinary dark-chocolate effect.

fit: chocolate craving and anxiety measured in a Parkinson case-control study
assessment: Chocolate craving was higher in Parkinson disease. Anxiety ratings were higher in a pooled food-addiction group. There was no estimate for dark chocolate intake and anxiety in the Parkinson group.

fit: high versus low flavanol dark chocolate
assessment: P-445 reports the FlaSeCo dark chocolate trial. Both groups ate dark chocolate with different flavanol content. The reported depression and cognitive outcomes supply no isolated anxiety result.

fit: dark chocolate and HADS anxiety in severe chronic fatigue
assessment: In a ten-person masked crossover, median HADS anxiety fell during high-cocoa treatment and rose during the simulated chocolate period. Period baselines differed. Within-treatment tests do not supply a separate paired treatment contrast.

fit: dark chocolate and biomarkers in a rotenone Parkinson model
assessment: The original report includes a chocolate group and several biochemical, microbiota and histology outcomes. It has no scored anxiety behavior or clinical anxiety measure.

fit: shiitake extract and cultured neuronal-cell outcomes
assessment: Viability and senescence changed after extract exposure. No dexterity was measurable in this design.

fit: shiitake constituent in Parkinson models
assessment: Reported mouse behavioral improvement includes pole testing context. Isolated lentinan and mouse locomotion do not establish an effect of roasting on clinical hand dexterity.

fit: coriander seed extract and drug-induced orofacial dyskinesia
assessment: The seed extract reduced induced excess orofacial movements in rats. Dried culinary leaf and reduced facial expression were not studied.

fit: coriander in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome
assessment: The menu lists coriander without specifying the plant part and the motor examination includes facial expression. Dried cilantro exposure and facial expression item changes are unavailable.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S1.97 proposes parsley as a possible dietary source of related Rubisco peptides while modelling spinach-derived rubiscolin. No parsley isolate, dose or Parkinson outcome is measured.

fit: Parkinson diet menu includes parsley and Table 4 reports medication
assessment: The report provides levodopa dose at follow-up and motor totals. It does not identify the parsley form, participant-specific parsley intake or hours in the OFF state.

fit: low
assessment: An outbreak investigation identified atropine and scopolamine in boiled-spinach and pastry leftovers. Poisoning supplies a food safety context and no Parkinson visual hallucination frequency estimate.

fit: low
assessment: Mandrake was detected among spinach and chard leaves. Hyperactivity or hallucination was reported jointly in acute poisoning. The source does not give a clean spinach exposure, visual modality, or Parkinson frequency.

fit: spinach and okra intake history and oxalate nephropathy
assessment: More oxalate-rich vegetables were consumed before kidney injury in a post-bypass patient. No single-food comparator, spinach preparation, dyskinesia or visual hallucination endpoint was reported.

fit: safflower oil comparator and Huntington bradykinesia scale component
assessment: The related motor examination includes body bradykinesia. Its separate outcome is unavailable, and the study population had Huntington disease.

fit: original article and linked trial context
assessment: The original review describes dysphagia as a nutritional barrier in neurodegenerative disease. Its separate safflower-fed amyloid mouse comparison measured brain inflammatory gene expression and lipid mediators, with no swallowing or bradykinesia result.

fit: safflower and spontaneous locomotion in developmental rats
assessment: Spontaneous locomotion did not differ. Novelty exploration was lower than on soybean oil or chow. Developmental fat composition and exploratory behavior differ materially from culinary oil and Parkinson's motor slowness.

fit: safflower-derived flavonoids in a Parkinson rat model
assessment: A flavonoid extract differs from culinary seed oil. The correction is linked with the source. Its text remains to be inspected.

fit: oral safflower oil comparator and episodic movements in Glut1 deficiency
assessment: The safflower period gave 11.8 disabling movement events per four weeks versus 14.3 in the drug period. These are episodic events in Glut1 deficiency. No bradykinesia or cold pressing was measured.

fit: safflower and open-field movement in healthy adult rats
assessment: More exploratory movement appeared in the exercise-plus-water group. Safflower group means did not establish a general motor benefit. The study used healthy animals and did not measure Parkinsonian bradykinesia.

fit: low
assessment: The human single-arm report applied commercial seed oil topically and measured aphthous lesions. It does not identify toasted oil or report salivary flow or drooling.

fit: low
assessment: The rat experiment measured salivary-gland histology after oral ethanolic extract of pumpkin flesh. The investigators removed seeds and peel. Gland structure is not secretion or drooling, and no seed oil was administered.

fit: low
assessment: Commercial oil administered orally reduced certain tongue tissue injury markers in rat paclitaxel groups. Pressing or roasting details were not verified and no saliva flow, drooling or Parkinson outcome was measured.

fit: soy oil vehicle and mouse motor assays
assessment: Original Methods and Table 1 assign 50 mg/kg to curcumin. Soy oil was the vehicle in control groups. Refined grade and levodopa-induced dyskinesia were not measured.

fit: food-related material in an imaging report
assessment: The original MR colonography study places excised pig colon specimens in soybean oil for imaging. This is a nonoral laboratory medium with no dose, grade or Parkinson symptom comparison.

fit: soybean comparator and orofacial movements in rats
assessment: Hydrogenated fat increased orofacial dyskinesia relative to the soybean feed. This was neither a Parkinson model nor levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

fit: long-duration diet comparison and rat orofacial movements
assessment: Older rats fed hydrogenated fat showed progressively greater orofacial movements in a study with soybean-oil and standard-chow groups. The oil grade and Parkinson treatment-related outcome were untested.

fit: ground soybeans plus levodopa and dyskinesia
assessment: Seven participants with Parkinson had lower mAIMS during the acute ground-soybean condition. Refined soybean oil and chronic dyskinesia were untested.

fit: distinct Prunus species and extract in cerebrovascular models
assessment: Two conference members describe Prunus cerasoides or prunetin and nonclinical outcomes. The model, species and forms differ from eating dried cherry and provide no apathy estimate.

fit: separate Prunus species and oral extract or constituent in a mouse vascular model
assessment: The author abstract and publisher excerpts report behavioral and tissue outcomes after carotid stenosis. The species, preparation, model and outcomes differ from dried cherry and Parkinson apathy. Likely report-family overlap with 2025 Brain PET member 0634 precludes counting independent replication.

fit: freeze-dried cherry powder in a formulated drink and self-rated mood
assessment: Some age groups reported improved mood or fitness items. The trial did not use an apathy scale and used a sweet cherry blend in healthy people.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S7.519 describes sweet cherry among fruit trees used for grafting work. No dietary cherry or measured neurologic symptom is present.

fit: injected Prunus stem and leaf extract in a mouse focal stroke model
assessment: The complete paper separates injected extract before or after stroke from constituent cell experiments. Its short-term injury and sensorimotor outcomes leave Parkinson apathy open and do not transfer to consuming dried fruit.

fit: sweet almond massage and depression in postmenopausal women
assessment: The reported depression score declined with almond-oil massage and stayed flat in the no-massage arm. The design did not isolate oil from massage and the BDI scale transformation is unclear.

fit: oral and injected almond oil in rat forced-swim behavior
assessment: Oral oil increased climbing without a clear difference in immobility or swimming. The high injected dose reduced immobility. The study did not test cold-pressed oil or clinical depression.

fit: unfragranced almond carrier and HADS depression during radiotherapy
assessment: Randomized aromatherapy arms gave no clear depression difference. Carrier grade comes from secondary study description. No isolated oral oil contrast.

fit: caregiver reports of balance across diagnoses and oil preparations
assessment: A minority of reports described Parkinson disease with cognitive impairment. Balance anecdotes were pooled with other diagnoses and oil preparations.

fit: same cohort family, self-reported supplement and composite progression
assessment: Unreviewed preprint reports slower total-score progression in a mixed model and inconclusive baseline differences. Oil grade and balance-specific result are unavailable.

fit: Parkinson baseline coconut oil frequency and self-rated balance
assessment: The item-specific graphic has a small inverse tile against the signed legend. No numerical coefficient, confidence interval, adjusted estimate, or refined grade is available.

fit: coconut oil supplement use and aggregate symptom score
assessment: The observational association favored users on total PRO-PD. The oil grade and separate postural-instability estimate were unavailable.

fit: coconut oil in mixed oral feeds and mouse rotarod retention
assessment: Coconut oil fell from 0.9 to 0.1 or 0.2 g per 100 g as several ingredients changed. Rotarod retention improved with the two altered feeds. No independent oil grade or human postural instability estimate.

fit: coconut oil frequency and baseline Parkinson composite
assessment: Table 2 gives an adjusted total-score association of −20.2 points per frequency step, 95% CI −31.0 to −9.4. Coconut oil grade and a separate postural instability estimate are unavailable.

fit: extra-virgin coconut oil and EGCG, balance in multiple sclerosis
assessment: Berg mean rose 49 to 52 on combination versus 43 to 43 on other fats and placebo. Reported tests were within-arm, baseline differed, and oil grade and population differ.

fit: fractionated oil and mixed diet
assessment: No clear between-group mobility difference. Refined coconut oil and postural instability were not isolated.

fit: acute swallowing difficulty after mixed seasoned meals
assessment: A mixed sauce included cumin and the case describes acute oral symptoms. Toasting, ingredient-specific causation and clinical Parkinson dysphagia remain unverified.

fit: healthy human salivary effect of three mixed cumin-ginger sprays
assessment: The study concerns spray formulation, salivation and safety. It supplies no swallowing test or isolated toasted-cumin exposure.

fit: Parkinson survey recording cumin use with aggregate nonmotor measures
assessment: Cumin intake was recorded and exploratory nonmotor comparisons were inconclusive after correction. No preparation or cumin-specific dysphagia estimate is reported.

fit: clinical salivary and dry-mouth response to a cumin and ginger spray
assessment: The crossover favored a mixed mouth spray for salivary flow. It did not compare oral toasted spice ingestion or assess a clinical swallowing endpoint.

fit: case of acute allergy after fried mixed food containing ground cumin
assessment: The report records acute anaphylaxis and sensitization to cumin. It supplies no toasted-seed or Parkinson swallowing assessment.

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking
assessment: Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

fit: rocket salad beverage and blood pressure in healthy adults
assessment: The post-beverage systolic pressure declined at 150 minutes. The beverage, posture, population, and endpoint leave fall frequency after raw leaves unmeasured.

fit: vegetable-group intake and injurious falls in older adults
assessment: Two analyses of one cohort relate vegetable diversity or vegetable-group intake to hospitalizations after falls. Salad greens are pooled and arugula is unnamed. No Parkinson subgroup or fall-frequency estimate was reported.

fit: rucola on an aggregate Parkinson diet menu
assessment: The article measures a global motor outcome without an arugula or fall-frequency contrast.

fit: fresh arugula in a nitrate-rich vegetable crossover
assessment: Thirty healthy adults. Post-lunch pressure changed during both active dietary periods. No isolated arugula, standing pressure or fall frequency result.

fit: isolated DHA and forceplate-detected dyskinesia
assessment: Dyskinesia was detected in three of nine assessed DHA recipients and six of fifteen assessed placebo recipients. The posted counts have incomplete follow-up and give no severity effect for baked trout.

fit: dietary protein redistribution and Parkinson dyskinesia
assessment: Small physiologic study describes more dyskinesia with lower daytime protein in participants with severe fluctuations. Meals and exposure were not baked trout. Full numerical table remains unavailable.

fit: chives on a Parkinson pilot diet menu and composite motor score
assessment: The Appendix A menu names chives. Both diet arms had lower UPDRS III scores over time without a chives-only contrast, a separately reported walking-speed outcome or a specified chive preparation.

fit: oral dried dill aerial-part and black rice extract, open-field movement after stroke
assessment: Total crossings, rearing, grooming and licking showed no clear change. The potentially overlapping PMID31827714 reports lower composite stroke scores at all doses without component estimates. Neither used fresh dill or measured bradykinesia.

fit: oral dill and black rice extract and aggregate stroke neurological score in adults
assessment: At one week high dose changed total NIHSS −87.50% vs −36.03% on placebo (p=.045). Later comparisons and the low dose were inconclusive. No isolated dill, motor subscore, fresh leaf or Parkinson comparison.

fit: maternal oral dill extract and developmental motor reflexes in offspring
assessment: The abstract describes better developmental righting, rotation and cliff avoidance following maternal extract exposure. These motor reflexes provide no Parkinson bradykinesia or fresh-leaf comparison.

fit: oral sowa extract and rotarod motor performance during withdrawal
assessment: The two extract arms had longer retention than withdrawal alone. This motor coordination task supplies no fresh leaf or clinical bradykinesia estimate.

fit: safflower oil mixed-meal crossover with peripheral biomarkers
assessment: Healthy participants received meals containing safflower oil, cocoa butter or no added fat. The abstract does not give an isolated contrast for the safflower arm, specify pressing method or measure the frozen Parkinson symptom.

fit: safflower oil and a Huntington psychiatric measure with an apathy item
assessment: Investigators report no clear comparative PBA-s change without numerical results or the apathy item. Its direction is unresolved.

fit: developmental safflower exposure and novelty exploration
assessment: Lower exploration favored a motivational proxy in one condition, while spontaneous locomotion was unchanged. The model measured neither Parkinson nor clinical apathy.

fit: isolated safflower pigment and depression-like measures in a Parkinson mouse model
assessment: Higher sucrose intake and lower immobility after the purified pigment are an opposite-direction clue at the level of depression-related measures. Neither the tested exposure nor endpoint is the frozen claim.

fit: acute extract trial with subjective fatigue planned
assessment: Healthy gamer crossover completed. Subjective fatigue was registered, with no results posted.

fit: planned chronic extract trial with fatigue endpoint
assessment: Subjective fatigue was registered as a primary outcome in healthy gamers. No results were available.

fit: Nepalese pepper extract and healthy adult task fatigue
assessment: Day-56 task fatigue favored extract. The groups differed on the baseline fatigue rating, and the trial did not enroll people with Parkinson’s.

fit: holy basil mixture and planned clinical falls outside Parkinson disease
assessment: No posted results. Uses holy basil and other ingredients with usual care in older adults with frailty, not dried sweet basil.

fit: oral sweet basil essential oil and induced rotarod falls in mice
assessment: The highest oral oil group fell more times and sooner on a rotarod than vehicle (p<.05), while the intermediate group showed no clear deficit. The study used oil distilled from dried leaves in mice without Parkinsonian induction. No culinary leaf or clinical fall frequency was tested.

fit: sardines among options and anxiety score
assessment: Advice to eat fatty fish yielded a higher anxiety point estimate with an interval crossing zero. Sardines were one option in an angina cohort.

fit: marine omega-3 capsule and Beck anxiety outside Parkinson disease
assessment: Table 5 log Beck difference −0.23 (95% CI −0.44 to −0.011). Commercial EPA-predominant blend, unknown fish species and no baked sardine comparison.

fit: sardine oil and postpartum mood
assessment: The sardine-oil versus perilla-oil postpartum depression threshold comparison was inconclusive. No standalone anxiety endpoint or baked sardine exposure.

fit: oily fish category and Parkinson anxiety instrument
assessment: The Parkinson clinical dataset contains a pooled oily-fish item that includes sardines and a HADS anxiety total. The publication has no sardine-specific estimate.

fit: registered six-herb oral capsule and secondary fatigue outcomes
assessment: Registry reports 93 enrolled and completed, with FSS and daily diary fatigue measures. No numerical results posted. The linked protocol describes a shorter duration than the current registry, and neither provides a separate ground cinnamon treatment.

fit: distilled cinnamon-containing mixture and rated fatigue in multiple sclerosis
assessment: Means moved 3.729 to 2.213 versus 3.520 to 5.066. Group p=.353, group-by-time p<.001. Printed SDs and intervals and the withdrawal counts conflict. Multiple ingredients and distillation prevent isolation of ground cinnamon.

fit: cinnamon intake as a group-visit dietary outcome
assessment: OA15.04 reports increased cinnamon intake in a 155-person randomized group-visit dietary secondary analysis for adults with chronic pain and depression; preparation and an isolated cinnamon symptom effect are not reported. The claim seeks ground cinnamon and fatigue severity.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-14-005 uses cassia bark and turmeric-root extracts in Aβ-exposed cells. P-14-016 and P-14-034 report different mixtures and models. The spice blend cannot identify an isolated ground-cinnamon effect.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1473 reports improvement of pediatric orofacial granulomatosis on elemental feeding followed by a diet avoiding both cinnamon and benzoates. It does not separate cinnamon from the other dietary changes.

fit: cinnamon in both diets and fatigue by diet
assessment: Both meal plans contain cinnamon. The 0.50-point fatigue item difference compares the assigned dietary patterns.

fit: pre-dose fatigue during withdrawal from habitual caffeine
assessment: Fatigue VAS on arrival was inconclusive across study conditions (p=.301). Ratings preceded the assigned dose at each visit. Supplements used flavored water in habitual users outside Parkinson disease.

fit: soluble caffeinated coffee and acute mental fatigue in healthy older adults
assessment: The randomized crossover reported a mean mental-fatigue change of −6.20 with caffeinated soluble coffee, +9.24 with ordinary decaf and +13.30 with placebo. The healthy population, soluble preparation and acute item differ from the claim.

fit: soluble decaffeinated coffee and isolated chlorogenic acids in healthy older adults
assessment: The crossover found no clear treatment or time-by-treatment effect for mental fatigue. The isolated compound had a separate result on a tiredness item. There was no caffeinated coffee arm.

fit: coffee reported among habitual foods in a Parkinson case
assessment: A single food-frequency assessment lists coffee with sugar. The report gives no repeated or isolated coffee exposure and no quantitative fatigue outcome.

fit: coffee as tongue-tip stimulus during swallowing rehabilitation
assessment: Coffee, soup and pickled plum were applied as taste stimuli in one stage V Parkinson case. The abstract gives no brewed coffee consumption, fatigue score or separate coffee result.

fit: indirect
assessment: Patient with drug-induced parkinsonism drank favorite coffee during multi-component care. Agitation was observed qualitatively; brew type and fatigue were unreported. No direction for brewed coffee and Parkinson fatigue.

fit: reported aggregate caffeine and nonmotor domains
assessment: The 62-person report associates caffeine with total nonmotor score and levodopa response. Brewed coffee and separate fatigue severity are unavailable.

fit: pooled coffee and espresso frequency and Parkinson fatigue
assessment: The published baseline heatmap shows an inverse correlation for the fatigue item. It gives no coefficient, uncertainty estimate, or breakdown by coffee preparation.

fit: whole coffee fruit extract blend and acute mental fatigue
assessment: The coffee fruit extract mixture lowered acute fatigue ratings in healthy adults. The intervention combined four extracts and did not test brewed coffee.

fit: reported coffee use and prescribed levodopa dose
assessment: Coffee predicted a higher prescribed dose in 129 charts. The article gives no brew type, coffee-specific coefficient or fatigue result.

fit: tube-administered tea caffeine and postprandial blood pressure
assessment: Powdered green tea was administered through existing feeding tubes to two Parkinson patients with postprandial hypotension. It provides no fatigue estimate or coffee exposure.

fit: paper-filtered coffee preparation during an occupational task
assessment: The thesis specifies electric drip and a paper filter. The outcomes are cooking performance scores. No assigned coffee consumption or fatigue result is available.

fit: separate coffee intake and fatigue reports from the same cohort
assessment: The cohort reports habitual coffee intake by diagnosis and fatigue trajectories in separate papers. The public reports do not link the participant coffee and fatigue measures or identify brewing methods. The study profile describes access by investigator request.

fit: self-reported coffee and combined sleep and fatigue domain
assessment: The UK cohort reported no clear domain differences after correction. It supplies no beverage-specific estimate or isolated fatigue result.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: T-Coffee is software and abstention from caffeine is an eligibility condition. S9.596 separately assays isolated chlorogenic acid from a food-chemistry perspective with no brewed-coffee or fatigue comparison.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-09-007 and P-09-023 use spent coffee grounds, and P-14-033 maps metabolites in green beans. A separate assay uses isolated caffeine. Brewed coffee and Parkinson fatigue are untested here.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1439 and P1595 record habitual coffee intake in inflammatory bowel disease and reflux work. Coffee-ground blood in separate emergency abstracts is a visual descriptor.

fit: older-adult sleep survey with coffee and tea prevalence
assessment: The authors report coffee intake in 68.8% of 381 older adults. They give no coffee-specific sleep or fatigue association, and preparation was unspecified.

fit: observational dysbiosis and reported beverage context
assessment: The poster reports a coffee association without an estimate and the later same-cohort paper focuses on sweeteners and metformin. It does not show a coffee-specific fatigue direction.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: An older-patient taste test uses coffee, tea or a malted beverage as a drink base for a milk or supplement comparison.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: OP-162-1-GE and OP-163-1-GE compare reported coffee intake with cardiac outcomes in overlapping UK Biobank work. Neither reports the frozen symptom.

fit: self-reported beverage-associated attacks in a familial dyskinesia pedigree
assessment: Coffee and black or green tea were reported as attack triggers in the Japanese family. Roasted green tea did not trigger the reported attacks. The cohort has familial episodic dyskinesia, with no Parkinson fatigue endpoint.

fit: coffee intake and glioma incidence in prospective managed-care cohort
assessment: Coffee exposure in a questionnaire was analyzed against incident malignant adult glioma. The matching 2005 abstract repeats the same cohort. Neither report measures Parkinson fatigue or establishes the brewing method.

fit: reported caffeine triggers in familial episodic dyskinesia
assessment: The authors distinguish triggers across genotyped family groups. The abstract has no separately assigned brewed coffee test or Parkinson fatigue outcome. Independence of all families relative to the historical literature remains unverified.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: Members test isolated caffeine in sleep, sensory gating and adenosine studies. These are compound comparisons, not prepared coffee in Parkinson disease.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S59 tests injected caffeine in an MPTP mouse model. Other members include acute memory and adenosine outcomes. The companion paper observes barrier and tissue endpoints.

fit: injected isolated caffeine and mouse striatal barrier outcomes
assessment: Barrier leakage, striatal physiology and tissue measurements in the MPTP study do not establish a brewed coffee or clinical fatigue effect. Companion to the 2008 meeting comparison.

fit: pooled beverage use in a shift-work survey
assessment: A self-selected sample of 260 workers reported energy effects and 35% reported coffee or tea use for symptoms. Reported beverage use is pooled and there is no response comparison. A parallel conference report shares the same survey.

fit: afternoon coffee break with social contact in a group-home case
assessment: Requests for pain relief initially decreased during a combined activity and then recurred. The subsequent history linked pain to the menstrual cycle. No dose, independent coffee effect or measured fatigue outcome was recorded.

fit: reported heartburn after coffee in an iron-deficiency case
assessment: The case includes a coffee-triggered heartburn report and an explicit denial of fatigue. It gives no clinical effect estimate for coffee on Parkinson fatigue.

fit: caffeine pill history alongside other exposures and anabolic steroid use
assessment: Caffeine was a reported pre-exercise exposure. The case did not isolate it from other exposures or measure Parkinson fatigue.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: PO1.119 measures a combined coffee/tea intake category after bariatric surgery. In PO1.121 only sweeteners in carbonated beverages associated with fatigue. Coffee/tea sweetener placement pertains to diarrhea, and gastric coffee-ground color is descriptive.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Beverage and diet studies measure coffee intake. P428 models weight change and Parkinson incidence while adjusting for coffee. These different members supply no brewed coffee exposure effect on fatigue.

fit: instant coffee versus water with arterial and ECG endpoints
assessment: The two abstracts report no arterial-wave or pressure difference and longer QTc after instant coffee at two points. They use overlapping protocols and may share participants. They give no brewed-coffee or fatigue result.

fit: filtered and unfiltered coffee in a coronary event case-control study
assessment: The authors observed different preparation associations in people with diabetes. A fatigue endpoint and directional test of the frozen exposure are absent.

fit: longitudinal habitual coffee and body-composition indices
assessment: In the same MONICA cohort, small concurrent adiposity associations had no consistent prospective counterpart. No fatigue endpoint or brewing method was verified.

fit: adult beverage survey with black tea, kefir and coffee
assessment: The study reports beverage use by sex. The methods and table contain different participant totals, and there is no matched gait, falls or fatigue endpoint.

fit: coffee consumption after acute fatigue began
assessment: The case history places extra coffee use after symptom onset in a tick-borne illness, with no measured change attributable to coffee. Preparation remains unspecified.

fit: coffee in a restricted diet associated with scurvy
assessment: Coffee was a reported dietary component after chronic diarrhea restricted intake. Treatment addressed vitamin C deficiency, and there was no isolated coffee-fatigue comparison.

fit: narrower same-cohort coffee and longevity comparison
assessment: In 970 men, those reaching age 90 reported 3.8 versus 4.1 cups daily, p = 0.13. No coffee-specific causal comparison or fatigue endpoint was reported. The parent registry and broader O-32 abstract do not create independent observations.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: OC27 includes a coffee drinking lifestyle measure while examining frailty in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. No independently reported coffee-fatigue result.

fit: reported midlife coffee and survival to 90 in Helsinki Businessmen Study
assessment: Lower consumption was reported in the long-lived group. This is an observational survival analysis without a Parkinson fatigue measure or brewing details. The later, narrower report shares the study family.

fit: caffeine constituent in multiexposure clinical vignettes
assessment: Workout supplement or analgesic cases report medications and caffeine as a constituent. They do not test brewed coffee or a Parkinson fatigue comparison.

fit: coffee subtype and cardiovascular event cohort
assessment: Subtype-specific coffee intake was self-reported. Some cardiovascular associations differed between caffeinated and decaffeinated types. Fatigue was outside the recorded endpoints.

fit: habitual coffee and Parkinson disease incidence in Moli-sani
assessment: The 2022 conference member and 2023 paper cover one cohort of 23,901 adults with 213 incident cases. Official supplementary models give rounded coffee-incidence estimates and multiplicity-adjusted p=.226 and .286 in the full models. Brewing and a fatigue severity outcome are unavailable in the accessible report and tables.

fit: coffee and tea as candidate factors in a young-stroke case-control report
assessment: The 1985 abstract lists coffee and tea together among candidate factors. It gives no coffee-specific estimate and does not measure Parkinson fatigue.

fit: coffee in the historical differential of paroxysmal movement attacks
assessment: The authors discuss coffee in the alternative diagnosis. The described five-person family's episodes are movement-triggered. The member does not establish a coffee effect in the five cases or in Parkinson fatigue.

fit: coffee intake timing and stroke onset in the SECRETO cohort
assessment: The poster reports the 598-person case-crossover coffee result and shares its sample with PMID:42274784. The endpoint and population differ from Parkinson fatigue.

fit: full SECRETO report of coffee and acute cryptogenic stroke
assessment: The linked article's one-hour coffee estimate is RR 1.73 (95% CI 1.06–2.83) in younger stroke patients. It does not measure fatigue, and the conference presentation is dependent.

fit: dihydroergocryptine and caffeine combination
assessment: A combination regimen reported an asthenia signal. Coffee, the effect of caffeine alone, and frozen fatigue severity were not isolated.

fit: isolated caffeine alongside Parkinson medication
assessment: The small primary report concerns motor response and dyskinesia. It provides no brewed-coffee fatigue comparison.

fit: isolated caffeine and blood pressure
assessment: A primary letter assessed postprandial hypotension after isolated caffeine. It did not measure brewed coffee and fatigue.

fit: added caffeine in decaf and sustained motor endurance in healthy participants
assessment: Twenty-three healthy crossover completers had inconclusive motor endurance and force comparisons. Decaf coffee was in both arms and no subjective fatigue severity was measured.

fit: caffeine from coffee and other sources in Parkinson progression cohorts
assessment: The two early Parkinson cohorts examined treatment initiation and UPDRS progression with aggregate caffeine exposure. They did not report individual fatigue outcomes or brewing information.

fit: coffee case with restricted primary access
assessment: A secondary institutional account reports daily function and excessive sleepiness context. The primary letter and any separate fatigue data remain unavailable.

fit: caffeine dose escalation and a recorded fatigue outcome
assessment: The primary report gives the baseline fatigue score. Its follow-up outcome and supplemental table were unavailable.

fit: isolated caffeine and fatigue severity in a randomized trial
assessment: At six weeks the fatigue estimate was −2.85 points with a credible interval spanning zero. The intervention was encapsulated caffeine.

fit: habitual black coffee and FACIT fatigue in hemodialysis
assessment: Mean fatigue scores 30.1 and 29.2, p=.745, in 67 coffee users and 19 nonusers. The observational comparison leaves causal effects and Parkinson transfer unresolved.

fit: reported caffeine during a randomized creatine trial
assessment: The LS-1 secondary analysis reported a caffeine association with worse composite progression in the creatine group. Brewed coffee and fatigue were not isolated.

fit: caffeinated versus decaffeinated brewed espresso and fatigue
assessment: Three of four participants had lower mean fatigue on regular espresso and one had higher fatigue. Both periods included brewed coffee. Fatigue was secondary, no pooled effect was reported and withdrawal is a plausible influence.

fit: coffee intake in a dietary case-control survey
assessment: The survey compared coffee consumption in Parkinson and control groups. It gives no within-Parkinson association with fatigue.

fit: coffee among hypotension management measures in an infusion study
assessment: The study reported fatigue under an infusion substudy. It did not isolate the effect of the coffee mentioned among management measures.

fit: registered fatigue item in an isolated caffeine capsule trial
assessment: The registry lists fatigue. The original reports daytime somnolence separately and does not give a fatigue-specific difference in its main tables. The identified supplement concerns adverse events and its bytes were not recovered from checked public routes.

fit: paper-filtered coffee and acute mental fatigue outside Parkinson disease
assessment: The 59-participant crossover reports lower mental fatigue with regular paper-filtered coffee versus flavored water. Participants did not have Parkinson disease.

fit: green coffee chlorogenic acid beverage and waking fatigue in healthy workers
assessment: A small crossover reports lower waking fatigue late in week two on the extract drink. The analysis has 15 healthy men and a distinct extract preparation and sample from brewed coffee and the later Umeda study.

fit: coffee history and current mental fatigue in two related Parkinson cases
assessment: Table 1 gives premorbid eight cups in case 1 and two to three cups in case 2. Current mental fatigue was 10.5 versus 10 out of 44. Preparation, timing and disease differences leave the exposure effect unresolved.

fit: reported coffee use and cognitive score in Parkinson disease
assessment: The 2020 preprint and 2021 article represent one cohort. Coffee use was associated with lower adjusted MoCA. The report gives no brewing method or fatigue analysis.

fit: canned coffee and striatal receptor occupancy in Parkinson disease
assessment: Five participants self-selected one or two cans. The article and conference report give receptor occupancy on PET and do not report fatigue.

fit: added caffeine in instant decaffeinated coffee and measured attention in Parkinson disease
assessment: Twenty-four Parkinson participants completed the crossover. Both arms used instant decaf and one included an added caffeine tablet. The main report and S1–S6 give task findings without fatigue severity.

fit: exceptional coffee intake and suspected drug-related toxicity
assessment: A single case reported acute signs after high intake with concomitant medicines and pre-existing sleepiness. It provides no comparative fatigue estimate.

fit: plant diet indexes and fatigue in older women
assessment: Separate fatigue HRs were 0.79 (95% CI 0.77–0.82) for the healthful index and 1.16 (1.12–1.20) for the unhealthful index, highest versus lowest quintile. Coffee and tea form a combined index item. No coffee-specific fatigue or Parkinson comparison was reported.

fit: injected caffeine and grip endurance in a mouse model
assessment: Caffeine alone increased grip time. The strength-over-time result improved only with caffeine plus haloperidol and with levodopa. The experiment used injected caffeine and no human fatigue ratings.

fit: coffee exposure and two PPMI imaging analyses
assessment: The two analyses used the same cohort release and assessed striatal outcomes. They did not report a separate fatigue result.

fit: reported coffee and caffeine challenge with tremor outcomes
assessment: The report contains both self-reported coffee-associated worsening and a separate acute caffeine challenge without detectable worsening of tremor. Fatigue was outside the comparison.

fit: reported coffee frequency and aggregate nonmotor symptoms
assessment: The coffee-frequency comparison gave an inconclusive total NMSS result and did not report fatigue separately.

fit: unfiltered coffee and acute fatigue outside Parkinson disease
assessment: The 52-participant unblinded crossover found no clear fatigue interaction for Turkish coffee versus water. Participants did not have Parkinson disease.

fit: coffee intake and fatigue as separate mortality predictors
assessment: The primary paper and supplement measure both coffee intake and fatigue in Parkinson disease. They estimate separate associations with survival, with no coffee-to-fatigue result or preparation information.

fit: reported aggregate caffeine exposure
assessment: Primary Table 4 gives a cross-sectional fatigue odds ratio of 0.94 (95% CI 0.37–2.35) for frequent versus infrequent caffeine use. It supplies no estimate for brewed coffee.

fit: dietary frequency and Parkinson fatigue in a case-control study
assessment: Fatigue was measured separately from daytime sleepiness. Coffee frequency was compared between cases and controls. Within-Parkinson symptom models used an overall diet score and supplied no brewed-coffee fatigue estimate.

fit: instant coffee and withdrawal drowsiness or fatigue in habitual drinkers
assessment: The combined withdrawal item favored regular instant coffee on two days. The separate fatigue scale shows no significance marks. Participants were healthy and the coffee was instant.

fit: daily coffee use and fatigue by sarcopenia status

fit: coffee history and Parkinson diagnosis in a case-control study

fit: qualitative caffeine avoidance during fatigue coaching

fit: Parkinson baseline oatmeal frequency and dyskinesia
assessment: The oatmeal tile is extremely close to zero on the inverse side. The separate cooked-oats field is not shown in the graph. No numeric coefficient or uncertainty is reported.

assessment: The adjusted aggregate symptom estimate crossed zero. Dyskinesia severity and oatmeal preparation were not modeled separately.

fit: oat-derived compound in cultured cells
assessment: Cellular oxidative-stress protection does not measure dyskinesia or cooked oats.

fit: boiled soy tempeh and human walking distance

fit: essential oil consumed in salad dressing
assessment: Three patients from the untreated poststroke aroma group described easier eating after essential oil was added. No Parkinson diagnosis, cracked pepper, random order, or quantified swallowing outcome.

fit: black pepper aroma within combined sensory care

fit: aroma sheet, oral care and exercise in psychiatric inpatients

fit: indirect

The distinct Parkinson case on the program page received ipratropium. No cracked pepper ingestion or corresponding Parkinson choking effect was studied.

fit: inhaled black pepper aroma and swallowing rehabilitation
assessment: Six patients had a history of aspiration pneumonia or cerebrovascular dysphagia. Saliva test and dysphagia grade improved before versus after, and water and food tests showed no detected differences. No Parkinson diagnosis or ingestion contrast was documented.

fit: bedside black pepper aroma in five inpatients
assessment: The uncontrolled pooled comparison gives less sputum and fever but nearly unchanged suction counts. Diagnoses, preparation, ingestion, and a measured swallowing result were unreported.

fit: black pepper aroma patches in 23 patients

fit: black pepper aroma patch in a neurological sample
assessment: One of three improved on a modified water screen and none improved on repeated saliva swallowing. Individual diagnoses were unreported. A patch does not establish an effect of eating cracked black pepper.

fit: inhaled black pepper aromatherapy oil in Parkinson with Lewy body dementia
assessment: Two of five enrolled improved on repeated saliva swallowing and swallow-time assessments, one was unchanged, and two discontinued. Uncontrolled and no raw scores. The oil was sniffed. Eating cracked black pepper was untested.

fit: inhaled black pepper oil after stroke
assessment: Measures of swallow reflex improved in a non-Parkinson population. Route and preparation differ.

fit: black pepper oil odor in pediatric tube feeding
