assessment: Fatigue went 49.34 to 45.88 versus 36.38 to 47.26 on control. The individual-timepoint comparisons gave no significant differences, with an unadjusted descriptive trajectory favoring oil.

fit: virgin coconut oil in a diet with a measured fatigue item
assessment: The plan naming virgin coconut oil improved fatigue by 0.50 points more than the low-fat plan on a descriptive item contrast. The assignment varied whole diets and cannot isolate the oil effect.

fit: coconut oil as a reported coping strategy for off periods
assessment: The survey pooled supplement responses and separately classified fatigue as a trigger. It gives no coconut oil and fatigue estimate.

fit: virgin coconut oil infection trial with daily fatigue reporting
assessment: Overall symptoms resolved at an inconclusive between-group rate. Individual fatigue severity was not given.

fit: fractionated oil and mixed diet
assessment: Sleep or fatigue scores worsened in participants in both study arms. The study did not separate the oil effect.

fit: oropharyngeal coconut oil application and suspected aspiration
assessment: An uncontrolled case reports suspected aspiration of applied coconut oil in a tube-fed adult and improved CT appearance after stopping use. It gives no edible grade, Parkinson group, fatigue measurement or comparative consumption result.

fit: oral virgin coconut oil with loratadine and rhinitis symptoms
assessment: In 52 adults the sneezing change favored control and other rhinitis symptoms were inconclusive. The mainly gastrointestinal effects did not supply a fatigue estimate. The thesis and article describe one non-Parkinson study.

fit: oatmeal and total self-reported Parkinson symptoms
assessment: The oatmeal coefficient was inconclusive and the paper gives no small-handwriting estimate.

fit: green oat capsules and computer-based tracking task
assessment: Some tracking and working-memory results favored extract. There was no handwriting or micrographia assessment.

fit: topical capsaicin and human thumb tracking accuracy
assessment: Healthy adults tracked visual targets more accurately in the capsaicin group after skin exposure and before and after training. No handwriting or consumed smoked paprika was measured.

fit: local hand capsaicin and precision pinch performance in humans
assessment: The pain group had better overall composite skill and similar training improvement in a cursor task. Pinch force and speed–accuracy do not estimate writing size after smoked paprika.

fit: mixed mango or passion fruit drink with soup outside Parkinson disease
assessment: The verified NCT06353984 registry lists HADS at nine weeks and no posted results. The full food program includes mango or passion fruit drink options. It does not assign fruit independently.

fit: dried mango fruit crossover with appetite and glucose outcomes
assessment: The separate dried-fruit arm confirms that preparation. Its endpoints were 90-minute satiety and capillary glucose, without mood or depressive symptom severity.

fit: fresh mango versus cookies and planned depression questionnaire
assessment: The open-label crossover registers depression scores at baseline and four weeks. The instrument and results are unavailable. The healthy adult exposure is fresh mango.

fit: non-soluble mango leaf extract and POMS Depression–Dejection in healthy adults
assessment: Supplementary File 4 gives treatment p=.398 and treatment-by-time p=.731. The design used acute concentrated leaf extract and did not measure dried mango flesh or depression in Parkinson disease.

fit: two soluble mango leaf extract doses and a transient mood-depression subscale
assessment: Group effect p=.401 and group-by-time p<.001. The Results report no clear post hoc difference between groups at any time point. The participants were healthy students and major depression was excluded.

fit: dried mango offered among optional snacks and aggregate affect
assessment: The randomized exposure was video content. The article aggregates intake across six snacks and measures momentary affect. It gives no individual mango exposure, separately attributable effect or depressive symptom severity.

fit: soluble mango leaf extract and exploratory POMS depression in healthy students
assessment: The treatment main effect had p<.001 and adjusted POMS depression scores were lower at three and five hours. The endpoint was exploratory without multiplicity correction. This does not estimate dried mango or Parkinson depression.

fit: isolated eugenol and gait-related tasks in MPTP mice
assessment: Eugenol pretreatment improved narrow-beam crossing and post-treatment worsened it. The rodent task and constituent provide no estimate for ground allspice in people.

fit: injected allspice leaf extract and gross motor depression in rats
assessment: High-dose intraperitoneal leaf extracts caused motor depression and reduced reflexes in general toxicology observations. Oral fraction study measured other outcomes. Ground fruit and clinical bradykinesia remain unresolved.

fit: lentinan and behavioral assays in Parkinson model mice
assessment: Behavioral improvement with isolated lentinan does not specify cooked food or rest tremor.

fit: lentinan carrier and Parkinson model behaviors
assessment: An engineered nanocomposite was used. The accessible abstract contains no food or rest-tremor comparison.

fit: lovage in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome
assessment: The menu lists lovage and the motor examination includes speech. Leaf and drying are unconfirmed and individual voice-volume change was not reported.

fit: filtered dried-marjoram tea and aggregate motor examination
assessment: The tea arm motor score decreased by 2.24 points, with within-arm p = .069. The available results omit walking-slowness and directly consumed dried leaf estimates.

fit: marjoram in a honey mixture evaluated in people with Parkinson disease
assessment: The Methods give a named marjoram exposure and follow-up in 35 patients. Leaf preparation and walking speed were unreported.

fit: reported marjoram use and broad motor symptom frequencies
assessment: Marjoram appears once in the use table. It cannot be linked to walking measures, dried preparation or an individual response.

fit: corn oil capsule comparator for cannabis use disorder pharmacotherapy
assessment: The protocol records sustained attention as a secondary outcome in a drug-versus-corn-oil comparison.

fit: corn oil ethyl esters as comparator with cognitive testing in deployed adults
assessment: The published abstract gives overall cognitive comparisons, using corn oil ethyl esters as the comparator. Attention-specific results and culinary refining are unverified.

fit: corn oil emulsion comparator and attention tasks in older adults
assessment: The corn oil comparator had a small, inconclusive within-phase attention change. The design has no oil-free arm, processing grade or Parkinson cohort.

fit: oral corn oil comparator and sustained-attention task
assessment: No clear performance difference emerged against two DHA doses in healthy children. Neuroimaging and fatty acid correlations do not estimate an oil-induced change in attention in Parkinson disease.

fit: oral Parkinson trial vehicle and aggregate cognition
assessment: All arms had corn oil and the aggregate cognition endpoint offers no attention task or attention-specific item result.

fit: reported pediatric exposure to product coded allspice oil
assessment: The proceedings list 234 exposures, with oral irritation, cough and vomiting most frequently reported for the oil. The source has no individual results for visual hallucination frequency, confirmed ground-fruit exposure or Parkinson cohort.

fit: Adults without diagnosed PD; multicomponent diet score with legume component; binary probable dream-enactment screen
assessment: The authors found no association between alternate Mediterranean diet adherence and probable RBD. This is not an isolated chickpea or canned preparation contrast, does not measure episode frequency, and is not a Parkinson cohort.

fit: 101 people with isolated polysomnography-confirmed RBD; general legumes and estimated prodromal Parkinson probability
assessment: Observed legume associations concern estimated prodromal Parkinson probability and marker count rather than dream-enactment episode frequency; no canned chickpea intake or diagnosed Parkinson cohort is established.

fit: Video-PSG isolated RBD vs controls; generic legumes on prior-year frequency questionnaire; prospective clinical conversion
assessment: The adjusted generic-legume frequency difference between iRBD and controls was inconclusive; RBD status and clinical conversion are not dream-enactment frequency, and canned chickpea exposure is unspecified. Food-group supplement is inaccessible.

fit: whole sweet pepper in two Parkinson diet menus and overall Part III motor examination
assessment: Capsicum occurred in both menus. Part III score changes were −8.58 and −6.27 (between p=.055). The report gave no gait-speed result or independent exposure to grilled peppers.

fit: oral Capsicum fruit extract and rearing in a rat motor model
assessment: Rats given two higher extract doses and extract with levodopa showed improved rearing. The tested Capsicum fruit cultivar was unspecified, contained capsaicinoids and was extracted. The outcome was not walking speed.

fit: purified nonpungent Capsicum and accelerometer-recorded activity
assessment: Ten-meter walking was a baseline eligibility measure. Light-to-moderate activity was measured after treatment, with a subgroup difference favoring extract (p=.050 in prose, p<.05 in Table 4) and no walking-time follow-up contrast in the report. The trial excluded motor disorders and walking aids.

fit: paprika vegetable in a Parkinson diet with gait in the motor examination
assessment: The intervention group improved on total UPDRS III (p=.0004). Diet alone p=.033 and diet plus bowel cleansing p=.005 were within-group comparisons. Gait-item results and paprika preparation were unavailable.

fit: isolated capsiate and timed short or middle distance running
assessment: After 12 mg capsiate, healthy active men completed 400 m in 66.4 versus 67.1 seconds (p=.046) and 3,000 m in 893.9 versus 915.2 seconds (p=.015). No whole pepper exposure or Parkinson gait measure.

fit: isolated capsiate and timed 10 km running
assessment: After two 12 mg doses of capsiate, the 10 km running time comparison was 45.07 versus 45.13 minutes (p=.828). The primary paper lists running and total 24 mg. No whole pepper or Parkinson gait measure.

fit: sweet pepper food frequency and timed 4 m walk within composite sarcopenia
assessment: The 2021 journal report adjusted OR at ≥2–3 times per week was 0.66 (95% CI 0.45–0.95) for sarcopenia, while the likely related 2019 abstract gives a nonsignificant sweet pepper result. Neither supplies a separate pepper coefficient for gait or a grilled exposure.

fit: patient-reported walking and slowness within overall Parkinsonism symptoms
assessment: The cohort included patient-reported difficulty walking and slowness and grouped vegetables showed an association with total symptom burden. The published questionnaire supplies no named pepper exposure and results give no walking-specific estimate.

fit: Thai Parkinson mobility and original vegetable questionnaire
assessment: The bilingual survey separately lists chili powder and records grouped vegetable intake. Mobility outcomes were analyzed without named bell pepper intake or a pepper-specific coefficient.

fit: cold-pressed turnip rapeseed oil and resting blood pressure
assessment: A 37-person crossover found the same mean resting systolic pressure after oil and butter. Postural change and lightheadedness were not evaluated.

fit: conventional canola in provided foods and resting pressure in peripheral arterial disease
assessment: The dissertation reports no clear treatment effect on blood-pressure change. The study did not use confirmed cold-pressed oil or report postural lightheadedness.

fit: canola and coconut mixed meal crossover with resting pressure and vascular measures
assessment: Kienēs and colleagues randomized the order of four mixed meals, each containing canola or coconut oil at one of two fat amounts. Twenty-nine participants with cardiometabolic risk completed all visits. The paper calls the coconut oil virgin cold-pressed and names Brölio canola without specifying a pressing grade. Resting blood pressure appears as a screening measure. Post-meal tests report carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity and augmentation index. No standing challenge or orthostatic lightheadedness measure was reported.

fit: ungraded canola menu and lightheadedness in Parkinson disease
assessment: Low-fat group lightheadedness was 2/23 and 4/23 across the two intervals, versus 2/24 in each ketogenic interval. Standing was not the prespecified trigger and the oil dose and grade were unavailable.

fit: pooled legumes in a sample menu and gait testing in a Parkinson nutrition cohort
assessment: The example dinner lists legumes and the cohort measured gait speed. The paper gives no canned lentil consumption or analysis linking intake to gait speed.

fit: lentils among Parkinson menu options and motor examination total
assessment: The plant menu group had a lower four-week motor total. The comparison does not isolate lentils or preparation, and walking speed was not reported separately.

fit: injected hydroalcoholic red lentil extract and cataleptic posture in rats
assessment: The source records persistence of an imposed posture after a perphenazine challenge. Walking speed and ordinary canned lentils were not tested.

fit: shared Parkinson vegetarian menu with lentils and motor composite
assessment: The two small groups improved on total UPDRS III. The study gives no lentil preparation, isolated intake or walking speed item contrast.

fit: lentils among prebiotic menu options and composite motor score
assessment: A four-week menu and lactulose intervention produced an inconclusive motor total change. Published data do not isolate lentil preparation or intake and omit individual walking speed changes.

fit: oral isolated cinnamaldehyde alone and with diazepam in mice
assessment: The full table and text report no standalone effect. Combination comparison favored more open-arm time. The abstract places a significant p sign beside its no-effect sentence.

fit: cinnamon capsules and acute state anxiety in healthy adults
assessment: State anxiety change differed inconclusively among assigned groups at p = .053. The abstract describes a single laboratory stressor.

fit: cinnamon intake as a group-visit dietary outcome
assessment: OA15.04 reports increased cinnamon intake in a 155-person randomized group-visit dietary secondary analysis for adults with chronic pain and depression; preparation and an isolated cinnamon symptom effect are not reported. The claim seeks ground cinnamon and anxiety severity.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-14-005 uses cassia bark and turmeric-root extracts in Aβ-exposed cells. P-14-016 and P-14-034 report different mixtures and models. The spice blend cannot identify an isolated ground-cinnamon effect.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1473 reports improvement of pediatric orofacial granulomatosis on elemental feeding followed by a diet avoiding both cinnamon and benzoates. It does not separate cinnamon from the other dietary changes.

fit: isolated oral cinnamaldehyde and elevated-plus-maze behavior
assessment: Inconclusive alone. The compound blocked an antagonist-induced increase in open-arm exploration. No independent ground cinnamon or human result.

fit: injected beta-caryophyllene and acute mouse behavior
assessment: More open-arm time and less immobility in behavioral tests followed injection of isolated beta-caryophyllene. This does not establish a clinical outcome from the food preparation.

fit: cinnamon consumption and nonmotor anxiety context in a Parkinson survey
assessment: The report describes inconclusive corrected comparisons and no separate cinnamon-specific HADS anxiety estimate.

fit: isolated cinnamaldehyde and anxiety-related behavior under mouse stress
assessment: Some maze and open-field measures favored the compound and distance traveled was inconclusive. The experiment used an isolated compound.

fit: cinnamon extract and anxiety-related maze behavior in brain injury model
assessment: Primary abstract and accessible figures show no clear group open-arm anxiety comparison. Full original body remains gated. Trauma model and extract differ from frozen claim.

fit: isolated cinnamaldehyde and open-field activity in MPTP mice
assessment: Figure 2 reports crossings and rearing. Urination comparison is inconclusive. Abstract anxiety claim cannot be isolated from measured activity.

fit: shiitake in a mixed-diagnosis choking series
assessment: Five of 15 patients had Parkinson disease and one obstruction involved shiitake. The abstract gives no patient-to-food attribution, preparation, or swallowing severity comparison.

fit: uncut shiitake and human small-bowel obstruction
assessment: Two people without teeth or dentures developed downstream obstructions. The report did not identify roasted shiitake or measure Parkinson swallowing.

fit: shiitake texture testing for dysphagia diets
assessment: Some formulations met IDDSI Level 5 criteria and some did not. Printed puree and food texture tests are distinct from a clinical swallowing outcome after roasted mushroom.

fit: shiitake variety and printed dysphagia texture
assessment: Selected printed material reached IDDSI Level 5 in food tests. The study did not compare the severity of patient swallowing difficulty.

fit: enzyme-softened shiitake in food texture tests
assessment: Vacuum- and enzyme-treated samples reached IDDSI Level 6 criteria without any Parkinson swallowing measure.

fit: rice bran oil comparator and aggregate motor examination
assessment: The trial prespecified Part III and reports total MDS-UPDRS. No facial expression item, oil-grade specification, or independent oil exposure effect was available.

fit: mixed seed extract and rat locomotor activity
assessment: Figures 1 and 2 report less catalepsy and higher activity with a mixture of almond, peanut and watermelon seed extracts. No arm tested watermelon alone or raw flesh. Animal locomotion differs from measured bradykinesia in patients.

fit: isolated oral lycopene and locomotor tasks in MPTP mice
assessment: The source reports timed beam crossing and open-field activity in mice. Only an isolated constituent was administered and neither task establishes clinical bradykinesia after raw watermelon.

fit: watermelon intake frequency in a descriptive Parkinson cohort
assessment: Among 40 participants, 15 reported weekly watermelon, 9 monthly, 16 rarely or never and none daily. Preparation and an intake-linked bradykinesia contrast are absent.

fit: watermelon juice and open-field activity in an anemia model
assessment: The university project reports increased activity after juice in phenylhydrazine-exposed rats. Arm accounting and figure details were incomplete. Clinical bradykinesia was outside the study.

fit: fish group and composite symptom score
assessment: Nonfried fish frequency associated with lower aggregate symptom scores. It did not estimate a canned sardine fatigue effect.

fit: canned sardines and processed sardine products
assessment: The sardine-enriched diet included canned sardines and foods made from them. The diabetes trial measured metabolic and microbiota outcomes rather than fatigue.

fit: canned sardine feeding and metabolic outcomes
assessment: The 152-person trial assigned canned sardines in olive oil. Fatigue severity was absent and tiring of the intervention was a withdrawal reason.

fit: canned sardine botulism and acute fatigue
assessment: A child with clinical foodborne botulism had fatigue after reported canned sardine exposure. Child-specific laboratory confirmation and a fatigue severity score were absent.

fit: fish-meat peptide tablets and fatigue VAS in healthy adults
assessment: The registry reports a favorable fatigue contrast without exact arm data. Fish species remains unverified. The processed tablet and healthy population do not test canned sardines or Parkinson fatigue.

fit: dried summer savory infusion and awake rat activity
assessment: Open-field squares crossed declined after seven days. The animals were awake and the study measured neither sleepiness nor Parkinson disease.

fit: veterinary reference context only, without a tested Parkinson comparison
assessment: The poisoning entry names chives among foods hazardous to dogs and cats. This is veterinary species-specific source context with no observed Parkinson falls.

fit: purified oral compound and rotarod latency in MPTP mice
assessment: Purified ferulic-acid groups generally stayed on the rod longer than the MPTP-only group. Rotarod latency and spontaneous fall frequency differ. The study used no dried chives.

fit: measured ferulic acid in common chive tissue
assessment: Ferulic acid was measured at 22.22 to 28.79 mg/kg fresh weight in green tissue. This establishes constituent presence under the study conditions. The study measured no dried exposure or falls.

fit: Parkinson case with narrative insomnia outcome
assessment: The clinical timeline reports improvement at about one week with daikenchuto and rehabilitation. Different pepper species and combined treatment limit attribution.

fit: hydroalcoholic fruit extract and drug-induced loss of righting in mice
assessment: The high extract dose shortened drug-induced loss of righting. The onset cell and narrative disagree on significance. The assay, plant preparation and population limit transfer to insomnia after eating toasted Sichuan pepper.

fit: planned healthy-gamer sleep-disturbance measure
assessment: PROMIS Sleep Disturbance was registered for a Nepalese pepper extract. No results were posted.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-14-005 studies a joint cinnamon and turmeric-extract blend. Other posters concern isolated curcumin in prostate cancer or cell and platelet experiments. No Parkinson symptom comparison is supplied.

fit: isolated curcumin pretreatment in cultured human endothelial cells
assessment: The original congress member reports curcumin among inhibitors of linoleate-induced LOX-1 expression. The later abstract describes classes of inhibitors. The cell outcome does not answer a culinary turmeric symptom claim.

fit: isolated curcumin and hepatic glucose production
assessment: The later article reports lower glucose production and lower PEPCK activity in a specified condition. The related original abstract reports no PEPCK effect. Experimental differences and any link to culinary turmeric remain unresolved.

fit: curcumin extract alongside a weight-loss diet in PCOS
assessment: No separate Parkinson symptom or culinary turmeric result was recorded. Within-group metabolic changes do not establish a between-group clinical response.

fit: turmeric-colored bread and child sensory preference
assessment: Children chose yellow bread less often. The study concerns colour and liking, without a swallowing or other relevant clinical endpoint.

fit: curcumin and falls or dizziness in Alzheimer disease
assessment: One combined fall-or-dizziness event in each of three arms: placebo, 1 g/day and 4 g/day curcumin. Separate or recurrent fall counts and culinary ground turmeric are absent.

fit: solid lipid curcumin and human balance
assessment: Rapid-step balance and gait speed changes were inconclusive in healthy adults. There was no fall frequency measure or culinary exposure.

fit: intravenous curcumin and rotarod latency
assessment: The isolated compound prolonged mouse time on a rotating rod. Forced-task latency differs from human fall frequency and delivery was intravenous.

fit: PD saffron capsule; Part III motor total; no speech-item or voice-volume estimate
assessment: Registered Part III contains a speech item incorporating volume, but accessible composite result cannot determine a direction for low voice volume; ground preparation is unverified.

fit: PD Sargol powder tablet; planned composite MDS-UPDRS; no speech-item estimate
assessment: Part II and III speech items address broader speech than volume; no item-level data available and tablet regimen differs from ordinary culinary use.

fit: injected carvacrol and drug-elicited vacuous chewing
assessment: Carvacrol prevented increased oral movements after reserpine. The preparation and dyskinesia model differ from dried savory and Parkinson.

fit: herb named in a mixed Parkinson menu
assessment: Total UPDRS III and the menu do not estimate individual freezing frequency after chervil.

fit: shared sesame oil vehicle and composite neuropsychiatric results in Parkinson disease
assessment: The registry reports NPI totals and the trial does not isolate hallucination frequency or oil exposure.

fit: roasted whole flaxseed and measured sleep latency in students
assessment: Polysomnography sleep latency changed from 14.8 to 10.39 minutes (p < .001), while global sleep quality showed no clear change (p = .635). This was uncontrolled and tested whole seed in students with poor sleep.

fit: flaxseed oil plus carnitine in migraine trial with planned PSQI
assessment: The shared registration connects the PSQI protocol to a results paper on migraine, mood and quality of life. The paper provides no sleep value, and the intervention combined oil with carnitine.

fit: flaxseed powder and Insomnia Severity Index in migraine
assessment: The eight-week mean Insomnia Severity Index change was −4.6 with flaxseed powder versus −1.6 with roasted wheat powder (p = .029). The intervention used the seed matrix and did not enroll people with Parkinson’s.

fit: organic flaxseed oil vehicle in a mixed uncontrolled hemp sleep study
assessment: The mixed formulation includes flaxseed oil as its carrier and supplies no isolated oil comparator.

fit: unspecified vegetable oil test food and planned sleep outcomes
assessment: The two periods compare test food after dinner with no test food. Before applying the trial to flaxseed oil insomnia or canola oil daytime sleepiness, the oil identity and result measures must be established.

fit: Parkinson dyskinesia diary during broccoli and ground white mustard tea
assessment: The single illustrative Table 1 self-rating remained 2 across all weeks. There was no controlled comparison or mustard-only arm. Whether cohort members overlap an earlier case series remains open.

fit: cabbage-derived fibers and Parkinson fecal fermentation ex vivo
assessment: The investigators measured SCFAs in samples. No sauerkraut ingestion or salivary outcome.

fit: fresh versus pasteurized sauerkraut in healthy adults
assessment: Actual fermented food was consumed. Gut microbiota and metabolites were measured; drooling and cultivar were unreported.

fit: shredded sauerkraut compared with nonfermented pickles in dysphagia-risk adults
assessment: Gut outcomes and feasibility were reported. No Parkinson subgroup or clinical drooling assessment.

fit: isolated orange juice fraction and experimental gut outcomes
assessment: PF01.04 studies nanovesicles isolated from orange juice in a diet-induced obesity model. Acridine orange in a different member is a dye. The food fraction and endpoints differ from raw orange.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-09-014 assesses essential-oil extracts from sweet-orange peel and albedo. P-09-007 uses citrus residues without an isolated whole-orange intervention.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1323 administers mixed orange–lemon juice before imaging in a 24-person pancreatic study. P1611 uses orange juice to check a pH device. Xylenol orange is a dye.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: P305 combines orange juice and germinated legumes against folic acid or apple juice and measures folate and plasma metabolites. The matrix contrast does not estimate raw orange and the named Parkinson symptom.

fit: orange juice as rescue during closed-loop insulin delivery
assessment: Orange juice was offered on four occasions when glucose was below 60 mg/dL. The study concerns insulin control, without a matched raw-fruit exposure or related Parkinson symptom outcome.

fit: carotenoid food recalls and macular pigment measurements
assessment: The participant records name several food sources and the authors report no detected association with optical pigment density. No assigned food preparation or relevant Parkinson symptom was measured.

fit: orange juice during two episodes of symptomatic hypoglycemia
assessment: A patient with diabetes and end-stage kidney disease had symptom relief after juice at two low glucose measurements. This is one case with a different product and cause, without raw-orange falls or constipation measurement.

fit: isolated ascorbic acid and levodopa exposure
assessment: The study found increased levodopa exposure in a low-baseline-absorption subgroup and no clear change in the full sample. Falls and whole orange were untested.

fit: oranges and upper gastrointestinal symptoms outside Parkinson disease
assessment: Survey participants reported food-associated symptoms. Falls were outside the study.

fit: oranges plus other citrus and first fall hospitalization in older women
assessment: The adjusted hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI .99–1.04) per 20 g/day, p=.345. No orange-only result, recurrent falls or Parkinson cohort.

fit: orange in Parkinson dietary surveys
assessment: Two primary surveys measured orange intake and reported no fall estimate.

fit: orange and juice combined in a Parkinson mortality cohort
assessment: The cohort analyzed mortality after diagnosis. It did not report raw orange and falls.

fit: baseline olfaction in a post-stroke inhaled pepper trial
assessment: Olfactory identification appears only among baseline characteristics. The trial measures subsequent swallowing and related outcomes, with no oral pepper or clinical olfaction change.

fit: isolated piperine and mouse odor-guided behavior
assessment: Oral isolated piperine shortened buried-pellet search latency and changed odor preference in Thy1-SNCA mice. Ground black pepper and human smell impairment were outside the comparison.

fit: ground black peppercorn used as an experimental odor
assessment: Food odors were presented in bottles to young adults for perceptual discrimination. Participants did not consume pepper and olfactory impairment was screened out.

fit: practitioner survey with authenticated sumac fruit and voice indications
assessment: Fifty-six of 100 practitioners cited fruit infusion. The survey contains no patient-level symptom change or intelligibility assessment.

fit: adult suspected allergy after a sumac-containing meal
assessment: Throat itching and breathing difficulty were recorded during suspected acute food allergy outside Parkinson disease. Speech intelligibility was not measured.

fit: oral sesame oil and forced-swim behavior in rats
assessment: Climbing time and immobility gave different results against the active control. Processing grade and clinical depression were unmeasured.

fit: refined sesame oil and depression in a fatty liver diet trial
assessment: Original abstract concludes lower depression with sesame than sunflower. The specific test for p=.013, arm estimates, and the full statistical plan remain unverified. Matching trial reports identify both oils as refined.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: Sesame oil acts as an injected vehicle in rat corticosteroid or AF64A experiments, with no oral oil comparison.

fit: shared sesame oil vehicle and depressive symptoms in Parkinson disease
assessment: Depression scores were inconclusive in both arms and oil was present in both. The oil-specific contrast is unavailable.

fit: oral caraway polyphenols and open-field activity in healthy mice
assessment: Open-field tile crossings increased. The experiment measured neither freezing episodes nor toasted caraway in Parkinson disease.

fit: celery suggested in a multimodal lifestyle program and a walking testimonial
assessment: One Parkinson participant described better walking, without individual celery consumption, timed walking, a raw stalk exposure or a comparison group.

fit: oral solvent extract of whole celery and narrow-beam crossing in MPTP mice
assessment: Beam crossing latency fell in the 250 and 375 mg/kg groups. The task reflects balance and speed in a toxin model. It did not measure human walking slowness.

fit: raw celery stalk in a human mixed-salad crossover
assessment: The trial measured vascular outcomes. There was no Parkinson or gait-speed measure.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide and an off-medication non-tremor subtotal
assessment: The subtotal includes gait alongside 11 other items. No isolated gait score or timed walk and no culinary raw celery stalk exposure.

fit: celery included on a Parkinson vegetarian menu
assessment: Composite UPDRS III improved. Neither celery stalk preparation nor gait speed was reported separately.

fit: aqueous parsley seed extract and arterial pressure
assessment: The extract lowered arterial pressure in anesthetized rats. No dried leaf meal, standing pressure or orthostatic lightheadedness was assessed.

fit: dried parsley blood pressure trial, withdrawn
assessment: Registration planned blood pressure and urine comparisons in adults with hypertension. The withdrawn trial enrolled zero and specified no standing measure or orthostatic symptoms.

fit: dried parsley leaf and asparagus clinical surveillance
assessment: In six-week surveillance of 163 patients, a dried parsley leaf and asparagus root product had no clinically useful antihypertensive effect. Seven withdrew with renal complaints. No standing pressure or orthostatic lightheadedness was reported.

fit: aqueous aerial extract and arterial pressure
assessment: Oral extract lowered pressure in normotensive and induced-hypertensive rats. Parkinson lightheadedness, standing response and dried culinary parsley were outside the study.

fit: other species model; methanolic leaf extract; motor tests; no human OFF duration
assessment: Haloperidol rat rotarod and catalepsy outcomes are not daily OFF time in people consuming dried basil. Reports are likely duplicate publications of one study; group-size and timing reporting unclear.

fit: other species model; injected hydroethanolic aerial extract; motor tests; no human OFF duration
assessment: Rotenone rat motor tasks do not measure daily OFF time or ordinary dried basil consumption; abstract combination claim is not supported by displayed five-group tables and methods conflict on sex and formulation.

fit: self-reported dry mouth and swallowing measures in an independent Parkinson cohort
assessment: Swallowing complaints and measured questionnaire dryness scores were associated in an independent Parkinson survey. The study did not assign oil and cannot estimate a response to oral lubrication.

fit: sunflower food frequency and composite Parkinson symptom burden
assessment: The poster reports +2 total PRO-PD points per intake frequency category (95% CI −10 to 13, p=.787). The cross-sectional exposure did not specify an oil grade. It gives no individual swallowing estimate.

fit: oral high oleic sunflower comparator and adherence-related inability to swallow oil
assessment: Participants swallowed high-oleic sunflower oil as an active comparator. Sparse oil-swallowing adherence events use a restricted denominator and do not estimate a symptom effect.

fit: dry mouth and self-reported swallowing difficulties in Parkinson disease
assessment: In the Parkinson cohort, subjective dry mouth and dysphagia were associated. The connection supplies clinical context for the patient-reported rinse result.

fit: sunflower oil mixed food bench texture IDDSI preparation
assessment: The product formulation reached several physical texture classifications. It supplies no patient swallowing comparison.

fit: oral sunflower oil and infant aspiration-related pulmonary outcomes
assessment: The case series documented repeated oral sunflower oil and silent aspiration in two infants with lipoid pneumonia. There was no oil-grade information, counterfactual group or evidence that oil caused a change in swallowing function.

fit: cold-pressed sunflower rinse and perceived swallowing ease
assessment: In a medication-related xerostomia crossover, eight of 24 reported easier swallowing after sunflower rinse versus two with water (p=.031, unadjusted). The oil was cold-pressed from roasted kernels and spat out. No instrumental or Parkinson-specific result was given.

fit: abdominal pain in two acute hazelnut food allergy cases
assessment: Both described abdominal pain during identified hazelnut-food anaphylaxis. The cake and cookie do not verify isolated oil or cold pressing, and the cases provide no pain severity or Parkinson comparison.

fit: oral cold-pressed hazelnut oil and measured gastric tissue injury
assessment: The lower and higher oil arms had smaller ulcer areas than ethanol alone, with reported p<.001. The experiment measured injury area and histology without pain behavior or a Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: celery named in a Parkinson diet with aggregate speech-inclusive motor scale
assessment: The celery plant part and preparation are unspecified and speech intelligibility was not separately reported.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes facial expression, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: standardized ginger powder tablets and total MDS-UPDRS
assessment: The registry shows recruitment complete and gives no results or separate dyskinesia measure.

fit: ginger in a combined formula
assessment: Completed registry record and protocol. No posted results or linked outcome paper located.

fit: two ginger extract capsule strengths and composite motor complications
assessment: Official other outcomes list change in MDS-UPDRS Parts I–IV at 12 weeks. The record gives no separate dyskinesia item outcome, ground ginger, inactive comparator or results.

fit: isolated oral zingerone and observed post-levodopa hindlimb behavior
assessment: The companion report describes no suppression of hindlimb stiffening in several lesioned mice. No arm counts, severity scale or ground ginger comparison were provided.

fit: dried ginger in four-herb ethanol extract and general motor tests
assessment: The abstract calls the finding dyskinesia, and the reported tests are pole descent, rotarod, grip and traction. There was no abnormal involuntary movement score or ginger-only arm.

fit: dried-rhizome extract and abnormal involuntary movements in levodopa-treated mice
assessment: Inventor Table 12 reports AIM AUC 144.00 ± 15.56 versus 276.75 ± 26.00 with levodopa alone. The extract is distinct from ground ginger and the disclosed animal comparison leaves route, n and masking unverified. The later Korean patent repeats the same experiment.

fit: adult beverage survey with black tea, kefir and coffee
assessment: The study reports beverage use by sex. The methods and table contain different participant totals, and there is no matched gait, falls or fatigue endpoint.

fit: oral black tea extract and spontaneous locomotion and circling in 6-OHDA rats
assessment: Primary Fig. 1 shows about 190 rotations per 30 minutes after lesion alone versus 143 and 102 with 1.5% oral extract started post- and pre-lesion. Secondary preparation sources suggest a daily water brew and ad libitum access. The experiment does not provide a walking-speed contrast.

fit: unspecified tea exposure and time to Hoehn and Yahr stage 3
assessment: Tel Aviv retrospective study of 278 PD patients found an inconclusive association with stage progression. A companion article explicitly repeats the same cohort for its onset analysis. Neither establishes black tea or walking speed.

fit: caffeine dose escalation with Timed Up and Go and patient-rated mobility
assessment: Timed Up and Go baseline was 10.39 seconds (SD 3.04). The main text gives no follow-up number. PDQ-39 mobility improved 2.8 points among those tolerating 400 mg/day of caffeine in the single-group trial.

fit: isolated theaflavin and narrow-beam crossing in an MPTP mouse model
assessment: Oral 10 mg/kg theaflavin shortened beam crossing and reduced slips at p < .05. The figure declares six per group while methods state twelve were assigned and all had behavioral tests. The task measures balance and coordination in mice and the preparation was isolated theaflavin.

fit: randomized caffeine and UPDRS III gait in Parkinson disease
assessment: The week-six examiner-rated gait contrast was −0.28 points (95% interval −1.16 to 0.59). The study used caffeine capsules and provides no timed gait speed or brewed tea estimate.

fit: grouped black and oolong tea and clinical gait assessment in older adults
assessment: Adjusted Table 3 gait B=.01, SE=.006, p=.02. The paper gives a different p-value in prose. The fixed-distance task used qualitative gait scores with a grouped exposure and no Parkinson subgroup.

fit: randomized caffeine capsules and walking-related composite items in Parkinson patients
assessment: No individual MDS-UPDRS Part II components differed clearly after six months. There was no reported timed-walk value or black-tea arm.

fit: caffeinated tea and progression to Hoehn and Yahr stage three
assessment: Ever versus never caffeinated tea HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.51–1.71, p=.82). Exposure and outcome lacked black tea and walking-speed specificity.

fit: laboratory green and fermented tea extracts and reported animal behavior
assessment: Supplement Fig. S1 shows 100 mg/kg/day orally per extract. Primary Fig. 4A shows about 300 seconds for fully fermented black tea versus 55 seconds for model alone, with all tea arms sharing one significance letter. The motion-test protocol and gait-speed fit remain unresolved.

fit: regular black tea in distinct Parkinson populations with composite follow-up
assessment: Two exploratory LRRK2 samples reported lower log MDS-UPDRS II levels with black tea while two idiopathic samples were inconclusive. No walk or gait item coefficient, tested brew or tea-by-time slope was reported.

fit: black tea intake and MDS-UPDRS motor examination in Lithuanian dietary cohort
assessment: Black tea 26.67 versus 13.33 mL/day in cases versus controls (p=.008). The motor regression is for the dietary score, and symptom-specific black tea comparisons were not reported.

fit: oral ethanol black tea extract and catalepsy and locomotion in haloperidol mice
assessment: Day 12 bar time decreased from 237.14 s to 76.4 and 64.28 s with 4 and 8 mg/kg. Ten-minute beam breaks increased from 107.83 to 191.42 and 247.28. The extract and test differ from brewed tea and clinical walking speed.

fit: Pinta sprout extract and rat melatonin biomarker
assessment: In Experiment 1, fasted rats given Pinta sprout extract had plasma melatonin about 16% higher than the chow control and 2.9 times the fasting group at 90 minutes. Neither sleep behavior nor insomnia was measured. The treatment was an extract from sprouted beans, with no boiled-pinto or Parkinson comparison.

fit: student sleep-quality cross-section with legume preference
assessment: Table 2 OR 1.59 (95% CI 1.22 to 2.08) refers to dislike of grouped beans, chickpeas and lentils. The pooled rice, pasta or beans meal item cannot identify pinto or an isolated ingestion effect. The study does not test Parkinson insomnia.

fit: parallel bean and sleep measures with fecal bacterial comparisons
assessment: Tables 3 and 4 compare fecal Akkermansia with sleep category and canary bean frequency separately. Supplement S1 names no pinto and gives no bean-by-sleep or preparation data. The older-adult cohort does not establish a Parkinson-specific insomnia effect.

fit: uncontrolled kidney bean yogurt and sleep quality
assessment: The conference report and article describe one 17-person older-adult cohort. PSQI fell from 8.06 to 4.88 over two weeks without a control. The fermented kidney bean preparation, population and global sleep outcome differ from the frozen pinto and Parkinson claim.

fit: whole MIND diet contrast and grouped bean score in diabetes
assessment: The sleep paper favors the diet assignment for adjusted PSQI. Companion reports concern grouped bean score, cardiometabolic markers and quality of life. All share one trial. Actual pinto-specific records and an ingredient-specific insomnia effect remain unverified.

fit: registered pinto crossover with vascular and metabolic outcomes
assessment: The thesis describes boiled pinto consumption. The official registration lists phytochemical, arterial stiffness and satiety measures. The trial completed without posted results and does not register insomnia or enroll Parkinson participants.

fit: PD pooled bean category and whole-diet insomnia association; no pinto exposure estimate
assessment: The cross-sectional whole-diet insomnia association does not identify boiled pinto consumption or its independent effect.

fit: registered Mucuna and soybean beverage with planned sleep measure
assessment: The randomized comparison plans sleep-quality assessment in healthy adults. Each drink includes soybean and the active beverage adds Mucuna. No results are published, and neither genus or preparation matches boiled pinto beans.

fit: canola-containing diet in shift workers with sleep-disturbance label
assessment: The registry lists melatonin and cardiometabolic endpoints without daytime sleepiness, verified refining grade or posted results.

fit: canola oil supplement comparator and caregiver daytime sleepiness in preterm toddlers
assessment: The secondary sleepiness comparison between omega 3-6-9 and canola was imprecise. The trial used an unspecified-grade oil in toddlers and had no oil-free control.

fit: canola oil in the low-fat menu and daytime sleepiness by diet
assessment: The ketogenic group improved more on the daytime sleepiness item. The low-fat plan names canola oil of unspecified grade, with no separate exposure estimate.

fit: canola comparator and PSQI daytime dysfunction in healthy older adults
assessment: Preprint daytime component changes were +.09 canola versus +.08 ketone ester. The peer-reviewed report gives no clear PSQI or subdomain difference. No grade, oil-free arm, dedicated sleepiness result or PD cohort.

fit: unspecified vegetable oil test food and no separately named daytime sleepiness outcome
assessment: Healthy adults compare test food with no test food. The public record gives no oil identity or separately specified daytime sleepiness, and no results are posted.

fit: pharmaceutical compound and composite motor outcome
assessment: A retrospective adjunct study assessed motor scores. It did not test culinary celery or isolate the named symptom.

fit: pharmaceutical adjunct and total UPDRS
assessment: Dai and colleagues reported lower total UPDRS under the pharmaceutical adjunct in Parkinson dementia. The accessible report gives no separate bradykinesia estimate.

fit: pharmaceutical adjunct and total UPDRS
assessment: Liu and colleagues reported a favorable UPDRS total with the pharmaceutical adjunct. The public abstract gives no bradykinesia item.

fit: whole dried celery methanolic extract in an MPTP motor model
assessment: Beam latency and grid-walk faults improved at some doses. The preparation was whole-plant extract and human bradykinesia was not measured.

fit: synthetic drug adjunct with off-medication non-tremor motor subscore
assessment: Table II reports -7.14 +/- 5.81 versus +0.50 +/- 9.48 at week 24 (p < .001, n=43 and 60). This subscore combines bradykinesia, rigidity, speech, face, gait and other items. It gives no isolated bradykinesia or culinary celery leaf effect.

fit: celery named in a Parkinson diet with composite bradykinesia-inclusive motor scale
assessment: No isolated celery arm, fresh leaf detail or separate bradykinesia change was published.

fit: pharmaceutical compound and composite motor outcomes
assessment: Retrospective comparison found lower composite motor scores with the adjunct and reported no separate bradykinesia estimate.

fit: pharmaceutical comparison and total UPDRS
assessment: Wang and colleagues compared butylphthalide with donepezil. Table 1 gives the UPDRS total without a bradykinesia item.

fit: formulated thyme drop and perceived talking comfort
assessment: Half reported greater talking comfort with the drop versus 16.7% with placebo after vocal loading. No listener-rated intelligibility or Parkinson’s participants.

fit: formulated thyme lozenge and voice measures
assessment: Subjective hoarseness and dryness improved while objective voice measures did not clearly change. The study did not measure listener-rated intelligibility.

fit: ground anise powder and SF-36 vitality in dyspepsia
assessment: Week-12 SF-36 vitality favored anise. The generic vitality domain and dyspepsia population differ from Parkinson fatigue severity.

fit: anise oil and 0–10 tiredness in a three-arm IBS trial
assessment: Tiredness at week 4 and follow-up was 3.15 and 2.74 with oil versus 3.94 and 3.54 with placebo. The table gives three-arm p<.001. A later review disagrees. Oil and IBS limit transfer.

fit: low
assessment: Mechanically ground anise fruit in capsules was compared with milled-rice placebo in a menopause trial. The reports supply a total MKI and mood subscales, without a separate fatigue severity estimate. Treat the May and October papers as one study.

fit: anise seed in a honey mixture evaluated in people with Parkinson disease
assessment: The preparation was unspecified. Fatigue was a survey category with no separate estimate for mixture recipients.

fit: patient- and physician-rated pain during diclofenac withdrawal
assessment: Table 2 assigns the 0.37-point physician pain change to fish oil. Corn oil shows +0.58 patient-rated (p=.007) and +0.47 physician-rated (p=.06) during diclofenac withdrawal. Between-oil changes were inconclusive; refining and Parkinson pain were unverified.

study: BNA2019 injected oil or preference member
fit: animal vehicle or flavored-milk preference outside the frozen preparation
assessment: PT080 and another member report injected corn oil as vehicle or control in a perimenopause model. The oil route, associated interventions and measures differ from oral corn oil.

fit: corn-oil high-fat rodent comparison
assessment: Muscle molecular markers differ across high-fat oils. The active comparator and molecular outcome do not estimate an isolated refined corn oil and Parkinson endpoint effect.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: Corn oil is used in rat lipid comparisons, feeding paradigms and a toxicant vehicle. No Parkinson clinical endpoint was measured.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Carney 2009 combines sertraline with corn oil; other original or protocol records use different lipid mixtures and symptom scales. The review cannot isolate the oil or a Parkinson endpoint.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: P210 compares EPA/DHA-enriched high-fat chow against corn-oil high-fat chow for muscle transcriptome and proteins. No separate frozen patient outcome.

fit: corn oil as high-fat diet control and partial marine-lipid substitution
assessment: Corn oil was one base formulation, with and without different marine PUFA fractions. Adiposity and lipids were measured. The possibly overlapping article concerns the same broad research and a refined corn oil symptom effect is unresolved.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: P233 is appended in the complete PMC HTML for this oral-key record and separately printed in the poster supplement. It compares corn and fish oil during shared exercise for strength and mechanistic outcomes. One study family.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Printed P233 reports an omega-3 versus corn-oil comparator during shared resistance training. Its strength findings are distinct from the frozen clinical outcomes. The other PMC key reproduces this member.

fit: corn-oil control during exercise training
assessment: The final isometric interaction is p=.015 and the corn arm changed −1.4%. P233 uses −0.3%. Body strength during shared training does not measure any frozen Parkinson endpoint in these claims.

fit: oral corn oil emulsion in Sjögren trial
assessment: The abstract reports no clear muscle or joint pain difference against gamma-linolenic acid. Both arms used active oils and the grade is unspecified.

fit: locally instilled corn oil and colonoscopy procedure pain
assessment: Procedure pain favored adding oil as local lubricant. The route, cause of pain, and unspecified grade leave the frozen oral hypothesis unresolved.

fit: corn oil as a shared carrier
assessment: Physical discomfort did not clearly differ. The trial had no independent oil or pain-specific contrast.

fit: oral corn oil comparator, osteoarthritis pain trial
assessment: VAS and WOMAC comparisons were inconclusive. The oil arm averaged 4.5 to 4.6 on VAS. There was no oil-free control and no specification of refining grade.

fit: separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context
assessment: A tumor experiment incorporates corn oil in control or combined diets involving EPA and aspirin. The study does not assign the frozen preparation and clinical endpoint.

fit: injected bromelain and rat stepping and forelimb movement
assessment: Pretreatment improved rat motor performance without clear dopamine preservation. The enzyme was injected. Raw pineapple and clinical dexterity were untested.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet with pineapple and composite motor examination
assessment: The diet lists pineapple and the composite motor examination contains finger and hand tasks. No pineapple intake, preparation, arm or individual hand-item result was reported.

fit: injected grapeseed oil drug carrier and an orofacial movement outcome
assessment: Grapeseed oil nanocapsules carrying haloperidol only partly attenuated acute vacuous chewing and all loaded formulations prevented excess chewing subchronically. The study counted involuntary jaw movements in rats. Speech, articulation and oral oil ingestion were unmeasured.

fit: fresh petiole composition and shared flavone markers
assessment: Fresh petioles contain apigenin and luteolin, also measured in the whole-plant mouse extract. Fresh tissue and dry extract have different denominators and preparation. No bridge establishes the mediator, equivalent exposure, or human rest-tremor outcome.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide adjunct with UPDRS III total
assessment: The 100-person retrospective comparator reports motor totals. The discrepancy between the two motor sections and lack of a separate item prevent a rest-tremor estimate.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide add-on and aggregate UPDRS
assessment: The original abstract reports 90 randomized participants and post-treatment totals 33.28 versus 41.26. Full tables and trial dates remain gated. It supplies no raw stalk exposure or separate rest-tremor outcome.

fit: synthetic racemic butylphthalide plus donepezil and aggregate UPDRS
assessment: Liu randomized 84 Parkinson dementia patients. Table 2 gives week-12 total UPDRS 20.32 versus 35.12 for adjunct and comparator (p<.01). Rest tremor is an eligibility or baseline phenotype and does not have a follow-up item estimate.

fit: pharmaceutical adjunct in Parkinson dementia with broadly defined motor score
assessment: The 73-person original author abstract reports a composite improvement without item, score values or timing. The full paper remains gated. The pharmaceutical treatment differs from raw celery stalk.

fit: public report of perceived general benefit from seed extract
assessment: The participant described prior tremor, no diagnosis and several concurrent products. No individual tremor outcome is attributed to celery and the preparation is a seed extract.

fit: human plasma after a blanched parsley meal
assessment: Original author abstract reports mean peak plasma apigenin 127 nmol/L (SD 81) at mean 7.2 hours (SD 1.3) in 11 healthy adults. This supplies matrix-specific exposure context with no raw celery stalk or resting-tremor comparison. Body access remains unverified.

fit: quantified butylphthalide in fresh raw stalk and raw leaf
assessment: Original Table 2 gives 0.29 mg/kg in raw stalk versus 0.87 mg/kg in raw leaf. These are whole-material chemistry measurements. The 2018 motor experiment did not quantify this compound in its administered extract.

fit: human plasma after a celery leaf meal
assessment: Cao Table 3 on p253 and Zhao 2008 Table 1 on p447 share all 35 numeric time-point cells, mean peak time and area under the curve. The reported denominators differ (20 and 10). This is one plasma-result lineage with unresolved participant provenance. Hydrolyzed plasma apigenin confirms dietary leaf exposure without a motor outcome.

fit: Parkinson dementia with multi-drug butylphthalide combination
assessment: Static tremor is an eligibility feature in the 60-person Baoding trial. Follow-up uses cognitive and dementia scales. There is no isolated drug, food or rest-tremor contrast.

fit: isolated celery-associated drug in a transgenic mouse motor test
assessment: Rotarod retention favored isolated butylphthalide in A53T mice. The separate rest-tremor and raw-food endpoints were not measured.

fit: human apigenin metabolites after different culinary matrices
assessment: Original Methods and Results compare metabolite timing after parsley drink, parsley in yogurt and chamomile tea. Circulating apigenin-4-prime-glucuronide peaks at four, six and two hours, respectively. The preparations differ in matrix and glycoconjugates. No raw celery stalk exposure or Parkinson motor endpoint is tested.

fit: isolated drug and toxin-model motor proxies
assessment: Figure 1 separates rod, beam and strength results from background discussion of quiescent tremor. No raw celery or separate rest-tremor evaluation.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide in a Parkinson dementia cohort
assessment: The 126-person Zhengzhou report lists tremor phenotype at baseline and reports an unitemized total UPDRS at follow-up. It gives no raw celery-stalk exposure or separate tremor measurement.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide within adjunct cognitive treatment
assessment: The 119-person Chengdu study lists resting tremor in a multi-symptom response rule. Its follow-up figure reports UPDRS II and III totals without a separate tremor item estimate.

fit: oral extract of whole celery and scored rest tremor in MPTP mice
assessment: Figure 4a plots lower separately scored rest tremor under whole-plant methanol extract in MPTP mice. At day seven the mean bars are approximately 4.7 with vehicle versus 2.1 in the highest extract group (n=8 per group, figure read). The extract contains measured apigenin and luteolin. Their presence in fresh stalk does not establish the causal constituent, matched exposure, or a human effect.

fit: raw celery stalk in a human mixed-salad crossover
assessment: Vascular measurements supply exposure context without a rest-tremor endpoint.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide and motor tremor composite
assessment: The off-medication subtotal combines rest with action and postural items. Table II nearly reproduces PDQ-39 and gives baseline means above the stated maximum of 28. A separate baseline sleep row also duplicates depression scores. The rest item remains unverified.

fit: celery included on a Parkinson vegetarian menu
assessment: No ingredient-specific effect or rest-tremor comparison was reported.

fit: Oral butylphthalide and total UPDRS in Parkinson dementia
assessment: Seventy-six randomized participants had total UPDRS reported at 12 weeks. Neither individual rest tremor nor a food exposure was tested.

fit: pepper-leaf tea and Insomnia Severity Index in primary insomnia
assessment: n=30. Day-14 ISI 5.33 with leaves and 5.60 with chamomile, p=.81. Leaves differ from ground peppercorns and the primary insomnia cohort does not identify PD.

fit: oral three-botanical formula with black pepper and PSQI
assessment: 50 adults in a single-arm course reported mean PSQI 12.22 at baseline and 5.30 after week 4. The formula also contains gotu kola and lotus and the study includes no PD subgroup or isolated pepper estimate.

fit: pepper extract and measured mouse sleep under acute caffeine challenge
assessment: Oral pepper extract plus caffeine increased non-REM sleep and lowered wake time versus caffeine alone. EEG gives no extract-only estimate and the intervention and outcome differ from ground pepper and clinical insomnia.

fit: black-pepper-containing turmeric powder and a measured insomnia scale outside Parkinson disease
assessment: All 45 patients received multicomponent dietary advice and were offered Curcuma Latte, containing turmeric and black pepper. Thirty-two had lower Oviedo insomnia scores, with no control arm or pepper-specific dose, processing or outcome contrast. The cohort had rheumatic chronic pain, not Parkinson disease.

fit: oral multiherb formula containing pepper fruit and PSQI in chronic insomnia
assessment: The n=60 open-label trial found within-arm improvement with all three active treatments and between-group post-treatment p=.27. Black pepper was one of twelve botanicals in one arm. No PD subgroup.

fit: lovage in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome
assessment: The menu lists lovage and the motor examination includes gait. The paper reports no stride measurement or separate effect of fresh leaves.

fit: cooked chervil soup allergy case
assessment: Acute allergy symptoms after cooked soup do not establish pain after eating fresh chervil.

fit: methanol extract of culinary chervil in enzyme and cell assays
assessment: Keratinocyte inflammation and enzyme results are not pain severity outcomes.

fit: French tarragon tincture in experimental nociception
assessment: The primary synopsis describes fewer acetic-acid writhes after intraperitoneal 40% and 70% ethanol tincture. This acute animal pain proxy does not measure Parkinson pain or culinary ingestion.

fit: oral tarragon and evoked pain in diabetic rats
assessment: Formalin response improved in both phases after one month. The 2004 and 2006 reports had overlapping investigators and methods and may describe one cohort. Culinary form and Parkinson pain were unresolved.

fit: separate topical tarragon versus sesame oil knee osteoarthritis study
assessment: The registry targets 90 adults and lists WOMAC pain. Recruitment is complete and no verified outcome report was located. The comparator and ethics approval differ from the 2026 almond-oil cohort.

fit: topical tarragon gel and dental injection pain
assessment: The registration separates tarragon-only, jujube-only, combination, lidocaine and vehicle arms. It lists pain three minutes after dental injection and no result. Neither route nor pain source matches the frozen claim.

fit: oral ethanolic tarragon extract and sensory thresholds in diet-induced neuropathy
assessment: Table 3 shows partial normalization of light-touch allodynia and thermal and pressure hypoalgesia after extract. The distinct evoked thresholds do not measure fresh culinary tarragon or spontaneous Parkinson pain.

fit: injected tarragon extract and evoked mouse pain
assessment: The higher tested doses reduced chemical nociceptive responses and increased hot-plate latency. Preparation, route and model differ from the claim.

fit: oral dried tarragon aerial extract and evoked nociception
assessment: Oral aqueous extract lowered evoked formalin scores in fructose-fed rats versus fructose alone. No fresh leaves or human Parkinson pain.

fit: topical tarragon oil extract and human knee osteoarthritis pain
assessment: The randomized trial found lower knee osteoarthritis pain immediately after topical treatment, with no clear later difference. The 2021 registry and paper differ on timing, allocation, schedule and blinding. They describe the same cohort and are counted once.

fit: rosmarinic-acid-rich lemon balm extract and cognitive composites in mild Alzheimer dementia
assessment: The report found no clear group difference on composite cognition and gives no separate intelligibility measure or fresh leaf exposure.

fit: red raspberry vinegar and scheduled blood pressure in an incomplete eight-week trial
assessment: The deposited author abstract says blood pressure was measured; pressure and postural symptom results are absent. The comparison used vinegar and cranberry juice. The body remains open.

fit: Himalayan raspberry consumption and blood pressure in hypertension
assessment: The five-person case series reports lower pressure over time, asymptomatic low readings in three and medication changes in two. It gives no orthostatic test, lightheadedness outcome, species assignment or frozen preparation.

fit: oral raspberry challenge and blood pressure during allergy
assessment: Blood pressure remained normal during a challenge that produced respiratory allergy symptoms in one patient. This case has no orthostatic measurements or Parkinson cohort.

fit: freeze-dried black raspberry slurry and crossover-sequence safety data
assessment: The registry records 0 of 5 participants with serious events and 0 of 5 with other events in each sequence. Each sequence received both treatments. The posted data provide no treatment-specific orthostatic estimate.

fit: frozen raspberry beverage and resting blood pressure
assessment: Flow-mediated dilation improved without a clear central or peripheral BP effect. The healthy-men crossover used drinks made from frozen fruit and did not measure orthostasis.

fit: freeze-dried red raspberry and blood pressure in hypertensive mice
assessment: Systolic pressure was 137 ± 4 mmHg with freeze-dried raspberry and 185 ± 4 mmHg with angiotensin II alone (p < .0001). This mouse model measured induced high blood pressure without an orthostatic endpoint.

fit: freeze-dried raspberry and systolic blood pressure in hypertensive rats
assessment: Final systolic pressure was 20.8% lower than angiotensin II alone (p = .03). A potentially overlapping 2024 report found lower week-seven systolic pressure in raspberry-only and combined berry groups. No orthostatic symptom endpoint was measured.

fit: raspberry snack and resting blood pressure in diabetes
assessment: Four-week raspberry supplementation showed a tendency toward lower resting systolic pressure. There was no standing blood pressure or lightheadedness outcome.

fit: frozen raspberry and seated blood pressure
assessment: The time-by-treatment systolic interaction was p = .03 and treatment main effect p = .37. Neither standing blood pressure nor symptoms were assessed.

fit: freeze-dried raspberry and blackberry and blood pressure in high-fat-fed mice
assessment: Systolic pressure was 98.9 ± 6.25 mmHg with raspberry alone (p < .0001) and 106.0 ± 9.10 with both berries (p = .002), versus 120.6 ± 6.79 with the high-fat, high-sucrose diet alone. Standing symptoms were unmeasured.

fit: canola-containing diet and facial-expression domain in Parkinson disease
assessment: The published Part III motor aggregate included a facial-expression item. The item estimate and canola processing were unavailable. The randomized comparison was between whole diets.

fit: cassia-containing formula and composite oral function in older adults
assessment: The aggregate oral score includes facial expressiveness but item changes were unavailable and the intervention combined 12 botanicals.

fit: possible companion Parkinson-only manometry study
assessment: The 1998 proceedings and investigator bibliography verify the title and page. The original Parkinson-only body and any overlap with the mixed cohort remain open.

fit: mashed potato in a Parkinson manometry study
assessment: Twelve Parkinson participants without dysphagia were tested with mashed potato and water. The reported pressure table pools water only. No potato-specific outcome or baked preparation.

fit: mashed potato as a soft-food questionnaire example
assessment: The questionnaire includes mashed potato in a mixed soft-food category. The study supplies no potato bolus or Parkinson-specific food result.

fit: potato paste swallowing ratings in healthy adults
assessment: Participants reported no clear difference in ease of swallowing across four pastes. The preparations and population differ from the frozen statement.

fit: food-specific boluses during dual-task endoscopy
assessment: White bread caused more observed residue. Green jelly and dyed liquid had more spillage. The overall score differed inconclusively and the study used no potato.

fit: boiled potato instrumental texture tests and classification by healthy older adults
assessment: Boiled potato passed fork cut and failed fork pressure, while healthy older adults placed it across several texture levels. Instrument results and perceived texture do not estimate clinical dysphagia severity.

fit: meal-related cough or choking and bolus texture comparison by diagnosis
assessment: The expanded survey reports mealtime coughing or choking in 24% of 435 Parkinson and 49% of 82 PSP patients. The separate eight-person Parkinson imaging comparison used simulated textures. No baked potato, food-by-case attribution or food-level severity estimate.

fit: soft food category in a Parkinson swallowing questionnaire
assessment: The soft-food response differed across groups while both medians were zero. Mashed potato was an example, and the direct swallow test used water.

fit: water and wafer endoscopy in Parkinson disease
assessment: The study assessed water, thickened water and wafer, without a potato comparison.

fit: clinical videofluoroscopy corpus with Parkinson-coded records
assessment: The public index identifies eight adults under Parkinson or PKD labels. Food-level transcripts require registration. Potato exposure remains unverified.

fit: milk-free mashed potato in Parkinson endoscopic swallowing assessment
assessment: The 24-person study used mashed potato, water and a salted cracker. Table 4 gives four people with aspiration across the assessment and no food-level response or baked potato.

fit: gummy chewing performance and nutrient intake in Parkinson disease
assessment: Ten participants with Parkinson scored 2 versus 6 among 24 comparison participants on the gummy chewing test. The diet questionnaire pools tubers and the paper reports nutrient estimates. It gives no baked-potato-specific result.

fit: starch-thickened contrast and penetration in Parkinson disease
assessment: Pudding-viscosity contrast reduced penetration relative to thinner contrast and increased some residue measures. The study used no potato. The 2019 and 2020 reports share cohort details, and the dissertation likely overlaps.

fit: foil-baked potato sensory variation across cultivars
assessment: A trained sensory panel found that varieties differ under the same foil-wrapped baking procedure.

fit: choking by bolus consistency in a single Parkinson case
assessment: Clinical choking persisted with an unnamed solid after therapy, while liquid and pasty choking were absent at reassessment. No individual food or baked potato was identified.

fit: modified oral food textures and enteral support in one Parkinson case
assessment: The case describes swallowing difficulty and a modified-food plan, without measured change or a baked potato exposure.

fit: caregiver-reported dry and moistened baked potato in Parkinson disease
assessment: A caregiver reported choking with dry baked potato and no difficulty with moistened baked potato in one person. The account gives no clinical confirmation, standardized swallowing assessment, or comparison with foods other than baked potato.

fit: biscuit and liquid boluses with endoscopic airway invasion results
assessment: Five cases underwent endoscopy. Figure 2 gives one penetration with a quarter biscuit, no aspiration with a half biscuit and two liquid conditions with penetration and aspiration. The 20 mL liquid bar total conflicts with cohort size. No potato was tested.

fit: indirect
assessment: Fatal aspiration during eating with food recovered from airway in a woman with Parkinson disease and multifocal stroke. The meal ingredient was unreported, so this gives no estimate for baked potato.

fit: boiled potato food code and diagnosis-level intake
assessment: The 2023 supplement names boiled potato and two 2026 analyses give potato intake by diagnosis. They use one cohort. No baked potato or choking outcome.

fit: earlier Pará food consistency and choking questionnaire
assessment: Five of eight men with Parkinson disease reported choking. Four changed food consistency. No test food was named and overlap with the later 24-person endoscopy cohort is unknown.

fit: named sandwich obstruction and Parkinson diagnosis
assessment: An official inspection documented severe choking during a peanut butter and jelly sandwich meal with bread identified, in a resident with Parkinson disease and dysphagia.

fit: corrected food identity in a Parkinson choking event
assessment: The survey’s meal and witness evidence identifies honeydew where the hospital record described potato. It gives no comparative dysphagia measure.

fit: observed baked potato consumption in a resident with Parkinson disease and dysphagia
assessment: The inspection documents actual baked potato consumption. A family member attributed difficulty during the meal to the chicken nugget coating and described a separate prior choking episode on liquid. No potato-specific swallowing symptom, instrumented outcome or comparison is recorded.

fit: whole baked potato served in a dysphagia care record
assessment: The report documents serving a whole skin-on baked potato. It gives no Parkinson diagnosis for that resident and no potato ingestion or swallowing outcome.

fit: baked-potato soup and chips offered to a person with Parkinson disease and dysphagia
assessment: The inspection identifies the soup on the tray ticket and records the resident beginning the meal. It does not establish soup or chip intake or a swallowing outcome from either item. The agency narrative is publicly mirrored and the original PDF did not open.

fit: potato product on a menu and confirmed chicken obstruction
assessment: The general menu lists baked tater tots. The bolus removed from the resident with Parkinson disease was chicken, and the record gives no potato-linked outcome.

fit: diet records with a derived Parkinson potato-consumption lower bound
assessment: At least 19 of 21 participants with Parkinson disease ate potatoes under the usual rounding of the pooled count. Preparation and swallowing response are unavailable.

fit: distinct food in an autopsy with severe esophageal achalasia
assessment: The primary abstract identifies boiled rice and provides no comparison of swallowing by food or preparation.

fit: combined nutrition intervention and dysphagia prevalence
assessment: In 54 Parkinson clinic patients, dysphagia prevalence fell from 66.7% to 21.7% under a multifaceted program. There was no concurrent control or potato comparison.

fit: swallowing questionnaire in Parkinson disease with broad texture examples
assessment: Thirty-five of 200 scored above 11. Food examples are pooled within questions, and no baked potato comparison or attributable case was reported.

fit: premeal aroma exposure with solid-food swallowing tests
assessment: One Parkinson patient swallowed madeleine, yogurt and water more quickly after combined nasal aroma exposure. The qualitative comparison was inconclusive and no potato was tested.

fit: validation of swallowing questionnaire with named food examples
assessment: Meat and peanuts are examples of challenging foods, and compote is one medication-taking aid. The 19-participant study reports a swallowing subscale and no exposure-specific outcomes.

fit: videofluoroscopy during electrical stimulation
assessment: The thesis and later journal article describe the same small cohort and unnamed paste, solid and liquid boluses.

fit: yogurt and water contrast with bolus-specific aspiration
assessment: Figures report four patients with aspiration on barium-mixed yogurt and three on water. Denominators vary. Unnamed solids were omitted after no elicited swallow. There was no baked-potato comparison.

fit: levodopa response during videofluoroscopy with liquid and solid boluses
assessment: The 22-person report names no foods. The paired contrast estimates medication response.

fit: confirmed scalloped potato obstruction in a different population
assessment: Staff removed scalloped potato and the resident was admitted to intensive care with aspiration pneumonia. The decision lists Down syndrome and dementia, does not identify Parkinson disease, and does not specify the cooking method.

fit: observed preparation of a composite potato meal
assessment: Caregivers prepared a mixed potato and vegetable purée and observed other meal practices. No isolated or baked potato swallowing response was measured.

fit: clinical food textures in Parkinson and parkinsonism
assessment: Thirteen of 43 inpatients had food intake difficulty and received modified meals. The authors observed easier swallowing with semi-gelled textures than watery purees in severe cases. No named food, separate Parkinson count or quantitative swallowing outcome.

fit: fatal choking in a case of parkinsonian syndrome
assessment: The fatal event followed a change from porridge and soft dishes to regular meals. The obstructing food and idiopathic Parkinson diagnosis are unverified.

fit: jelly aspiration and positioning in one Parkinson case
assessment: An unnamed jelly produced penetration and aspiration at 45-degree cervical lordosis but neither at 30 degrees in the same patient. No baked potato, obstructive choking or across-food comparison.

fit: choking during texture-modified meals with multiple comorbidities
assessment: Rice porridge, chopped food and thickened fluid were prescribed before decannulation. The later choking and aspiration events did not identify the obstructing material. Parkinson had been raised in a prior evaluation.

fit: actual choking plus instrumental jelly aspiration in Parkinson
assessment: One patient with Parkinson and cervical osteophytes survived an obstructive choking event with unidentified food. Jelly aspiration and thickened water clearance were separate instrumental observations.

fit: hospital food-choking series including 11 parkinsonism cases
assessment: Of 119 selected incident reports, 11 coded parkinsonism. Choking materials are pooled across all cases and give no ingredient identity or denominator for baked potato. The program synopsis is the same study.

fit: senbei and manju considered feasible after postoperative VF
