assessment: Recognition and spatial tasks favored the oil groups in an ovariectomy and D-galactose model. The preprint and publication describe one study. The report did not assess Parkinson executive function.

fit: whole-fruit mixed menu and unreported executive outcomes
assessment: The same trial registration and publication planned or collected executive tasks. The article and supplement give no result for cognition, and the exposure is whole avocado plus mango.

fit: whole avocado and executive-task MRI and NIH Toolbox registration
assessment: No posted results in available official update, which shows Unknown status. The trial excludes Parkinson disease and assigns fruit rather than oil.

fit: whole avocado crossover with prespecified cognitive measures
assessment: Secondary CANTAB and flanker outcomes are registered without results. The study assigns whole fruit in prediabetes.

fit: maternal avocado oil and rat offspring recognition memory
assessment: Recognition memory improved in offspring of supplemented dams. Developmental exposure and recognition memory do not establish adult clinical executive function.

fit: oral cold-pressed avocado oil and mouse recognition memory
assessment: Oil-fed obese mice preferred the novel object. Figure 3A reports within-group recognition, with no direct treatment contrast shown. It does not test clinical executive function.

fit: avocado-oil mayonnaise in a ketogenic sample menu and narrative executive change
assessment: One Down syndrome and Alzheimer case describes executive change during a mixed diet without an isolated oil comparison, oil processing or quantified executive outcome.

fit: flaxseed oil compared with corn oil and registered executive composite
assessment: The mild cognitive impairment pilot defines a composite using Trail Making, digit span and category fluency. No posted results, pressing method or Parkinson intervention.

fit: oral Pazze flaxseed oil chow and fear extinction
assessment: The dissertation reports a diet main effect p = .726 during fear extinction. The task concerns aversive memory and cannot estimate Parkinson executive function.

fit: pooled omega-3 supplementation and cognitive trajectories by matched observational groups
assessment: MMSE, ADAS-Cog13 and CDR-SB had faster decline in pooled supplement users. No separate flaxseed oil estimate or processing specification. Observational confounding and whole-scale outcomes limit transfer.

fit: flaxseed table oil and executive function in healthy older adults
assessment: The flaxseed arm improved 0.30 on phonemic fluency versus 0.03 with corn oil (p = .049), with lower baseline fluency in the flaxseed arm. The total Frontal Assessment Battery comparison was p = .142. The trial had no Parkinson participants or documented pressing method.

fit: isolated marine fatty acids and Parkinson depression
assessment: The small DHA and EPA trial reported more Hamilton Depression Rating Scale responders than corn oil. No whole trout or poached preparation was assigned.

fit: supplied trout and the Geriatric Depression Scale
assessment: The adjusted GDS-15 contrast in 96 randomized adults was −0.17 (95% CI −0.48 to 0.15, p = .295). The trial does not identify the cooking method, species or a Parkinson population.

fit: whole trout and registered emotion outcome
assessment: Registered childhood and family intervention measures 12-week emotion score. Results are unposted and there is no Parkinson or poached-trout depression outcome.

fit: trout among options and depression score
assessment: Advice to eat fatty fish raised the depression score estimate in men with angina, with an interval crossing zero. Trout was one option and intake could be replaced by fish oil.

fit: fish oil and clinician-rated Parkinson depression
assessment: Fish oil improved two clinician-rated depression scales in a small Parkinson trial. Beck Depression Inventory results were inconclusive. The source fish was unspecified.

fit: EPA-rich and DHA-rich fish-oil capsules and depressive symptoms in older adults with mild cognitive impairment
assessment: Six-month primary depression score change favored DHA-rich capsules by 1.40 points and EPA-rich capsules by 1.23 points versus safflower oil after one improving control participant was excluded. Fifty were randomized and 40 completed. No poached trout or Parkinson cohort was studied.

fit: marine omega-3 capsules and depression risk
assessment: Marine capsules increased incident depression or clinically relevant symptoms in VITAL-DEP, with an inconclusive mean PHQ-8 change. The population and exposure differ from the claim.

fit: self-reported Parkinson urgency with mixed broccoli and white mustard tea
assessment: The 2021 eight-completer pilot reported better urgency and frequency. The 2024 report gives 13 of 14 with urgency attenuation and transient worsening in some participants exceeding the usual schedule. Participant overlap is unknown. Neither uncontrolled report isolates mustard or quantifies urgency frequency attributable to it.

fit: mustard constituent and voiding interval in rats
assessment: Intravesical allyl isothiocyanate increased voiding frequency. The experimental direction opposes the premise at the proxy level, but the direct bladder route did not measure human urgency or ground mustard ingestion.

fit: freeze-dried blackberry powder and executive-related tests in older adults
assessment: Fluid cognition composite p=.04 without a specified arm contrast. The poster reports no significant treatment effect on virtual-maze flexibility. An executive-domain estimate and independent reproduction remain open.

fit: blackberry diet and spatial working memory in aged rats
assessment: Short-term Morris water maze performance improved. The source is an aging animal model and exact diet preparation remains open.

fit: mixed thawed blackberry smoothie and executive task outcomes
assessment: Task switching had a treatment-by-session response-time interaction p = .001, but no clear treatment main effect. The healthy-adult drink used four fruits.

fit: multicomponent capsule including blackberry and executive testing
assessment: The capsule includes blackberry among numerous dehydrated fruit and vegetable ingredients. Favorable within-period TESEN changes do not isolate blackberry, a frozen preparation, or diagnosed Parkinson disease.

fit: aqueous marjoram extract and drug-induced catalepsy
assessment: Extract reduced time on the forced posture assay. The test does not rate dystonia severity in Parkinson disease.

fit: fresh orange juice versus coffee in surgical bowel recovery
assessment: The preprint reports 73 hours to first bowel movement with juice versus 47.5 with coffee, p < .001. Linked registry estimates 80, whereas preprint reports 476. No untreated comparison.

fit: orange scent conditioned cue in rat alcohol seeking
assessment: Original and linked journal reports share the cue statistic. The scent formulation is unspecified. It was not eaten, and the experiment measured conditioned lever responding rather than constipation.

fit: orange item and Rome III constipation in Brazilian older adults
assessment: Constipation was reported in 31/120 consumers versus 9/19 nonconsumers (unadjusted p=.054). The survey gives no confirmed raw preparation, adjusted effect, severity change or separate Parkinson cohort.

fit: orange-pomace beverage outside Parkinson disease
assessment: Stool frequency (p = .0281) and softer stool (p = .04) favored added pomace. Gas and bloating increased. NCT02979496 lists constipation severity, but its separate score result was unavailable.

fit: orange frequency and Bristol stool form in university students
assessment: The separate reported sample of 1,144 students gives orange p=.001 without a directional cross-tab. It excluded diagnosed constipation and diarrhea. Orange preparation and Parkinson constipation severity were outside the study design.

fit: blended orange and other fruits with physical therapy in Chagas megacolon
assessment: Constipation scores fell in 11 of 12 participants after six weeks (paired p<.0022). Four reported bloating or flatulence with the drink. The study groups multiple ingredients with physical therapy and has no control or Parkinson population. The 2010 thesis abstract describes the same cohort.

fit: pooled fresh fruit frequency and a binary constipation category
assessment: Daily fresh fruit was associated with the authors’ constipation category. The definition used non-daily or missing bowel reports, and raw oranges and constipation severity were not estimated.

fit: shared orange flavor in a Parkinson constipation trial
assessment: Weekly bowel movements favored the probiotic and prebiotic formulation. Orange flavor was present in both arms, and no raw-fruit effect was estimated.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1323 administers mixed orange–lemon juice before imaging in a 24-person pancreatic study. P1611 uses orange juice to check a pH device. Xylenol orange is a dye.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: P305 combines orange juice and germinated legumes against folic acid or apple juice and measures folate and plasma metabolites. The matrix contrast does not estimate raw orange and the named Parkinson symptom.

fit: orange juice as rescue during closed-loop insulin delivery
assessment: Orange juice was offered on four occasions when glucose was below 60 mg/dL. The study concerns insulin control, without a matched raw-fruit exposure or related Parkinson symptom outcome.

fit: carotenoid food recalls and macular pigment measurements
assessment: The participant records name several food sources and the authors report no detected association with optical pigment density. No assigned food preparation or relevant Parkinson symptom was measured.

fit: orange juice during two episodes of symptomatic hypoglycemia
assessment: A patient with diabetes and end-stage kidney disease had symptom relief after juice at two low glucose measurements. This is one case with a different product and cause, without raw-orange falls or constipation measurement.

fit: pasteurized orange juice products and stool frequency in healthy adults
assessment: Forty-eight adults consumed regular or levan-enriched lower-sugar orange juice. Table 3 reports p=.02 for time and p=.79 for product by time. Both arms received juice. This does not estimate the effect of raw whole oranges on Parkinson constipation.

fit: oranges and upper gastrointestinal symptoms outside Parkinson disease
assessment: The survey gives no constipation severity estimate.

fit: uncontrolled immature trifoliate orange extract in neurogenic bowel
assessment: Constipation score moved from 4.60 to 3.48 in 25 patients after two weeks (p = .04). No concurrent group; the plant, formulation and population differ from raw sweet orange in Parkinson disease.

fit: pasteurized orange juice and a bowel diary in ten healthy women
assessment: The baseline and day-60 ordinal frequency scores were 1.40 and 1.40. The reported diary comparisons were inconclusive across periods. A sequential design without a concurrent group cannot isolate the juice effect.

fit: whole raw orange, pomace comparators and acute glycemia
assessment: A 227 g Navel serving provided 5 g fiber, also delivered in a pomace treatment. The outcomes were glucose and insulin over two hours.

fit: orange reported in a Parkinson food frequency survey
assessment: The survey records orange frequency among 40 people with Parkinson disease. It gives no preparation or constipation outcome.

fit: orange-pomace beverage outside Parkinson disease
assessment: Primary stool-frequency interaction p = .46. Table S7 gives product main effect p = .004 for at least one no-movement day, with p = .40 for the interaction and a baseline imbalance. The prose gives p = .002.

fit: initial encounter constipation records and medicinal citrus prescriptions
assessment: The hospital study reports constipation in 1,022 of 3,206 initial encounters and counts Citrus aurantium entries in mixed decoctions. Records give prescription and symptom frequencies without measured citrus consumption or a constipation change.

fit: unprepared orange intake frequency and categorical Bristol stool form
assessment: The 100-person adult cross-sectional survey gives Pearson chi-square 56.548 on 35 df (p=.012). The cells and direction are unavailable. Parkinson disease and constipation severity were outside the study design.

fit: paprika xanthophyll and athlete endurance rather than everyday fatigue
assessment: Full-sample xanthophyll-alone versus placebo did not separate the lactate or heart-rate endpoints. Low-baseline-NAD subgroup findings are endurance proxies. The paper gives no subjective everyday-fatigue estimate or raw pepper intervention.

fit: red paprika xanthophyll drink and perceived postexercise fatigue
assessment: Subjective fatigue after treadmill exercise declined more with the extract in 14 athletes. Neither raw pepper nor Parkinson fatigue was tested.

fit: isolated capsinoid crossover and exercise metabolism
assessment: The preprint and journal abstract report a shift toward fat oxidation after exercise and inconclusive glycogen restoration. The strongly matched registry and publications describe one likely cohort and give no participant-rated clinical fatigue estimate.

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking
assessment: Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

fit: purified dihydrocapsiate in canola carrier and perceived exercise fatigue
assessment: A crossover compared 12 mg dihydrocapsiate in canola oil to cellulose placebo during cycling in adults with overweight or obesity. No perceived-fatigue difference was reported. This provides no raw bell pepper or isolated canola oil estimate.

fit: paprika xanthophyll with preregistered fatigue outcome not reported
assessment: The registry lists fatigue VAS as a secondary measure. The accessible respiratory report with 21 participants gives no separate fatigue estimate.

fit: paprika extract and everyday fatigue in a completed trial
assessment: The official registry lists 23 enrolled rather than its target 30, 9 mg daily extract or placebo for eight weeks, and an everyday fatigue VAS. Neither arm results nor a matching original report could be verified.

fit: walnut oil in a Parkinson diet menu with composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A names walnut oil and the motor examination includes bradykinesia. The paper gives no preparation, isolated oil exposure or bradykinesia item result.

fit: dietary cold-pressed walnut oil and locomotion in toxin-exposed flies
assessment: Cold-pressed walnut oil improved climbing relative to rotenone alone at both follow-ups, a movement signal opposite the frozen clinical direction in this model. The assay does not measure bradykinesia in people.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S2.146 and S9.719 study isolated resveratrol in pea mitochondria or rat nerve recovery. S9.660 identifies grapes as one source. Grape snail is unrelated terminology.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-07-009 and P-14-003 work with grape pomace or plant extracts. P-18-008 studies isolated resveratrol in old rat skeletal muscle. No dietary grape comparison measures Parkinson anxiety or rigidity.

fit: red grape juice and rotations in a separate 6-OHDA rat study
assessment: There were six rats per arm. Juice and juice with treadmill exercise reduced apomorphine-induced rotations relative to their own baselines. The reported paired tests do not estimate the juice-vs-lesion treatment effect. The study does not assess muscle rigidity and tests juice rather than frozen grapes.

fit: oral hydroalcoholic red grape seed extract and an ordinal rigidity proxy in 6-OHDA rats
assessment: Figure 2B reports a lower muscle-stiffness score after grape-seed extract relative to untreated and vehicle-treated lesioned groups (p<.01). The extract does not match whole frozen grapes and the endpoint is a rat behavioral proxy.

fit: juice plus exercise
assessment: The two papers describe one registered study. Juice supplied no clear added functional or cognitive benefit.

fit: clinical case or dietary history without a matched ingredient comparison
assessment: A restricted diet history includes a grape or olive. Grape-like morphology occurs elsewhere. The case supplies no grape-controlled comparative effect.

fit: cold-pressed topical coconut oil and childhood enuresis
assessment: A pediatric trial reported fewer bedwetting episodes with topical coconut versus paraffin. The trial excluded urgency and abnormal frequency. Its topical procedure and population differ from the frozen claim.

fit: self-reported coconut oil frequency and total Parkinson symptom score
assessment: The cross-sectional composite association specifies no virgin oil and does not count urinary urgency episodes.

fit: virgin coconut oil in a whole diet with a Parkinson urinary item
assessment: A ketogenic menu naming virgin coconut oil had a 0.70-point larger decrease on a multi-symptom urinary item. The trial did not resolve an independent oil effect or count urgency episodes.

fit: dried sage leaf capsules and cognitive or salivation outcomes
assessment: The grant report and 2010 investigator account describe one cohort. The posted attachment lacks its referenced secondary-outcome timetable. Neither account gives a fatigue estimate.

fit: one adverse-event case mentioning sage and fatigue
assessment: Four public FDA report versions trace to one case with multiple exposures, unspecified sage preparation, and no listed Parkinson diagnosis. The report does not attribute fatigue specifically to sage.

fit: dry sage extract and menopausal exhaustion
assessment: The post-treatment exhaustion comparison was inconclusive (p = .634) despite a within-group decrease. The trial does not identify fatigue in Parkinson disease.

fit: sage-containing beverage mixtures and acute mental fatigue
assessment: Two of three extract mixtures containing sage had lower task fatigue in healthy adults. The study did not isolate sage.

fit: two sage extracts and perceived exertion during cycling
assessment: Perceived exertion was 0.3 points lower with the mixture. The exercise endpoint, exposure and population differ from the claim.

fit: sage extract and fatigue in an uncontrolled menopause series
assessment: The within-group fatigue rating fell from 3.07 to 2.23. The study used an extract, lacked a concurrent control and gives no Parkinson result.

fit: common-sage extract chemistry and antiproliferative experiment
assessment: The author abstract confirms sage-derived extracts and chemical and cancer cell endpoints. P33 references this same report. It provides no culinary dose or Parkinson symptom comparison.

fit: Spanish sage essential oil and acute task fatigue in healthy adults
assessment: Planned comparisons after the single-dose crossover found less task fatigue on three of six repetitions at one hour and five of six at four hours. The species, oil and outcome differ from fresh culinary sage and Parkinson fatigue.

fit: concentrated fresh sage leaf extract and composite menopausal exhaustion
assessment: Exhaustion fell 0.8 points in the uncontrolled series. The item combines physical and cognitive complaints. Extract, single-arm design and menopause limit transfer to Parkinson fatigue.

fit: fresh sage tip extract and secondary menopause fatigue ratings
assessment: Secondary POMS fatigue favored fresh-sage-tip extract (p=.029), without a separately identified arm-by-time fatigue table. Menopause exhaustion improved nominally, while a separate sleep-exhaustion item was unchanged. Extract tablet, multiplicity and population limit transfer.

fit: Isolated cardamonin and general movement in mouse parkinsonism
assessment: Author abstract describes improved general motor activity with an isolated compound. The food preparation and a separate resting tremor measure are absent from the verified abstract. Publisher body remains open.

fit: cardamom listed in multicomponent Parkinson diet and composite UPDRS III
assessment: The composite improved and includes rest tremor. The authors did not report the tremor items separately or isolate cardamom.

fit: low
assessment: An infant exposed to mixed green anise and star anise infusion had acute systemic illness with seizures and nystagmus. The mixture and pediatric setting provide no ingredient-specific result or visual hallucination frequency in Parkinson’s.

fit: self-reported coconut oil use and overall PD symptom progression
assessment: Unreviewed observational preprint gives mixed-model total PRO-PD progression association, not an oil-grade or dream-enactment estimate; co-use and multiple tests limit inference.

fit: unspecified coconut oil and the self-rated REM behavior item
assessment: Inverse sign in the displayed baseline pair. The item gives no episode count, grade or within-participant change.

fit: self-reported coconut oil frequency and total Parkinson symptom score
assessment: The cross-sectional composite association gives no oil grade or dream-enactment frequency and cannot establish causation.

fit: ketogenic diet and one participant's reported sleep behavior; oil exposure unverified
assessment: Participant 008 reported ongoing episodes and little overall diet change, while a companion perceived less movement. The report identifies coconut or avocado oil use for participant 019, not 008; no virgin-oil exposure or before-after event count is established.

fit: thyme oil constituents and experimental cholinergic measures
assessment: The original abstract concerns synaptic and receptor effects of thyme oil and constituents. It supplies no human attention score or effect of fresh thyme consumption.

fit: isolated thymol and attention-related behavior in a juvenile rat model
assessment: The original author abstract describes favorable behavior. Task estimates, original methods and the 2023 correction content remain unresolved.

fit: dried thyme and perceived memory
assessment: The trial reports a self-rated memory score. There was no objective attention task, fresh preparation or Parkinson’s subgroup.

fit: isolated thymol and Y-maze alternation after propionic acid in rats
assessment: Isolated thymol increased spontaneous alternation 35% relative to model controls, a working-memory proxy. No fresh thyme or clinical attention measure.

fit: pinto among cooked bean rotation and signed stool changes
assessment: The pooled whole bean group more often reported increased stool frequency and short-term softening than rice; it also reported bloating. Pinto-specific constipation severity, Parkinson diagnosis and dietary attribution remain open.

fit: canned pinto and canned green bean crossover and stool-change questionnaire
assessment: The small crossover found no clear difference in combined stool changes. The preparation was canned and there was no clinical constipation direction or Parkinson group.

fit: mixed cooked pulses and constipation severity
assessment: An apparently linked conference abstract reports lower constipation severity after a rotation including pinto beans. This single-arm study cannot separate individual pulses or provide a Parkinson comparison.

fit: canned pinto beans and participant-reported stool changes
assessment: Pinto phases produced reports of stool changes, combined without a dependable constipation direction. The beans were canned and participants were outside Parkinson cohorts.

fit: cinnamon intake as a group-visit dietary outcome
assessment: OA15.04 reports increased cinnamon intake in a 155-person randomized group-visit dietary secondary analysis for adults with chronic pain and depression; preparation and an isolated cinnamon symptom effect are not reported. The claim seeks ground cinnamon and walking slowness.

fit: oral ground C.verum and movement outcomes after acute MPTP in mice
assessment: Ground cinnamon started three hours after MPTP and favored seven-day rotarod and open-field movement versus vehicle; Figure8 gives six mice/group. This early post-insult motor signal supports a limited favorable bridge without a clinical gait-speed estimate. Benzoate was a separate arm.

fit: oral ground C.verum and motor proxies after acute MPTP in mice
assessment: Ground cinnamon 100 mg/kg/day began three hours after MPTP for seven days. Figure 8 (six mice/group) favors powder for rotarod and rearing/grooming in Gfap-cre littermates. Rotarod genotype-by-treatment p=.021 supports the reported GDNF dependence; rearing/grooming interactions were inconclusive. Early post-insult motor evidence supports limited favorable transfer, not clinical gait velocity. Separate benzoate arms and cell experiments are not patient comparisons.

fit: oral ground C.verum and timed motor proxies in aged A53T mice
assessment: Ground cinnamon 100 mg/kg/day for 60 days favored rotarod and shorter pole turning/descent times versus vehicle in aged A53T mice; Figure 4 gives five or six/group. These timed agility/slowness proxies support a minimal favorable bridge without establishing clinical gait velocity. The 2025 correction replaces duplicated Figure 6 benzoate histology panels, not Figure 4 motor results; retain the reliability caveat and same-program dependence.

fit: canola, olive and fish oil feasibility trial and registered pain VAS
assessment: Official record links a design matching the existing P49 report. Result fields are empty and dose wording differs. Registry adds methods, not an independent trial.

fit: oral liquid canola oil and osteoarthritis pain
assessment: The three-arm 30-person feasibility study found no clear between-group difference in secondary measures that included pain. The abstract does not state cold-pressed grade.

fit: Sunola fish oil blend and clinical pain, plant identity unresolved
assessment: Primary report names Sunola and changes fish oil dose. Lead investigator used canola in an interview. Product plant identity remains unresolved.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Bot's rapeseed/MCT capsule and the Jazayeri rapeseed/fluoxetine comparator are separate families. Their depression endpoints and unverified oil processing supply no frozen effect estimate.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Rapeseed oil is a component of the multi-food SYSDIET comparison; ALA source discussion is supplementary. It is not an isolated grade-specific contrast for the frozen symptom.

fit: rapeseed and other foods in a Mediterranean diet with rheumatoid arthritis pain
assessment: Pain VAS favored the bundle. Cooking oils, formulated spread and foods changed together. No pressing grade.

fit: canola active comparator and osteoarthritis pain
assessment: Original abstract and secondary extraction distinguish the inconclusive COAT pain contrast and missing primary table. Grade and oil-free comparator unavailable.

fit: raw, steamed and boiled Brussels sprout volatiles
assessment: Sulfides changed with preparation, but roasting and human smell ability were not tested.

fit: thawed Brussels sprout sampling and retronasal flavor
assessment: The sprouts were not roasted. Change in liking did not track retronasal intensity for this vegetable; olfactory impairment was not assessed.

fit: microwave-cooked Brussels sprouts in healthy sensory panel
assessment: Retronasal odor liking related to food liking. No roasted exposure or clinical olfactory impairment.

fit: raw and cooked Brussels sprout volatiles
assessment: Food volatile differences do not measure the ability to smell after eating.

fit: oral avocado oil comparator and written symbol-count task
assessment: The timed symbol substitution test reports accuracy and completion, with 90 seconds in journal Methods and 60 in the registry and protocol. Scores increased in both arms. The report gives no character size or clinical micrographia measurement and no refined oil specification.

fit: black pepper oil odor and whole saliva secretion
assessment: The author abstract reports higher saliva output after black pepper oil odor. Sixty healthy students were randomized to oil odors or water. The complete tables, clinical drooling and culinary ingestion remain outside the verified result.

fit: whole pepper aroma and combined capsaicin care
assessment: Combined treatment was stopped in one patient after drooling increased. No Parkinson diagnosis, cracked pepper ingestion, or independent pepper effect.

fit: spinach-enriched chow and conditioned eyeblink learning
assessment: Aged rats showed better conditioned eyeblink learning after spinach-enriched chow. This reflex is distinct from spontaneous facial expressiveness.

fit: spinach listed in a mixed Parkinson diet and total motor score
assessment: The menu lists spinach but gives no individual intake or cooked preparation. Total UPDRS III includes facial expression, while no separately reported item or isolated spinach result is available.

fit: chervil in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome
assessment: The menu lists chervil and the motor examination includes rigidity. The paper does not establish fresh chervil exposure or report item-level rigidity change.

fit: pooled fish intake and overactive bladder
assessment: Higher fish intake was associated with lower odds of a composite overactive bladder outcome in NHANES. Grilled sardines and urgency without leakage were not separated.

fit: oily fish category and Parkinson urinary score
assessment: Parkinson clinical records include pooled oily fish and the SCOPA urinary domain. The paper does not estimate a fish-specific association or separate urgency.

fit: extra-virgin olive oil in a multidomain trial with planned insomnia scale
assessment: Table 1 recommends extra-virgin olive oil in the MIND dietary component and the schedule includes the Insomnia Severity Index. Older adults at dementia risk are the study population. Posted outcomes and oil-specific effects remain open.

fit: oral ungraded olive oil comparator and primary insomnia sleep scores
assessment: Sleep diary efficiency in the olive-oil arm was 81.5% to 85.1%. The comparison uses an active mixture in the other arm and cannot isolate the oil effect or extra-virgin grade.

fit: refined olive-oil placebo and actigraphy in healthy adults
assessment: The oil arm was explicitly refined. Its actigraphy includes measured sleep latency and efficiency, but the comparators were marine oils, with no Parkinson insomnia.

fit: topical extra-virgin oil and PSQI in dialysis patients
assessment: The local thesis extract records 42 oil and 39 saline participants versus 86 planned. Adjusted four-week PSQI changes were −2.863 and +0.126 within arms. No direct between-arm coefficient is reported in the table. The oil was applied to itchy skin.

fit: shared olive-oil advice and sleep adverse events during Parkinson diet phases
assessment: Table 3 lists mild intermittent insomnia during the ketogenic phase as possibly related to the overall diet. The MCT phase lists a separate serious insomnia and psychosis event after deep brain stimulation, judged unrelated. Phase completion and post-visit counts differ. Olive oil was encouraged in both diets with no isolated effect on insomnia severity.

fit: topical ozonized extra-virgin olive oil and pressure wound resolution
assessment: The paired human wound comparison reports no significant resolution difference between topical oils. It does not address dietary cold-pressed or extra-virgin oil or a Parkinson symptom.

fit: topical extra-virgin oil comparator and rat wound microbiology
assessment: No difference between the topical product groups was detected for microbial colonization. The population, route and endpoint differ from the frozen claim.

fit: topical extra-virgin olive oil comparator and rat tail withdrawal
assessment: The different topical products gave no significant separation in thermal latency. Sample independence from the related microbial abstract is unresolved, and the model supplies no oral oil or Parkinson symptom estimate.

fit: olive oil as part of Mediterranean diet adherence by young volunteers
assessment: Among female respondents, anxiety was inversely associated with total diet adherence. Olive oil is a dietary component and its isolated effect, oil grade and Parkinson fit remain unverified.

fit: olive-oil-enriched diet and incretin response in normal rats
assessment: The early GLP-1 increment was higher, and glucose tolerance improved at day 36. Gut tissue GLP-1 content was comparable at day 50. The original congress report and paper are one family. Bowel motility and oil grade were unverified.

fit: olive-oil-enriched diet in a separate streptozotocin rat model
assessment: The rat cohort had greater acute GLP-1 release with oil but lower chronic weight gain, lower intestinal GLP-1 content and no improvement in oral glucose tolerance. The outcome and model do not answer the frozen symptom.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Separate depression comparator studies use olive oil and olive oil ethyl esters. The diet trial additionally contains extra-virgin olive oil alongside other foods. No indicated preparation-specific Parkinson anxiety or insomnia outcome.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: MS food-intake reporting and a hydroxytyrosol animal study are distinct exposures. Neither assigns matched oil grade and Parkinson outcomes.

fit: olive oil within a supplied 28-day Mediterranean diet
assessment: In 22 men, systolic pressure was lower after the mixed diet. No ingredient-specific comparison or bowel, anxiety or insomnia outcome was reported.

fit: olive-oil comparator capsules for a fish-oil metabolic study
assessment: The olive-oil group was an active dietary comparator, with no oil-free arm and no matched symptom measure.

fit: structured lipid blend including olive oil in a mouse diet
assessment: A modified mixture containing olive oil, soy oil and crambe oil was studied. It cannot identify an isolated olive-oil effect or any of these symptoms.

fit: different olive-oil feed matrices and mouse liver proteome
assessment: Fat dose and matrix differ between the mouse diets. Reported metabolic and hepatic findings do not establish an oil-preparation or clinical symptom direction.

fit: olive oil in a composite dietary score among older coronary patients
assessment: The outcome is reported by Mediterranean dietary score and diabetes status. No grade, oil-specific estimate or Parkinson symptom result was reported.

fit: dietary questionnaire grouped by fat sensitivity
assessment: The original fat-sensitivity and food-frequency poster lists olive oil. Its grade is unspecified and it estimates dietary reports by sensory group without the frozen symptom comparison.

fit: cannabis in olive-oil vehicle and acute drowsiness in headache
assessment: The primary abstract compares active cannabis formulations. Short-term drowsiness is described in the alternate transcription. There is no plain-oil comparison, confirmed grade, or measured insomnia outcome.

fit: extra-virgin oil item and cross-sectional sleep score
assessment: Two consumption items were inversely associated with poor sleep score in bivariate analysis. No assigned preparation or Parkinson insomnia result.

fit: lycopene-enriched oil and nocturnal actigraphy
assessment: Nighttime activity declined in both groups while duration and depth did not clearly change. Both groups received fortified oil.

fit: whole Mediterranean score and self-reported insomnia
assessment: Fox Table 2 gives a MEDI-score insomnia coefficient of -1.07 with Holm-adjusted p=.02. The separate unspecified olive oil items estimate total PRO-PD only. The study cannot determine any effect of extra-virgin oil on insomnia.

fit: shared ungraded olive carrier and insomnia severity in a two-dose case series
assessment: The three-person higher-dose group had a within-group ISI change at day 60 (p=.03). The cohort compares two active cannabis doses in olive oil, without olive-only or olive-free group, so the association cannot identify oil direction.

fit: separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context
assessment: P0635 uses olive-oil-containing intravenous emulsion in hospital nutrition. Route, mixed composition and endpoints differ from oral olive oil in the frozen claim.

fit: oat bran comparator with cognition measurements
assessment: Official protocol lists oat bran powder and a different active comparator. No posted results, cooked whole oats or separate hand dexterity test.

fit: oatmeal and total Parkinson symptom burden
assessment: The survey reports an inconclusive composite association and no separate dexterity measure.

fit: green oat extract and computer tracking in healthy adults
assessment: Some cursor-tracking results favored extract, without clinical dexterity testing or cooked oats in Parkinson's.

fit: combined flaxseed-derived omega-3 and vitamin E with Parkinson total score
assessment: The aggregate change favored the combination. The first public registry omitted UPDRS and specified a different dose and clinic. The 2019 revision postdates the paper. No rigidity item, verified cold pressing or oil-only comparison.

fit: independent combined flaxseed-derived omega-3 and vitamin E trial in Parkinson disease
assessment: Part III mean changes were −1.9 and +3.1, with p=.05 as printed and no clear part-level benefit in the authors’ interpretation. No separate rigidity, verified oil pressing or oil-only estimate.

fit: plasma alpha-linolenic acid and the examiner-rated Parkinson rigidity item
assessment: Rigidity correlated inversely with ALA in the age-adjusted analysis (ρ = −.331, p = .046), with a weaker sex-adjusted estimate (ρ = −.278, p = .096). The small cross-sectional cohort provides no oil ingestion comparison.

fit: possible cold-pressed flaxseed blend in an uncontrolled combined Parkinson regimen
assessment: Case 4 describes less rigidity and Case 5 less arm stiffness after an oral and intravenous regimen. Product exposure at case level and an independent oil effect are unresolved.

fit: baked eggplant acute adverse case with a different endpoint
assessment: The reported acute allergy supplies no dystonia outcome and does not isolate roasted eggplant.

fit: eggplant extract in a rotenone cell model
assessment: Oxidative and cell-survival results do not measure dystonia or roasted eggplant exposure.

fit: raw carrot aroma stimulus and trained panel ratings
assessment: Characterizing raw carrot aroma did not test a change in eater olfactory impairment.

fit: clinical olfaction and nutrient-density comparison in newly diagnosed Parkinson disease
assessment: The case-control study assessed smell identification and dietary nutrient density without isolating raw carrot as an exposure.

fit: carrot frequency model and independent rhinitis-olfaction model
assessment: The carrot odds-ratio text is inconsistent, and the separate rhinitis-to-smell association does not establish a carrot effect. Preparation, temporality and Parkinson applicability remain unresolved.

fit: coriander listed among seasonings of a mixed Parkinson vegetarian diet
assessment: The diet lists coriander without confirming plant part, dried preparation or consumption; there is no post-treatment drooling outcome or isolated ingredient effect.

fit: living coriander plant exposure and salivary analyte concentrations
assessment: There was no ingestion or reported salivary flow or clinical drooling measure; biochemical saliva concentrations are different outcomes.

fit: pea protein in a mixed sachet and registered walking speed
assessment: Plant blend, whey and control sarcopenia protocol specifies six-meter walking speed. No posted results or sample taking cooked peas alone.

fit: pea proteins among several active ingredients and gait within SPPB
assessment: Completed prototype powder trial with separate ingredients and no posted results. Does not test whole cooked peas or Parkinson gait.

fit: pea beverage and registered walking tasks after resistance exercise
assessment: Three beverages combined with exercise and timed gait assessments in older adults. Recruiting and no posted results. No cooked-pea Parkinson comparison.

fit: isolated pea lectin and forced stepping in rats
assessment: The paraquat plus pea lectin group had a lower forced-stepping score. The lectin-only group had no clear decrease. No cooked peas or human walking speed were tested.

fit: isolated lectin and forced forelimb placement
assessment: The combined paraquat and lectin arm developed forelimb placement deficits. No cooked peas or human walking velocity was measured.

fit: Green-tea polyphenols and aggregate motor outcome
assessment: The registry has no posted results. The investigator deck links the same trial and gives no separate rest-tremor result. The funder describes total UPDRS under the delayed-start design. This is a green-tea extract.

fit: Tea use and on- and off-levodopa motor examinations in Taiwan
assessment: The registry records unspecified tea use and UPDRS III in both medication states. There is no posted result, black-tea preparation or stated tea-by-rest item analysis.

fit: Black tea questionnaire and Parkinson motor examination in PROBE-PD
assessment: The study records black tea and clinical rest tremor. No registry results are posted. A 2024 prevalence abstract and 2026 insecticide preprint supply no black-tea rest-severity result.

fit: Black tea intake and incidence in the Singapore Chinese Health Study
assessment: The highest intake category had adjusted relative risk 0.29 (95% CI 0.13–0.67) for incident Parkinson disease. Tremor enters diagnosis, with no severity estimate after disease onset.

fit: Black tea as a shared or optional beverage in a clinical breath-test protocol
assessment: Tremor was recorded in clinical assessment, but the beverage options were unassigned and reported analyses are not tea-specific.

fit: Black tea with carbamazepine and induced tremor onset in rats
assessment: Mean onset was 2.60 minutes with black tea versus 1.40 with water in the drug-treated groups. Significance notation compares with challenge alone. This is induced-seizure tremor rather than Parkinson rest severity.

fit: Isolated caffeine and total Parkinson motor responder outcome
assessment: Twenty-one days yielded 12/15 versus 2/12 total motor responders. Baseline categories differ and the adverse-event denominator conflicts across sections. Tea was restricted. Rest tremor measured within the test is not separately reported.

fit: black tea frequencies and separate rest tremor history in a Parkinson database protocol
assessment: The official questionnaire separates black tea type, frequency and duration from a yes/no rest tremor history field. The protocol gives no planned tea-specific model, brewing method, severity estimate or reported tea–tremor result.

fit: isolated caffeine and Parkinson rest tremor in single-group dose escalation
assessment: The first two weeks showed a within-group reduction of 1.18 rest-tremor points (SD 2.4, p=.01), and worsening parkinsonian or physiological tremors were among reasons for discontinuation. No concurrent group or assignment to black tea.

fit: randomized caffeine and UPDRS III rest tremor in Parkinson disease
assessment: The week-three rest tremor contrast was −0.32 points (95% interval −0.73 to 0.10) and week six was −0.28 (−0.83 to 0.27). The intervention was isolated caffeine.

fit: caffeine capsule randomization and daily-living tremor in Parkinson patients
assessment: The six-month trial found inconclusive individual MDS-UPDRS II comparisons. Overall adverse events occurred in 29/60 versus 31/61. The main text lists tremulousness among queried events without giving its count. The registered record has no posted results and the separate examination rest item remains unavailable.

fit: Reported black tea intake and composite PRO-PD burden
assessment: Adjusted +8.4 points per frequency-category step (95% CI −2.5 to +19.3). The contrast is cross-sectional, with no separate rest-item coefficient or brewing method.

fit: coffee consumption and clinician-rated rest tremor in newly diagnosed Parkinson disease
assessment: Rest tremor 1.49 versus 2.41 raw mean points in ever coffee drinkers versus nondrinkers, adjusted p=.001. The adjusted dose gradient was clear in men only. The beverage is coffee.

fit: acute oral caffeine and coffee perception in tremor
assessment: Six percent of Parkinson survey respondents perceived worse tremor after coffee. A separate acute oral caffeine test reported no increase. PubMed and publisher HTML differ in listed assessment times. Full body, groups and separate rest outcome remain open.

fit: regular black tea in Parkinson disease with daily-living motor composite
assessment: LRRK2 subgroups show lower log MDS-UPDRS II composite levels, with inconclusive idiopathic comparisons. The questionnaire's tremor item is not examination-rated rest tremor, and no black-tea item contrast was supplied.

fit: measured caffeine variation and constituent load in brewed black tea
assessment: Ayakdaş and Ağagündüz used chromatography to compare brewed teas. Their serving-form comparison found black tea cup-sized bags averaged 39 ± 9.9 mg caffeine per 200 mL and loose-leaf samples 24 ± 7.2 mg under the reported controlled brewing conditions. Brew time and format affect the measured content and black tea also contains theanine. The isolated caffeine Parkinson comparison used 200 or 400 mg daily. This supports caffeine as one possible link to the beverage and shows why the dose and mixture cannot be assumed comparable. No study participants or motor outcomes were part of the chemistry experiment.

fit: black tea intake and motor examination among Parkinson cases and healthy controls
assessment: Food recall compared 59 cases with 54 healthy controls for black tea intake. Public motor associations were based on a diet-wide score and supply no rest-tremor contrast for black tea.

fit: individual Parkinson symptoms and diet scores
assessment: The study gives a whole-diet fatigue association without a dried chervil estimate.

fit: garden chervil leaf and stem chemical analysis
assessment: Lyophilized chervil material was evaluated in chemical and cell assays, without fatigue measurements.

fit: dried sage capsules and cognition in Parkinson
assessment: Memory and salivation contrasts are reported, without a named apathy result. Secondary timetable unavailable.

fit: sage capsule trial and cognitive outcomes in Alzheimer disease
assessment: The completed registry record has no results or explicit apathy measure.

fit: registered sage extract and computerized cognition
assessment: The trial is recruiting in middle-aged adults and gives no Parkinson apathy endpoint.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: The treatment section mentions two Salvia species for dementia behavior or cognition, with no new primary clinical cohort.

fit: sage extract and Alzheimer cognitive rating
assessment: Composite cognitive results favored extract. No explicit apathy outcome.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S7.519 describes sweet cherry among fruit trees used for grafting work. No dietary cherry or measured neurologic symptom is present.

fit: sweet cherry extract and movement in rotenone-exposed flies
assessment: Extract-treated flies showed better spontaneous and induced movement during rotenone exposure. This assay did not measure dystonia or test dried cherry.

fit: systemic capsaicin and motor activity in rats
assessment: Spontaneous activity declined in intact rats and levodopa-elicited activity declined in reserpine rats. Walking speed and culinary smoked paprika were unmeasured.

fit: intraperitoneal capsaicin and locomotor activity in 6-OHDA rats
assessment: The authors report improved locomotor measures, opposite the proposed direction on that surrogate. No walking-speed estimate after smoked paprika was available.

fit: systemic capsaicin and levodopa-elicited motor activity in rats
assessment: Capsaicin reduced the measured high motor activity. The study did not quantify clinical dyskinesia or test paprika.

fit: intraperitoneal capsaicin and abnormal involuntary movements in 6-OHDA rats
assessment: Abnormal involuntary movements decreased in the model. Exposure and endpoints differ from culinary paprika and Parkinson clinical dyskinesia.

fit: oral almond oil vehicle across estradiol and lesion comparisons in rats
assessment: The matching dissertation confirms oral almond oil in all four groups. Basal cardiovascular and baroreflex measures did not clearly differ. No oil-free contrast or clinical orthostatic-lightheadedness outcome was available.

fit: thyme-containing mixed diet; aggregate nonmotor score
assessment: The Part I total includes hallucinations and psychosis but does not isolate visual hallucination frequency; individual thyme intake and effects are unreported.

fit: blueberry powder in juice and different outcome
assessment: A possible preliminary gait report was located. No speech-intelligibility estimate is available.

fit: blueberry-containing diet in a corticobasal degeneration case
assessment: One patient with autopsy-confirmed corticobasal degeneration was essentially mute at a visit when the diet included blueberries. Preparation and earlier intake are unspecified and there is no causal or idiopathic PD comparison.

fit: mixed dietary patterns include optional uncooked blueberries; aggregate motor score
assessment: The total motor score provides no listener-scored intelligibility or blueberry-specific comparison, and individual berry intake is unverified.

fit: oral flaxseed oil and exploration or locomotion in rotenone mice
assessment: The authors report greater line crossing and rearing with oil than with rotenone alone. The measured activity score combined exploration and movement. The oil was uncharacterized and no clinical bradykinesia was tested.

fit: competitive oral flaxseed and corn-oil comparison with motor sequencing outside Parkinson
assessment: The Frontal Assessment Battery motor series result was inconclusive (p=.140). This is a learned movement sequence and not examiner-rated bradykinesia.

fit: combined flaxseed-derived omega-3 and vitamin E with Parkinson total score
assessment: The reported composite cannot locate a change in bradykinesia. The intervention combines vitamin E with flaxseed-derived omega-3 and oil pressing was not identified.

fit: flaxseed-derived omega-3 plus vitamin E and Parkinson motor examination composite
assessment: Part III changed −1.9 with the combination and +3.1 with placebo (printed p = .05). The authors found no clear Part III effect. Individual bradykinesia scores, oil-only arms and pressing history were unavailable.

fit: plasma alpha-linolenic acid and the Parkinson body bradykinesia item
assessment: Body bradykinesia and hypokinesia ρ = −.230 (p = .171) adjusted for age and −.151 (p = .372) adjusted for sex. The chair-rise item correlated inversely but is a distinct measure. No oil ingestion contrast was tested.

fit: oral Pazze flaxseed oil chow and open-field movement
assessment: The dissertation reports no clear diet main effect on line crossings (p = .595) or rearings (p = .976). The model is early life stress and the outcomes are general activity.

fit: isolated alpha-linolenic acid and behavior in an LPS mouse model
assessment: The authors report partial recovery of motor deficits across a battery including pole, rotarod and open-field tests. Individual task estimates and administration route remain unavailable from the primary abstract. The intervention was isolated ALA.

fit: oral isolated black-pepper ALA and motor behavior in MPTP mice
assessment: The original preview identifies greater than 98% pure ALA and reports significant mitigation of model behavior deficits. Task-level estimates were not available and the preparation was isolated ALA rather than flaxseed oil.

fit: whole hazelnuts offered and Parkinson motor composite includes facial expression
assessment: The dietary Appendix lists hazelnuts with nuts and seeds. The motor score contains facial expression, without a published separate facial result or a hazelnut oil assignment.

fit: potato-fiber buns in a crossover with appetite and stool outcomes
assessment: In the full report, satiety increased with one preparation. Stool form and fecal fat did not differ across groups, and sleep was not assessed. The poster, trial and publication share one comparison.

fit: combined potato preparations and sleep efficiency
assessment: Completed official trial, no posted results. Protocol pools baked, boiled and mashed potato and registers sleep efficiency.

fit: boiled or mashed potatoes and prospective sleep duration
assessment: Adjusted sleep duration was +0.9 minutes/day per 80 g/day (99% CI −0.6 to +2, p=.1). The questionnaire did not report a roasted-potato category, an insomnia scale or a Parkinson-specific result.

fit: genetically proxied potato preference and insomnia
assessment: Two-variant preference instrument has OR 1.17 (95% CI 1.10–1.25). No measured intake, culinary preparation, Parkinson population or insomnia severity result.

fit: clinical case or dietary history without a matched ingredient comparison
assessment: Two original clinical histories report potatoes or chips as part of highly restricted diets. The form is incompletely characterized and a food-specific direction is absent.

fit: oral cinnamon and bladder nociception in rat cystitis and uninflamed controls
assessment: Cinnamon decreased a distension response in cystitis and increased it in uninflamed rats. The study gives no clinical urgency outcome.

fit: topical cinnamon patch and urinary urgency in overactive bladder
assessment: The urgency-frequency item favored the patch at two weeks. Daytime voiding frequency was inconclusive. The intervention was topical and no Parkinson subgroup was reported.

fit: cinnamon-containing Gosha-jinki-gan and urinary urgency
assessment: In a single-group study urgency and overall scores improved. One of the reported adverse symptoms was urinary frequency. No isolated ground cinnamon arm.

fit: cinnamon consumption and urinary nonmotor domain in a Parkinson survey
assessment: The cohort reported cinnamon and included a urinary symptom domain. It gives no urgency item result for cinnamon.

fit: oral cassia bark powder and void counts in acute cystitis mice
assessment: Powder decreased experimentally elevated void frequency. The mouse assay measured voids rather than perceived urgency.

fit: nigella oil and forelimb skill learning in healthy mice
assessment: Reaching success increased late in training in the oil group. This is skill acquisition with an oil exposure and no Parkinson impairment.

fit: ground culinary shiso as an odor stimulus in healthy women
assessment: Smelling steam from rice with ground shiso increased pleasantness ratings. The study did not test impairment of smell after eating dried leaves or Parkinson disease.

fit: isolated inhaled perillaldehyde and required smell pathway
assessment: Induced anosmia prevented the compound's forced-swim response. It was an experimental manipulation and not a restored-smell endpoint.

fit: isolated capsiate and willingness to invest effort in healthy men
assessment: The publisher abstract reports no change in readiness to invest effort during repeated cycling after 12 mg capsiate. No published arm estimates, clinical apathy rating, or roasted pepper exposure.

fit: Parkinson dietary crossover with baseline apathy and no identifiable bell-pepper contrast
assessment: Interviewed participants described pre-existing apathy as a barrier. The trial registered a Starkstein scale, and the report gives baseline prevalence without a post-diet group response and with no assigned roasted bell pepper.

fit: baked sweet pepper in Parkinson menus and Part I apathy item within a total score
assessment: The ketogenic menu bakes stuffed sweet peppers and the low-fat plan bakes capsicum as a topping. Published item-level results did not include apathy. The diet comparison cannot distinguish a pepper effect.

fit: purified nonpungent Capsicum and POMS2 vigor-activity in older adults
assessment: The randomized older-adult sample produced no significant between-arm vigor-activity comparison. The study used extract, supplied no apathy-scale result and excluded motor disorders.

fit: motivation or initiative within Parkinsonism symptom score and vegetable groups
assessment: Motivation or initiative was included in the patient-reported symptom checklist. Regression results for vegetables targeted the total score and provided neither a roasted pepper exposure nor an individual apathy item estimate.

fit: individualized plant-rich timed diet and rated apathy in a Parkinson cohort
assessment: Apathy changed from 13.65 to 9.0 in the diet group and 13.05 to 13.6 in controls. Narrative and tabulated post-treatment comparisons conflict. The intervention did not quantify roasted bell pepper exposure.

fit: Parkinson case with formula during levodopa treatment
assessment: The report is a levodopa and Japanese-pepper combination lead. It gives no recorded dyskinesia outcome or ground Sichuan pepper exposure.

fit: related Japanese pepper in an animal motor model
assessment: The intranasal preparation was evaluated with pole and rota-rod tasks. The experiment contains no levodopa-induced dyskinesia endpoint.

fit: topical macadamia carrier and composite hand sensation in cervical myelopathy
assessment: Right-hand grip was higher by week eight in one uncontrolled case. Subjective rating bundled fine tasks with other complaints. The regimen combined hands-on treatment and essential oils and the oil was applied topically.

fit: topical macadamia carrier and qualitative fine hand tasks in carpal tunnel syndrome
assessment: Writing and pinch tasks were reported to improve with mixed treatment in one patient. Figure 1 gives a descriptive right-grip increase of 0.8 kg. This is a different route, condition and intervention with unspecified pressing.

fit: planned postmeal psychomotor vigilance after oral macadamia oil
assessment: The registry plans psychomotor vigilance testing for alertness after liquid or powdered oil meals in healthy adults. No results are posted, and a vigilance task does not measure Parkinson manual dexterity.

fit: injected sesame-oil rotigotine formulation and rat drug exposure
assessment: An oil suspension changed peak and decay of rotigotine levels. It did not measure clinical OFF time or a toasted food preparation.

fit: aqueous spearmint extract and POMS depression/dejection in older adults
assessment: Day-90 changes were +.30 placebo, +.81 at 600 mg and −1.51 at 900 mg with overall p=.0862. Dose and baseline differences limit inference. The trial used extract in a non-Parkinson population.

fit: extract blend and depression scales in adults with sleep complaints
assessment: Both adjusted depressive symptom comparisons spanned zero. No fresh spearmint or Parkinson population.

fit: peppermint extract and tail-suspension immobility in male mice
assessment: Peppermint extract plus rotenone produced 183.67 seconds mean immobility versus 251.48 with rotenone alone (p<.001). The same animals improved locomotion. This is a different species, extract, animal assay and exposure from fresh spearmint in people.

fit: topical macadamia oil control and anxiety assessment in fibromyalgia
assessment: The five-person fibromyalgia analysis found no clear difference in STAI state or trait anxiety between topical macadamia oil and the same oil plus geranium (p = .09 and .63). The 2021 registry and university dissertation are earlier reports of the same crossover. The study did not test ingestion or an oil-free comparator.

fit: macadamia oil active comparator and state anxiety
assessment: State anxiety did not differ clearly between macadamia oil and krill oil (group p = .8611). Both groups received oil and no Parkinson cohort or oil-free comparator was studied.

fit: canine hindlimb paresis after raw or roasted kernels
assessment: Thirteen dogs had acute hindlimb paresis, recumbency or joint pain after kernel exposure. Freezing of gait and expressed oil were outside the case series.

fit: acute hindlimb weakness and ataxia after macadamia kernels in dogs
assessment: Canine field cases showed ataxia and experimental dogs became too weak to stand normally. The experiment exposed dogs to roasted kernels and did not count Parkinson freezing episodes.

fit: plasma piperine and total MDS-UPDRS Part III in PD
assessment: In 13 patients with both genetic variants r=−.466, p=.108. The direction is descriptive. Exposure source and particle size are unknown and there was no reported isolated hand-dexterity estimate.

fit: preliminary drug-induced sleep assay of tarragon tincture
assessment: The 50 mg/kg behavior-study dose was selected in preliminary induced-sleep testing. Drug names differ between report and dissertation Contents, and no tarragon sleep values are accessible. Parkinson insomnia and ordinary sleep remain untested.

fit: injected essential oil and acute mouse sedation
assessment: Overt sedation and reduced rotarod performance followed some doses of intraperitoneal essential oil. The study provides no baseline insomnia, sleep duration or spontaneous sleep measure.

fit: combined cruciferous vegetable frequency and drooling measured in a Parkinson cohort
assessment: The original dietary abstract pooled cauliflower and broccoli. The likely overlapping journal report supplies a clinical drooling scale and no relationship to cauliflower or its preparation.

fit: injected drug with peanut-oil carrier and later visual hallucinations in recurrent mania
assessment: The original Methods and case describe the peanut-oil vehicle and visual hallucinations after active drug withdrawal in the same study. It gives no isolated oil effect, oral cold-pressed exposure or Parkinson symptom-frequency estimate.

fit: historical topical drug exposure and observed visual behavior
assessment: The 1947 letter describes apparent visual behavior and separately identifies arachis oil as the contemporary vehicle. Exact batch and oil grade are unverified. The drug poisoning, topical route and non-Parkinson population preclude attribution to edible oil.

fit: Cinnamon appears in both multi-food PD diet plans; Part II composite rather than handwriting-size result
assessment: A combined activities-of-daily-living score cannot identify handwriting change, and the diet comparison cannot isolate ground cinnamon.

fit: commercial watermelon juice and supine blood pressure
assessment: Ten young adults in a crossover. Two-hour estimate -13.1 mm Hg (95% CI -24.09 to -2.11, p=.02); the overall interaction was p=.91. No measured lightheadedness or postural test.

fit: fresh diced watermelon and resting pressure in a fixed-order comparison
assessment: The Results and Table 1 show no clear within-watermelon pressure change. Cookie-phase pressure rose. The study did not measure standing pressure or lightheadedness.

fit: oral pasteurized watermelon juice and vascular outcomes in postmenopausal women
assessment: The companion paper found no clear ambulatory pressure or vascular difference. The trial did not measure orthostatic pressure or lightheadedness.

fit: watermelon flesh beverage and ambulatory pressure in adults with elevated pressure
assessment: The 24-hour, daytime and nighttime comparisons were inconclusive. No postural test or lightheadedness endpoint was reported.

fit: incidental watermelon mention and orthostatic blood pressure in a dementia case
assessment: The original letter reports 130/84 mmHg supine and 114/79 mmHg standing during medication review in a posterior cortical atrophy case. The watermelon episode illustrates a visual error. The report gives no ingestion time or change in lightheadedness after a food intervention.

fit: oral peanut oil comparator and grip strength in sarcopenic older adults
assessment: The standard-care control arm had no clear physical-function change. The trial measured grip strength rather than dexterity, excluded Parkinson disease and had no matched oil-free arm.

fit: mixed meal containing caraway and acute allergic oral symptoms
assessment: The case describes oral burning and respiratory symptoms after a meal containing caraway seasoning. It did not measure swallowing performance or specify ground caraway.

fit: Human Parkinson study with rice bran oil placebo and global score
assessment: Global MDS-UPDRS results were reported without Part II handwriting item 2.7, objective letter size or oil-grade data. The active oil carrier is unspecified.

fit: acute upper-airway reaction with macadamia kernel and prior topical oil exposure
assessment: A child had coughing, lip swelling and severe hoarseness after chewing and spitting out a kernel. The earlier oil contact was topical. The primary report does not document oral oil or formal swallowing testing.

fit: drooling in anaphylaxis after macadamia-containing ice cream
assessment: A three-year-old developed excessive drooling, generalized erythema and hypotensive shock after eating ice cream containing macadamia nuts. There was no formal swallowing exam or isolate of cold-pressed oil.

fit: filtered marjoram tea and motor examination in Parkinson
assessment: Accessible report gives no facial expression score or fresh-leaf comparison.

fit: encapsulated ginger extract and Beck anxiety scores in migraine
assessment: The reported day-90 comparison was inconclusive (p = .46) and the registration lists different outcomes. The population had migraine and used an extract.

fit: ginger rhizome powder and Hamilton anxiety with concurrent SSRI use
assessment: The publisher abstract explicitly identifies IRCT20201108049306N1 and reports increased active-arm scores while concluding anxiety decreased. The registered powder, SSRIs and Hamilton measures do not resolve the direction without the original tables or a correction.

fit: dried extract plus propranolol and Beck anxiety scores in migraine
assessment: The original paper gives a day-90 comparison of 17.2 versus 17.1 points (p = .84). Its registered outcomes list migraine and the published population differs from Parkinson disease.

fit: oral dried ginger suspension and elevated plus-maze behavior
assessment: Both ginger groups spent longer in open arms than the water group in Table 1. Methods conflict on group count and oral dose. This powdered suspension in mice leaves grated ginger and Parkinson anxiety unresolved.

fit: oral aqueous extract of supermarket ginger and rat maze
assessment: Open-arm time averaged 30 versus 20 seconds, with no significant open-field crossing difference. Filtered extract and a rat maze cannot identify a clinical effect of eating grated ginger.

fit: anxiety outcomes in a Parkinson formula trial with unresolved ingredients
assessment: The official abstract reports Hamilton and self-rated anxiety differences. Publisher metadata identifies legacy PDF record 8908, which was unavailable. Ginger, formula composition and numerical outcomes remain unverified.

fit: ginger extract and mouse dark-box anxiety model
assessment: Open-arm time means were greater after extract. The same experiment describes movement differences and gives no extract preparation method, route or dosing duration.

fit: ginger extract and listed MDS-UPDRS Parts I–IV
assessment: The scale includes anxious mood but the official record has no separately listed item outcome or posted results. The dosing arms compare two strengths of ginger root extract.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-862 reviews ginger and weight or fat loss, without a frozen Parkinson endpoint.

fit: oral ethanolic rhizome extract and mouse maze behavior
assessment: Open-arm occupancy increased at both tested extract doses. The paper reports no significant 60-minute locomotor difference but gives no numerical locomotor values. No fresh grated or clinical Parkinson contrast.

fit: isolated ginger compounds and artificial permeability
assessment: The contemporaneous related abstract reports an artificial membrane assay. The original journal article is restricted and no clinical anxiety or grated ginger effect is established.

fit: four-herb ginger blend and Hamilton anxiety in opioid dependence
assessment: The abstract reports favorable time-by-treatment p=.035 for the mixture with only 41 of 81 completing. No estimate specific to ginger or Parkinson disease.

fit: topical fresh ginger juice in a mixed IBS treatment and anxiety-related quality of life
assessment: The author abstract reports favorable between-group anxiety-related item scores at days 7 and 28. The plaster contains other herbs and no oral ginger-only arm. Separate tabular results remain open.

fit: intraperitoneal isolated 6-shogaol and anxiety-like behavior after mouse head injury
assessment: Open-arm entries increased versus the injured control while ambulation fell in the tables. The Results prose conflicts with both a significance marker and the direction of ambulation. No clinical anxiety or grated ginger exposure was measured.

fit: ginger oral capsules and Spielberger anxiety in burn inpatients
assessment: Ginger and placebo had inconclusive visit-level differences through day 6. The report does not specify ginger species or preparation. This cohort was treated for burns.

fit: randomized ginger extract drink and postoperative HARS categories
assessment: No-anxiety category 18/20 to 20/20 versus 14/20 to 14/20. The post-only comparison p=.0293 has baseline imbalance and does not supply an adjusted anxiety severity estimate.

fit: standardized ginger root powder and a secondary anxiety outcome in healthy adults
assessment: The original manuscript and indexed journal table give DASS-21 anxiety median change −1 versus 0, Mann–Whitney U = 286, p = .511 in the thesis and .51 rounded in the journal. Low baseline scores, a short study, and healthy adults limit the comparison.

fit: standardized ginger root powder and HADS anxiety during chemotherapy
assessment: All three reported HADS anxiety differences have confidence intervals crossing zero. The time-by-group test gave p = .352. The protocol included this as a secondary outcome.

fit: inhaled ginger essential oil and nervousness during an acute cognitive stressor
assessment: In a crossover of 20 male students, task-time nervousness ratings were 35.0 with ginger aroma and 32.4 with scentless control. Subjective condition comparisons were inconclusive. Selected physiological stress response contrasts favored ginger.

fit: bitter-ginger extract and HADS anxiety in cancer
assessment: The uncontrolled study reports improvement with a different Zingiber species. Sixteen of 35 completed eight weeks. Exact anxiety changes and full formulation details remain unavailable.

fit: dietary gingerol-enriched extract and open-field behavior in diabetic rats
assessment: Figure 1 reports more center time and entries in extract-treated neuropathy rats. Methods describes eight weeks, while Results references five. Open-field measures and concentrated extract do not resolve culinary ginger and clinical anxiety.

fit: oral gingerol extract and open-field behavior in female rats with nerve ligation
assessment: Center entries increased for the higher dose versus ligation vehicle at week four in Figure 2, p < .05. The abstract describes both doses more broadly. Concentrated extract and a pain-model behavior do not establish an effect on Parkinson anxiety.

fit: oral ginger extract and anxiety-like behavior in a prenatal valproate mouse model
assessment: The original abstract describes favorable anxiety-like behavior after four weeks. No numerical result, clinical anxiety scale or fresh culinary exposure is available.

fit: combined standardized ginger and ginkgo extract in rat maze
assessment: The combined preparation increased open-arm behavior at a lower dose and decreased approach at a higher dose. The 1 mg/kg finding was inconclusive. The effect of freshly grated ginger alone and clinical anxiety were not assessed.

fit: ginger and ginkgo extract ratios in rat maze
assessment: The 2.5:1 mixture at 1 mg/kg increased open-arm behavior. Other ratios gave no detected effect. This experiment does not isolate ginger and differs from the earlier experiment at the same total dose.

fit: single-dose standardized ginger extract drink and postoperative patient-rated anxiety
assessment: Supplemental Table 1 gives VAS means of 2.00 vs 1.21 (p = .420) on day one and 1.62 vs 0.71 (p = .266) on day two, n = 24 each. The trial reports no baseline-adjusted anxiety-change contrast. This is the same already catalogued perioperative cohort.

fit: cold-extracted pumpkin seed oil and diastolic pressure in a cardiometabolic cohort
assessment: Mean diastolic pressure declined about 3.3 mmHg in the oil group and 0.6 mmHg in controls. The primary analysis does not establish an adjusted change between groups. No orthostatic outcome was measured.

fit: oral pumpkin seed oil and weekly tail-cuff pressure in hypertensive rats
assessment: At week 8 the oil group was at 134.20 versus 149.40 mmHg in hypertensive controls. The abstract cites a week-5 control. Cold pressing and orthostatic symptoms are unverified, and the Methods describe one oil administration inconsistently.

fit: regulatory adverse-event table for a commercial ethanolic seed extract
assessment: The assessment names hypotension in a 2,245-patient uncontrolled seed-extract series without event counts or orthostatic context. The 2000 author abstract likely overlaps and does not enumerate adverse event types. No cold-pressed oil or Parkinson comparison.

fit: pumpkin seed oil capsules and blood pressure in premenopausal women
assessment: The completed record lists systolic and diastolic pressure changes at 12 weeks. No results were verified and no orthostatic symptom was specified.

fit: pumpkin seed oil versus raw seed and resting blood pressure
assessment: The primary 2018 abstract reports no clear blood-pressure change in the oil arm. No orthostatic outcome was reported and the linked dissertation remains inaccessible.

fit: oral pumpkin seed oil and resting pressure in postmenopausal women
assessment: The abstract reports lower brachial and central systolic pressure after oil and no clear heart-rate variability or stiffness change. Standing pressure and lightheadedness were not measured.

fit: pumpkin oil-enriched diet and seated blood pressure measurement in hyperlipidemia
assessment: The registry specifies seated pressure after rest. The published abstract omits arm-specific values, and the verified four-page supplement reports fatty-acid laboratory results only. Main clinical tables, processing grade and standing symptoms remain unverified.

fit: oral pumpkin seed oil and resting diastolic pressure in postmenopausal women
assessment: Mean diastolic pressure fell from 81.10 to 75.67 mmHg in the oil arm. The 12-week arm contrast was inconclusive and neither standing pressure nor lightheadedness was assessed.

fit: branded pumpkin seed oil capsule and measured seated pressure versus placebo
assessment: Seated systolic change was −1.2 versus +1.0 mmHg (p = 0.496); diastolic change was −0.1 versus −0.8 (p = 0.813). No pressure after standing or scale for triggered lightheadedness. The complete capsule formula and pressing grade are unverified.

fit: oral pumpkin seed oil and dizziness reporting with active drug comparison
assessment: Zero of 39 oil participants and two of 34 tamsulosin participants reported dizziness. The active-drug comparison gives no measured orthostatic symptom or cold-press grade.

fit: refined olive oil and dementia composite score
assessment: Dementia severity ratings improved within both oil groups. No apathy-specific estimate or Parkinson participants.

fit: multicomponent Parkinson diet and baseline apathy
assessment: Published material includes a baseline Starkstein Apathy Scale and no isolated refined-olive-oil or follow-up apathy contrast.

fit: olive oil in a composite dietary score among older coronary patients
assessment: The outcome is reported by Mediterranean dietary score and diabetes status. No grade, oil-specific estimate or Parkinson symptom result was reported.

fit: Mediterranean diet adherence and apathy outside Parkinson disease
assessment: Table 4 adjusted OR 2.76, 95% CI 0.83 to 9.21, p=.099 for diet nonadherence and apathy during quarantine. The prose describes an association. There is no oil-specific contrast.

fit: Parkinson cohort diet scores and individual apathy assessment
assessment: Recovered institutional Table 4 covers 162 participants and MDS-UPDRS I item 1.5. Lifestyle-adjusted MIND, DII and HDI p=.612, .687 and .369. The models use entire dietary patterns and supply no separate oil-grade result.

fit: Parkinson dietary patterns, olive oil questionnaire and patient-rated motivation
assessment: The two diet scores show lower difficulty on the motivation or initiative item at p<.001 each. The supplements list olive oil questions but report question-level estimates only against the aggregate PRO-PD measure. The food processing grade and separate oil-to-apathy estimate are absent.

fit: apathy during sublingual cannabinoid treatment with olive oil carrier
assessment: Apathy decreased in one uncontrolled Alzheimer cohort. Same cohort as the 2022 preprint. Formulation uses unspecified olive oil as carrier and there is no carrier-only arm.

fit: low
assessment: The report used dyskinesia in a five-case peripheral neuropathy syndrome in men with diabetes. Product form and motor phenomenology remain unverified. It did not measure Parkinson or levodopa-induced dyskinesia after toasted groats.

fit: whole celery extract and gait task performance in mice
assessment: Grid foot faults decreased and beam crossing improved at some doses. No stride length was measured.

fit: celery named in a Parkinson diet with a gait-inclusive motor scale
assessment: The composite motor score improved. The study gives no confirmed fresh leaf exposure or stride length value.

fit: pomegranate peel extract and sucrose consumption in stressed mice
assessment: The primary report highlights a greater sucrose response with flax and imipramine, while pomegranate peel changed selected biomarkers. Sucrose intake is a reward-related measure, without clinical apathy or raw fruit.

fit: nanoemulsified pomegranate seed oil and planned Parkinson mood and apathy domain
assessment: The planned NMSS covers loss of interest. No item-level result or trial outcome publication was verified. The intervention is a nanoformulated oil capsule.

fit: multi-ingredient pomegranate-acai product and registered motivation
assessment: The single-arm healthy adult registration lists self-reported motivation. There are no posted results or isolated aril comparison.

fit: rosemary extract and prospective bowel adverse-event surveillance
