assessment: Combined diarrhea or constipation item, active without results, methanolic extract and type 2 diabetes cohort. No severity estimate.

fit: rosemary-containing abdominal aroma massage and constipation in older adults
assessment: Constipation scores and stool frequency favored the blend. The intervention combined three oils with massage.

fit: rosemary-containing aroma massage and functional constipation in students
assessment: Both massage groups improved over time. The formula combined four oils and did not estimate ingested rosemary.

fit: abdominal massage and bowel outcomes in Parkinson disease
assessment: Inconclusive between-group change in a 32-person pilot. The intervention tested massage with advice and assigned no rosemary.

fit: rosemary leaf extract and laxative or antidiarrheal responses in animal studies
assessment: Lower levels of the extract increased laxation and higher levels reduced transit in distinct models. The study used extract and gives no Parkinson symptom estimate.

fit: rosemary essential-oil massage and reported defecation benefit
assessment: Figures suggest 12 and 9 reporting benefit in groups of 15, but outcome and allocation are weak and there is no sham group. Preparation and route differ.

fit: Dill extract and involuntary contractions of isolated visceral smooth muscle
assessment: A methanol extract of dried aerial parts inhibited experimentally induced and spontaneous intestinal smooth muscle contractions. This ex vivo result provides no neurological dystonia evidence.

fit: Oral sowa extract and experimental motor behavior
assessment: The animal withdrawal study used motor coordination and locomotor measures without a neurological dystonia endpoint or culinary foliage verification.

fit: acute and repeated cognitive function with black cardamom extract
assessment: Both reports use the same registration family and measure timed cognitive-task outcomes. They provide no sleepiness scale and use aqueous black cardamom rather than ground green seed.

fit: cardamom crude extract and pentobarbital-induced sleep in mice
assessment: The extract lengthened drug-induced sleep. The study did not measure waking sleepiness in Parkinson’s.

fit: topical mustard constituent and elicited swallow reflex in rats
assessment: Topical allyl isothiocyanate triggered reflex swallows and local TRPA1 antagonism reduced them. Reflex counts and direct chemical application do not measure food swallowing safety.

fit: topical mustard constituent after experimental rat pharyngolaryngeal injury
assessment: The injury comparison prolonged allyl isothiocyanate-evoked swallow latency without changing swallow count. The design did not test culinary mustard in Parkinson disease.

fit: mustard sauce and allergic swallowing symptoms
assessment: The primary abstract verifies three systemic allergic reactions. A later case table attributes acute dysphagia to two patients. Parkinson disease and a ground-mustard comparison were absent.

fit: saffron capsules and composite Parkinson motor score
assessment: The eight-week motor total comparison was inconclusive, F=.53 and p=.424. The accessible report supplies no separate facial-expression item 3.2.

fit: saffron plus chamomile and composite outcomes
assessment: Registered combination and constituent comparisons. No posted results.

fit: isolated constituent and composite motor score
assessment: Within-group composite motor improvement. No ingredient-level or symptom-specific treatment estimate was available.

fit: brewed green tea after a fatigue task in healthy adults
assessment: The small crossover reports a decline after green tea with no reported beverage-by-time interaction.

fit: matching brewed exposure and fatigue outcome
assessment: Mean FSS rose 28.4 to 32.1 in 14 participants. The original Iowa State dissertation gives the same cohort and medians of 27 and 30.5. Its appendix reports demographics and medication without individual paired FSS. The comparison has no control, paired-change variance or exact fatigue p-value.

fit: observational tea analysis or prediabetes egg program
assessment: An observational member reports current green tea drinking and odds of cognitive impairment. No Parkinson population, fatigue outcome or olfactory endpoint is supplied.

fit: tencha and acute task-related mental fatigue in healthy men
assessment: The patent describes lower mental fatigue qualitatively. Its numeric comparisons concern arithmetic task scores. Its design differs from UMIN000034209.

fit: green tea frequency and Parkinson fatigue
assessment: The published baseline heatmap shows an inverse correlation for the fatigue item. Brewing is unspecified, and the figure gives no coefficient or uncertainty estimate.

fit: concentrated tea polyphenols and Parkinson progression
assessment: The accessible results give no individual fatigue estimate.

fit: green tea and chicory extracts with collagen in an insomnia crossover
assessment: The official protocol lists 5 g green tea extract, 1 g chicory extract and 5 g collagen peptides. The current registry supplies three fatigue subscales. The journal found no clear difference in general fatigue (p=.79), lower physical fatigue with supplement (model contrast −0.67, 95% CI −1.3 to −0.1), and inconclusive mental fatigue. This crossover outside Parkinson disease did not test brewed green tea.

fit: fermented tea extract and task-related fatigue in a healthy crossover
assessment: Sixteen adults received fermented tea extract and its unfermented comparator. Figure 3 reports a smaller POMS fatigue rise graphically with no specific p value or significance mark. The figure's p < .1 indication concerns total mood or other subscales. The products have different GABA contents.

fit: tube-administered powdered green tea and blood pressure
assessment: In two tube-fed Parkinson cases, the post-feed pressure drop lessened after powdered green tea. Fatigue and oral brewed tea were outside the comparison.

fit: matcha suspension and fatigue in healthy men
assessment: The trial measured lower pre-exercise fatigue in week one. Powder suspension, concurrent training and participants without Parkinson disease limit applicability.

fit: green tea and fatigue during mental tasks in healthy men
assessment: Fatigue increased during water and green tea sessions in a fixed order. A comparative effect of green tea is unresolved.

fit: green tea and acute drowsiness or local discomfort in healthy adults
assessment: Drowsiness decreased during the tea session while local pain or dullness increased. Fixed session order and the absence of a between-condition change estimate limit inference.

fit: self-reported green tea and combined sleep and fatigue domain
assessment: The UK cohort reported no clear domain differences after correction. Brewing and the separate fatigue outcome are unresolved.

fit: isolated fermented GABA beverage and POMS fatigue in the Yoto citation trail
assessment: In nine preselected fatigued healthy participants, Table 2 gave fatigue T-score change -5.11 with the 50 mg GABA drink versus +4.00 with control, p=.0001. The 25 mg comparison was inconclusive. This was an isolated fermented ingredient in a sweetened beverage, without brewed green tea or Parkinson fatigue.

fit: brewed green tea and fatigue ratings during short mental tasks
assessment: The 18-person crossover measured fatigue VAS and POMS fatigue-inertia. The reported cross-beverage mood and POMS changes were inconclusive, with no fatigue-specific estimates. Composite mood and salivary stress-marker results are separate, and healthy students differ from Parkinson participants.

fit: pooled green tea and extracts for weight outcomes
assessment: The weight and body-composition intervals span zero. The result is not a comparison of brewed green tea and Parkinson fatigue.

fit: powdered matcha capsules and sleep quality in older adults with cognitive decline
assessment: Uchida et al. report a 0.86-point favorable between-group PSQI change after twelve months with an interval spanning zero; the two primary cognitive and daily-living outcomes had no clear differences. UMIN000035658 covers the same cohort. The study measured sleep quality rather than Parkinson fatigue and used capsules.

fit: powdered matcha capsules and morning refreshment in adults without Parkinson disease
assessment: Baba et al. report +3.47 versus +5.12 points for morning refreshment (p=.39) and -2.0 versus -2.9 for daytime sleepiness (p=.54) after four weeks. Registry UMIN000052248 calls the first scale fatigue recovery. The published outcome is refreshment on rising with powdered capsules, without a brewed-tea Parkinson fatigue estimate.

fit: acute asthenia recurring after a mixed tea infusion was resumed
assessment: Asthenia and jaundice reappeared about two weeks after resuming a 75% green tea and 25% peppermint infusion. Suspected liver injury, the blended exposure and the single case limit interpretation of fatigue in Parkinson disease.

fit: asthenia during liver injury associated with multiple green tea infusions
assessment: Asthenia accompanied a severe hepatitis presentation in a person reporting six to seven cups daily of several green tea infusions. The case gives no standardized fatigue severity or Parkinson comparison.

fit: presenting fatigue during hepatitis after prolonged green tea with lemon intake
assessment: The patient presented with weeks of fatigue after six months of tea consumption. Liver tests normalized after cessation and supportive care. The case provides no graded fatigue change or Parkinson diagnosis.

fit: isolated caffeine and fatigue severity in a randomized trial
assessment: The fatigue estimate was uncertain at six weeks. The comparison used encapsulated caffeine and did not test brewed green tea.

fit: green tea with mucuna and adjusted levodopa in a Parkinson case
assessment: The published letter gives lower total UPDRS and Part IV scores under the combined regimen. It supplies no separate fatigue outcome or isolated tea contrast.

fit: standard versus reduced-caffeine green tea and accumulated fatigue
assessment: In 19 analyzed healthy adults, low-caffeine brewed tea was associated with lower Monday accumulated fatigue than standard tea, p=.015. Friday p=.074. Both groups consumed tea and the products differed in several constituents.

fit: green tea extract capsules and muscle electrical fatigability
assessment: The placebo-controlled athlete study assessed experimentally induced fatigue through muscle electromyography. It gives no subjective clinical fatigue result for an ordinary brew.

fit: green or white tea allowed in a mixed multiple-sclerosis diet measuring fatigue
assessment: NICE lists optional tea in the prescribed diet and an inconclusive unadjusted MFIS endpoint. The original abstract reports a favorable separate comparison. No measured intake, separately assigned brewed tea, or Parkinson fatigue estimate.

fit: brewed green tea versus water and daily fatigue after gastrectomy
assessment: Of 80 randomized, 77 were analyzed. Figure 3C reports lower fatigue on days 3–6 and a repeated-measures comparison p<.001. The official ChiCTR1800018294 WHO mirror lists fatigue as secondary in a retrospective registration from September 2018. The open-label postoperative trial gives no Parkinson effect estimate.

fit: matcha powder and task-related fatigue in healthy adults
assessment: The two-week study found no clear effect on task-related fatigue.

fit: blended tea catechins and ornithine and exertion during cycling
assessment: The acute combination lowered perceived exertion by 0.5 points (95% CI 0.2 to 0.8 lower) during fixed-load cycling. A separate cycling test had no clear exertion or performance difference. The formulation and population are indirect.

fit: reported aggregate caffeine exposure
assessment: Primary Table 4 gives a cross-sectional fatigue odds ratio of 0.94 (95% CI 0.37–2.35) for frequent versus infrequent caffeine use. It supplies no estimate for brewed green tea.

fit: isolated EGCG and motor behavior in PINK1 flies at author-abstract depth
assessment: The abstract describes locomotor and neuroinflammatory outcomes in flies and names tea for traditional fatigue use. It gives no brewed-beverage symptom fatigue estimate. The original body and detailed tables remain gated.

fit: practitioner-reported green tea in capsule or tea form
assessment: The questionnaire names Camellia sinensis and the formulations. It reports no patient-level fatigue data.

fit: separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context
assessment: P1263 tests isolated EGCG in mouse chemotherapy mucositis with mucosal and tissue outcomes. It supplies no brewed green tea or Parkinson fatigue comparison.

fit: high-theanine green tea and fatigue in healthy students
assessment: All four public versions describe a four-condition crossover and supply no result. The tea comparison in a later patent uses a different design, sample and arms.

fit: powdered green tea and unreported fatigue in healthy adults
assessment: The Methods name a fatigue VAS and the human outcome tables give no estimate for it.

fit: red raspberry powder and spatial working memory
assessment: The 36-person crossover reports fewer spatial working memory errors and better strategy at p < .05 after a freeze-dried raspberry powder meal. The 2019 registry and 2026 paper are one study.

fit: black raspberry powder and global clinical dementia rating
assessment: Global CDR fell from .5 to 0 in 11 of 11 active participants versus 0 of 10 controls. Executive performance was not reported separately and participants had mild Alzheimer-type dementia.

fit: freeze-dried red raspberry and learning and memory in high-fat-fed mice
assessment: Raspberry-supplemented mice retained novel object recognition and high-fat-fed supplemented mice found the Barnes maze escape hole faster. These tests measured animal learning and memory after freeze-dried fruit.

fit: mixed thawed raspberry smoothie and executive tasks
assessment: Task switching response time improved within the mixture arm late in the session. The four-berry drink and healthy-adult population cannot isolate frozen raspberry.

fit: multicomponent capsule including raspberry and executive testing
assessment: The capsule includes raspberry among many dehydrated ingredients. The favorable TESEN changes are within-period results in healthy adults, with no contribution estimated for frozen raspberry.

fit: freeze-dried red and yellow raspberry and working memory in mice
assessment: The Alzheimer-model experiment found no clear diet effect on object recognition or spatial memory. The animal model and freeze-dried preparation differ.

fit: strain-defined fermented milk
assessment: The trial measured bowel function, anxiety and composite nonmotor symptoms for a distinct preparation.

fit: commercial kefir in myeloma and planned patient fatigue measures
assessment: Official protocol names fatigue. No primary result or exact product grade was verified.

fit: kefir during cancer treatment and aggregate physical symptoms
assessment: The fourth-cycle physical symptom outcome favors the kefir arm. Tiredness is one physical item and is not given separately. Product flavor and contribution of extra contact remain unclear.

fit: commercial kefir and registered PROMIS Global Health
assessment: A planned fatigue item in a broader outcome supplies no result. Observational protocol without a parallel untreated comparison group.

fit: kefir bolus and instrumented swallowing test
assessment: The study compared swallowing under different food and liquid textures and measured no fatigue.

fit: formulated kefir and treadmill exhaustion in healthy participants
assessment: The crossover likely corresponds to registry NCT04293666 based on design, sample and exact strains. Registry says freeze dried and paper says spray dried. Endurance was 11.76 versus 9.08 minutes with p=.0048 in Results and p=.0004 in abstract. No patient fatigue comparison.

fit: kefir after exercise and patient-reported fatigue in cancer survivors
assessment: The 24-person article abstract reports 39.3% fatigue improvement. The likely related 19-person dissertation reports an interaction p=.002. Product flavor, full article contrast and Parkinson treatment remain unverified.

fit: kefir, milk and water and acute postexercise fatigue
assessment: Postexercise fatigue improved with kefir and water before retesting. The author abstract does not show a clear kefir superiority estimate.

fit: kefir powder and planned fatigue visual analog rating
assessment: Physical fatigue is secondary in the 75-person powder protocol. Results are unpublished in the official record.

fit: hazelnut oil mixed into chocolate and measured secretion
assessment: Panelists licked and expectorated two same-sugar fat matrices. Replacing some cocoa butter with hazelnut oil gave no statistically clear difference in saliva per gram of sample. The experiment did not measure drooling or specify oil grade or Parkinson status.

fit: compound hazelnut-oil gargle and ex vivo tongue wetting
assessment: Higher liquid retention refers to formulated wetting in excised tissue. The preparation was mixed and its oil grade unspecified. It measures no saliva production or drooling.

fit: spearmint oil in registered dry-mouth blend
assessment: Multi-ingredient spray versus mint-flavored water in Sjögren syndrome registers unstimulated salivary flow. No posted results and no dried spearmint or clinical drooling outcome.

fit: gum chewing and swallowing in Parkinson participants
assessment: Swallows were more frequent and latency shorter during chewing. Flavor was unspecified in the public original abstract and drooling severity was not reported.

fit: spearmint-flavored gum and six-minute saliva volume
assessment: Flow rose from 0.85 to 4.03 mL/min with chewing. The six-minute flavor comparison had p=.091. There was no unflavored comparator or drooling measurement.

fit: spearmint-flavored gum and salivary flow
assessment: Collected salivary flow increased versus rest for all flavors. This possibly overlapping report describes an early peak and no significant late flavor differences. No dried leaf or clinical drooling outcome.

fit: commercial spearmint-flavored gum and saliva production
assessment: The randomized chewing experiment measured salivary secretion. Dried spearmint ingestion and Parkinson drooling were outside its design.

fit: cooked barley flour and HADS anxiety outside Parkinson’s
assessment: The crossover reported no clear between-phase anxiety difference for cooked barley flour versus rice flour in 23 adults. The whole grain form and Parkinson population were untested.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S6.390 compares barley chloroplast responses to light, and S6.415 and S11.760 study seed treatment or germination. These are plant studies without a dietary or anxiety comparison.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-09-018 names barley as a plant model for planned testing of a bacterial polymer. No grain feeding or measured anxiety outcome is supplied.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P1667 identifies barley prolamines in the dietary context of celiac disease. The microscopic-colitis series supplies no standalone barley comparison.

fit: veterinary reference context only, without a tested Parkinson comparison
assessment: Patulin is described as a contaminant of grains including barley. The dictionary supplies an exposure context without a grain intervention or a Parkinson anxiety observation.

fit: barley-derived beta-glucan and anxiety-like behavior in stressed mice
assessment: ICARE abstract A141 reports more typical maze behavior in stressed mice given barley beta-glucan (p<.05), without numerical group results. It tests a constituent outside a Parkinson model. Related abstracts may share animals.

fit: boiled waxy barley and self-rated anxiety change in healthy adults
assessment: The randomized contrast favored barley for change in POMS 2 tension–anxiety. Final group medians were both 43. In an exploratory trial with visibly different foods, eight protocol exclusions and no Parkinson participants, the contrast gives weak indirect evidence against worsening.

fit: low
assessment: The primary abstract describes qualitative anxiety improvement during a package of Persian barley water, lemon balm tea and lifestyle modification. A case of hyperthyroidism cannot estimate anxiety after isolated boiled barley grains in Parkinson’s.

fit: barley-based talbinah and two anxiety measures in older adults
assessment: Within the intervention period, DASS anxiety was inconclusive while POMS tension-anxiety decreased. The trial did not isolate boiled barley or Parkinson anxiety.

fit: shared pearl barley porridge and mouse open-field activity
assessment: All arms received porridge with peanut oil. The group contrasts were olanzapine and other added treatments, and the open-field outcomes were sector crossings and rearings. No assigned barley effect or clinical anxiety estimate.

fit: cooked waxy barley cultivars and general mental health
assessment: Both groups ate barley. A mental-health summary improved within one group, without a separate anxiety instrument, no-barley comparator or Parkinson subgroup.

fit: separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context
assessment: The clinical work includes barley in an allergen-testing panel, with gluten context separately. Neither this test route nor the aggregate outcomes measure eating barley for the frozen symptom.

fit: macadamia oil comparator and sleep-related impairment
assessment: There was no clear treatment-by-time effect on PROMIS sleep-related impairment (p = .6878). Neither oil-free exposure nor diagnosed insomnia was tested.

fit: oral macadamia oil and acute daytime ratings with pretreatment sleep information
assessment: Two healthy-student experiments found lower acute sleepiness and fatigue with a macadamia oil meal. The study family collected selected past sleep information and did not assess treatment-period insomnia or establish cold pressing.

fit: carrot juice and functional gait comparison
assessment: Usual gait speed in the carrot arm changed inconclusively (p=.350). Stride length, steamed carrot and a Parkinson cohort were absent.

fit: oral purple carrot extract in Parkinson model rats
assessment: Catalepsy and oral movements improved. No stride-length test or steamed carrot comparison was given.

fit: clove oil odor detection during an oxytocin crossover
assessment: Clove oil was a detection probe in a schizophrenia study of oxytocin. The abstract reports no clear clove threshold change. The later journal report has no clove threshold. Neither route nor endpoint matches the frozen culinary comparison.

fit: registered topical clove oil and dental pain
assessment: The registry plans a randomized topical clove-versus-olive-oil comparison. Results were unavailable.

fit: clove powder and hot-water nociception in mice
assessment: The annual report gives no analgesic effect in the hot-water assay. It prints 1 mg/kg powder, leaves that assay route unstated and provides no group counts, effect sizes or uncertainty.

fit: injected clove essential oil and mouse hot-plate behavior
assessment: Three essential-oil concentrations gave higher transformed latency responses than saline. The route was intraperitoneal and the outcome thermal response in mice.

fit: topical clove-derived eugenol and acute toothache
assessment: At five minutes 14/17 eugenol and 0/17 vehicle participants reported relief. Allocation and blinding details and uncertainty are unreported. The exposure was a constituent gel applied at the painful site.

fit: oral aqueous clove extract and experimental nociception
assessment: The author abstract reports favorable assay results overall and leaves species and test-level comparisons unclear. Publisher full article download returned 404.

fit: topical clove oil and pediatric nerve block pain
assessment: Clove oil and benzocaine gel showed inconclusive observer and self-rated pain comparisons (p=.326 and .714). No inactive comparison or oral ground clove.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: Abstract 65 identifies eugenol in clove oil and tests the oral isolated compound or its labeled analogue, without a tested clove food.

fit: topical ground clove and immediate dental pain
assessment: The ground-clove gel yielded lower needle-pain scores than placebo. A local dental procedure cannot establish the effect of eating clove on Parkinson’s pain.

fit: isolated oral eugenol and evoked thermal or mechanical rat responses
assessment: Day-five thermal latency 11.4 versus 6.1 seconds, p<.01. Mechanical tests were inconclusive and did not generate allodynia. The formulation differed from the saline comparator. Neither arm corresponds to ground clove or clinical Parkinson pain.

fit: topical clove oil cream and chronic anal fissure healing
assessment: The author abstract reports 60% versus 12% healing at three months and lower manometric pressures. The full paper is needed to verify a pain outcome separately.

fit: clove odorant among four scents and olfaction
assessment: Eugenol was one of four smelled odorants. The intervention measured olfaction and gives no pain estimate after ground clove.

fit: injected clove oil and mouse nociception
assessment: The oil group showed fewer writhes and longer hot-plate latency than saline. The article mentions sedation with higher doses. No ground clove or clinical Parkinson outcome.

fit: oral standardized clove extract and composite hangover symptoms
assessment: Mammen and colleagues reported a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover of standardized oral clove polyphenols in 16 men following a controlled alcohol challenge. The report gives an overall 55.34% reduction in composite hangover severity. No separate pain, ache, or headache contrast could be verified from the accessible report. The code printed with the study belongs to the ethics committee rather than an identified trial registry. Article access and the later reanalysis are documented separately.

fit: topical clove-papaya gel and pediatric dental injection pain
assessment: This pediatric active-comparator study tested a clove–papaya formulation, benzocaine and precooling. No separate clove effect or clinical Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: topical eugenol and needle pain in hemodialysis
assessment: The crossover enrolled 34 patients and reported mean pain of 3.29 with topical eugenol versus 5.03 without intervention. The publisher describes a lower score than placebo. The outcome is procedural pain and the exposure is a topical constituent.

fit: topical clove oil and pediatric dental injection pain
assessment: In a four-arm pediatric dental study, topical lignocaine gave lower self-rated and observer pain than clove oil. Clove oil versus ice was inconclusive.

fit: topical clove essential-oil gel and rat nociception
assessment: The gel lowered late-phase formalin pain scores. The paper found no clear early-phase composite or thermal latency effect. No ground-clove or clinical pain effect was measured.

fit: inhaled clove and postoperative headache
assessment: Overall three-arm contrasts were inconclusive at eight and 24 hours (p=.20 and .31). The study did not test ingested clove or Parkinson’s pain.

fit: topical clove oil and pediatric dental pain
assessment: Three active treatments had no statistically clear between-group difference. There was no inactive comparison or Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: injected clove distillate and experimental rat pain
assessment: The clove pharmacopuncture study evaluated a distilled injected formulation in cell and rat experiments. It increased thermal tail-flick latency and attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity after experimental inflammation. This records a local and preclinical analgesic signal with an exposure and outcome distinct from consuming ground clove for Parkinson pain.

fit: green beans in a Parkinson menu and aggregate motor scores
assessment: The Parkinson pilot offered green beans as one of many options. Aggregate motor change was inconclusive and individual facial-expression scores, steaming and participant-specific green bean intake were unreported.

fit: oral sweet basil extracts and beam motor coordination in an ischemia model
assessment: The 2009 poster and 2011 journal abstract share researchers and endpoint but differ in reported occlusion duration. Overlap unresolved. The accessible outcomes give no stride estimate or fresh-food exposure.

fit: oral sweet basil leaf extract after cerebral ischemia in mice
assessment: Author abstract reports improved motor coordination and a neurological severity score after post-ischemia treatment. Detailed results, fresh herb intake and measured stride remain open.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes gait examination, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: injected Capsicum fruit extract in a barbiturate challenge
assessment: Some extract and fraction groups showed a longer loss-of-righting interval. Natural sleep and clinical insomnia were outside this mouse assay.

fit: extract and a sleep diary in healthy athletes
assessment: An early within-group sleep-quality change appeared in the combined NMN and xanthophyll arm. The xanthophyll-only changes were inconclusive. Ground paprika and clinical Parkinson insomnia were not tested.

fit: hot sauce and mustard mixture and sleep in healthy men
assessment: The six-person experiment reported worsened sleep-stage and wake measures after the seasoned meal. Separate spice-specific and Parkinson effects were unmeasured.

fit: paprika oleoresin in a matched cannabinol crossover
assessment: The randomized comparison varied cannabinol. The paprika colorant was listed among excipients. There is no separate ground-paprika sleep effect.

fit: clove smell identification item and Parkinson freezing phenotype
assessment: The clove odor recognition contrast between freezers and non-freezers was inconclusive (p=.212). The study did not measure change in freezing after ingesting clove.

fit: filbertone profiling in cold-pressed hazelnut oils
assessment: Table VI measures semi-quantitative filbertone signals in some cold-pressed preparations. Raw-kernel oils in this study are below the quantification limit. No systemic uptake or tremor outcome was measured.

fit: isolated filbertone with rotarod and treadmill performance in a mouse model
assessment: The primary author dissertation for the same article shows behavioral task results. It supplies no oral hazelnut oil arm, human Parkinson cohort or resting-tremor comparison.

fit: isolated filbertone with biochemical endpoints in cell and mouse models
assessment: The full original gives biochemical and tissue markers. The preprint and article are one family. It provides neither a cold-pressed oil exposure nor a human resting-tremor result.

fit: whole hazelnuts offered and Parkinson motor composite includes rest tremor
assessment: The published composite motor score includes rest tremor. The menu lists whole nuts and separately lists other oils. There is no rest-tremor result by item or grade-specific exposure.

fit: cinnamon powder and honey with illustrative medication diaries
assessment: The case reported longer medication ON intervals. Both figures mark 15 minutes of dyskinesia and provide no severity rating or isolated cinnamon effect.

fit: cinnamon intake as a group-visit dietary outcome
assessment: OA15.04 reports increased cinnamon intake in a 155-person randomized group-visit dietary secondary analysis for adults with chronic pain and depression; preparation and an isolated cinnamon symptom effect are not reported. The claim seeks ground cinnamon and dyskinesia severity.

fit: self-reported coconut oil use and overall PD symptom progression
assessment: The observational total score does not isolate refined oil or listener intelligibility; baseline and progression models differ and uncorrected multiple testing limits inference.

fit: self-reported coconut oil frequency and total Parkinson symptom score
assessment: The cross-sectional composite association gives no refined-oil classification or listener-rated intelligibility outcome.

fit: virgin coconut oil within mixed ketogenic plan and composite motor score
assessment: The plan specifies virgin oil in recipes but not refined oil or confirmed individual intake; reported UPDRS motor totals do not isolate intelligibility.

fit: ketogenic diet and Parkinson patient-reported voice handicap
assessment: Reported VHI-10 means favor the ketogenic group after three months. The intervention does not assign a named coconut oil and the voice handicap instrument does not measure intelligibility.

fit: ketogenic diet and companion report of talking; oil exposure unverified
assessment: Participant 013's companion described better talking without listener-rated intelligibility or individual coconut-oil intake; participant 019 separately mentioned regular coconut or avocado oil.

fit: pineapple frequency and pooled urinary incontinence impact
assessment: One of eight mild and one of 12 severe impact participants reported pineapple weekly. Raw preparation, separate urgency counts and clinical Parkinson diagnosis were unmeasured.

fit: pineapple fruit and juice as reported bladder symptom triggers
assessment: Pineapple and juice were rated as worsening bladder symptoms in a painful-bladder cohort. No assigned intake, raw preparation or separate Parkinson urgency episode counts.

fit: pineapple or juice before pelvic pain and bladder symptom flares
assessment: Case-crossover odds were inconclusive overall and in participants reporting a possible dietary trigger. The dietary item pooled fruit and juice and the endpoint was a flare, without a Parkinson urgency estimate.

fit: pineapple juice sensitivity in veterans
assessment: The symptom survey recorded pineapple juice sensitivity in 42 interstitial cystitis participants and two in each comparator. It did not measure raw pineapple or Parkinson urgency.

fit: bromelain-containing mixture in bacterial and ex vivo bladder models
assessment: The mixture altered some bacterial and inflammatory measures. It provided no voiding or urgency outcome, no raw pineapple and no Parkinson participants.

fit: grouped high-acid foods and urgency urinary incontinence
assessment: Adjusted OR 1.29 (95% CI 1.03–1.62) for grouped high-acid foods. Pineapple membership and separate estimate unverified. The endpoint includes leakage.

fit: canola vehicle and acute throat symptoms during olive challenge
assessment: Acute symptoms followed a blend containing extra-virgin olive oil. No canola-specific voice estimate or designated processing grade.

fit: canola menu and speech domains in Parkinson disease
assessment: Part II and III include speech, but no separately reported speech item, sound-pressure data or processing-specific canola contrast was available.

fit: instrumented mouse stride length with equal soybean oil in two blends
assessment: The Angelman-model gait experiment measured longer strides on standard feed and shorter strides toward control with a safflower blend. Both experimental diets contained the same soybean oil amount, and the model had no Parkinson shortened-stride phenotype.

fit: dietary soybean oil substitution and ordinal stepping and coordination in rats
assessment: After spinal cord injury, scores on an ordinal measure of stepping and coordination were lower in soybean-oil-fed animals than in menhaden-oil-fed animals. No stride distances or soybean-oil preparation grade were reported.

fit: equal soybean oil and mouse treadmill stride variability
assessment: Curcumin changed stride variability while the diet oil amount was matched. The study did not isolate soybean oil or measure shortened clinical stride.

fit: soybean-oil laboratory chow and quantified treadmill gait timing
assessment: The study found no clear differences in propulsion, swing or braking time between soy-fat chow and a coconut oil/DHA/ARA developmental feed. No stride distance, oil processing grade, or Parkinson context was reported.

fit: Cuminum fruit water extract by gavage in MPTP mice; rotarod and activity endpoints
assessment: Motor activity tasks are not levodopa-induced dyskinesia; the extract, species model and preparation do not establish a toasted cumin effect in humans.

fit: Parkinson diet trial includes pan-heated cumin in soup; diet-level motor complication score
assessment: Heating in a mixed soup is not verified toasting; individual intake and a cumin-specific dyskinesia result are unavailable.

fit: UK Parkinson survey recorded cumin use in previous month; preparation and dyskinesia outcome unreported
assessment: Individual cumin use is reported but toasting, dose and dyskinesia severity are not assessed as a cumin contrast.

fit: oral extract of dried tarragon leaves and forced-swim immobility
assessment: Both extract arms under restraint had lower immobility than restraint alone, with similar total maze arm entries. This comparison concerns a concentrated extract and stress behavior rather than a clinical depressive symptom.

fit: oral tarragon tincture and rat forced-swim behavior
assessment: The paper reports no activity for the remaining preparations including tarragon in its forced-swim test, without raw tarragon estimates. The preparation and outcome differ from dried herb and Parkinson depressive symptoms.

fit: tarragon extract in feed and behavior after mouse social defeat
assessment: Social interaction and grooming improved in the behavioral model. Sucrose preference did not differ clearly. The results do not measure depressive symptoms in people with Parkinson disease.

fit: injected tarragon extract and behavioral immobility in mice
assessment: Extract reduced immobility in forced swim and at one tail-suspension dose. These are rodent proxies and do not test clinical depression or dried culinary tarragon.

fit: refined olive oil and 1-back task activation
assessment: The activation interaction was inconclusive. Imaging does not establish a clinical attention effect.

fit: MIND meals with extra-virgin olive oil and planned flanker testing
assessment: The registered outcome covers attention, but the intervention is a whole meal pattern and the oil is extra-virgin, with no posted results.

fit: olive oil shared in placebo and active arms with original attention measures
assessment: The 12-person comparator arm showed slower psychomotor vigilance and faster task switching at follow-up. Both arms contained olive oil and no verified refining grade was specified.

fit: olive-oil comparator and sustained attention battery
assessment: The full article reports fish-arm sustained-attention change. The table gives no corresponding olive-arm means, no oil-free control, and no verified oil grade.

fit: olive-oil comparator with letter cancellation and reaction times
assessment: The older-adult trial reports inconclusive secondary cognitive differences between fish and olive oil, with small descriptive changes in the olive arm. No standalone refined-oil estimate.

fit: olive comparator and complex reaction time in trained athletes
assessment: A fish-versus-olive contrast produced a group interaction. The original reports anomalous units and baseline spread. No verified refined grade, oil-free arm or Parkinson cohort.

fit: usual cooking olive oil and attention scores in a cross-sectional cohort
assessment: Higher adjusted attention scores were reported overall, with a larger association among women with HIV. The questionnaire did not separate oil grades.

fit: olive oil as a shared vehicle in an attention trial
assessment: The group-by-time complex attention interaction was p=.049 for the pearl formulation comparison. Both preparations were dipped in olive oil.

fit: refined-plus-pomace intake and adjusted attention change
assessment: The fully adjusted estimate for common olive oil was −0.006 z-score units per 10 g/day (95% CI −0.047 to 0.035). Refined-only intake was not modeled separately in the published comparison.

fit: refined oil taste and exploratory EEG
assessment: Six healthy adults tasted oils and underwent EEG. No functional attention score was measured.

fit: summer savory oil and rat rotarod motor coordination
assessment: Balance after lead exposure gives no dystonia measure.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: S7.478 orally administers oat-stem lignin to irradiated mice and S6.415 studies oat seed germination. Neither is a prepared oat-grain or Parkinson motor comparison.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-14-021 studies oat globulin hydrolysates and P-15-007 applies isolated oat phenolics to keratinocytes. Oat-beverage fermentation is another member. OATS also names a semen phenotype.

fit: oat bran as an option within a bundled Parkinson diet
assessment: The pilot had a small, inconclusive composite motor change. It did not quantify oat intake or individual rigidity.

fit: oat-containing synbiotic in a Parkinson rat model
assessment: The rat intervention combined oats with three probiotic strains and measured tissue and microbiota outcomes rather than rigidity.

fit: common-sage extract chemistry and antiproliferative experiment
assessment: The author abstract confirms sage-derived extracts and chemical and cancer cell endpoints. P33 references this same report. It provides no culinary dose or Parkinson symptom comparison.

fit: isolated ellagic acid gavage and measured stride in rats
assessment: Stride improved in a small lesion model after purified acid. A 2016 report shares the investigators and possibly the same cohort, so it is not counted as independent. Ground sage, dose correspondence and human stride remain untested.

fit: sage leaf extract and paw-print index after sciatic injury
assessment: Footprint index improved after extract. No stride length was measured.

fit: safflower oil capsules and bowel tolerability
assessment: Some volunteer participants reported bloating. No tally of constipation, bowel rate or stool consistency during the active period. The comparison did not establish oil refining.

fit: safflower oil comparator and constipation adverse event in Glut1 deficiency
assessment: Constipation was reported in 1 of 42 on safflower oil and 1 of 43 on triheptanoin during blinded exposure. This is an adverse-event count rather than a constipation severity comparison against no oil.

fit: safflower-containing comparator and registered bowel diaries
assessment: Protocol measures stool frequency and consistency in a synbiotic comparison. High-oleic safflower is one placebo ingredient. No posted outcomes.

fit: safflower oil frequency and composite PRO-PD
assessment: The adjusted composite difference was +6.8 points per frequency step (95% CI −6.8 to +20.5). No separate constipation or grade comparison is available.

fit: high-oleic safflower and canola in defined diet and stool characteristics
assessment: The blend with different fiber produced firmer stools and greater output per unit fiber. The formula varied several ingredients and did not measure Parkinson constipation.

fit: inhaled marjoram oil and resting blood pressure
assessment: In nine seated healthy adults, mean arterial pressure decreased versus plain air at the last two minutes. A separate supine comparison used baseline. Standing symptoms and oral fresh marjoram were outside the experiment.

fit: marjoram extract and aortic ring relaxation
assessment: Vascular tissue relaxation is not an orthostatic symptom measurement.

fit: filtered marjoram tea and composite nonmotor scale in Parkinson
assessment: The report gives no separate estimate for standing lightheadedness. It tested a dried-leaf tea.

fit: inhaled marjoram oil and mean arterial pressure
assessment: Rested between-group pressure change was inconclusive. No standing symptoms or food exposure.

fit: clinical allspice allergy case with limited access
assessment: The primary citation reports severe allergy. Preparation, swallowing data, and the full case history could not be verified.

fit: anise in a Parkinson honey mixture and broad sleep disturbance in an unlinked survey
assessment: The survey's sleep-disturbance category is not an exposure-linked dream-enactment count; ground preparation and individual intake remain unverified.

fit: older-men exercise comparison with a candidate cold-pressed pumpkin component in the control blend
assessment: The manuscript confirms the blend and brand. A matching 2015 NIH label names cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil. The specific lot is unverified. The trial measures strength and walking under exercise without handwriting or Parkinson outcomes.

fit: vegetarian Parkinson intervention naming pumpkin seed oil and a motor composite
assessment: Appendix A lists the oil among other foods, and supplement Figure S2 reports UPDRS III totals. The pressing process, individually consumed oil and handwriting outcomes are unreported.

fit: filtered marjoram tea and composite nonmotor scale in Parkinson
assessment: The reported NMSS total cannot identify a change in visual hallucination frequency.

fit: tested oral marjoram extract and behavioral observation in rats
assessment: The Methods specify female rats and a dried aerial-parts extract. General observation and acute mortality do not measure hallucinations. No Parkinson or fresh-leaf exposure.

fit: historical report of attempted use without verified hallucination outcome
assessment: An ethnobotanical article mentions alleged use with the intent to induce hallucinations. The description does not authenticate a marjoram species, clinical event, visual modality or preparation.

fit: cinnamon pen identification in recently diagnosed Parkinson
assessment: Table 3 reports 1/32 Parkinson and 17/24 matched controls identified cinnamon, p < .001. This is cross-sectional recognition with no ingestion measure.

fit: cinnamon odor identification in Parkinson disease
assessment: Four of 29 participants with Parkinson disease and 37 of 76 comparison patients identified cinnamon. The cross-sectional test used smell stimuli and did not administer ground cinnamon as food.

fit: cinnamon odor identification in early-onset Parkinson
assessment: Cinnamon recognition was 43.9% in an early-onset cohort of 156, and the original figure shows about 56% errors. No item denominator, food intake or cinnamon-specific duration estimate was reported.

fit: mixed oral oils and planned adverse smell changes
assessment: First posted in 2026 after reported completion. The mixed essential oil study schedules adverse smell checks and has no posted results. The independent cinnamon effect and Parkinson olfaction remain unresolved.

fit: cinnamon odor as a diagnostic stimulus
assessment: The stimulus helped distinguish existing olfactory deficits and does not estimate an ingestion effect.

fit: cinnamon odor among pooled diagnostic stimuli
assessment: Cinnamon was one of twelve scent stimuli. The report gives aggregate identification scores, without cinnamon-specific results or ingestion.

fit: cinnamon pen identification in Parkinson and other cohorts
assessment: The author workbook confirms 17/54 Parkinson, 16/54 iRBD and 25/54 control correct responses. The primary report's three-group p value is .154. Cinnamon intake is not recorded.

fit: self-reported cinnamon use and recognition in adult volunteers
assessment: Table 1 reports 98.0% correct recognition in 102 self-reported users and 93.3% in 15 nonusers, nonsignificant. The study provides no Parkinson cohort, dose or change over time.

fit: cinnamon used as a diagnostic smell stimulus
assessment: Both cohorts took two test batteries with different odors. The comparison assesses existing olfaction and does not estimate an ingestion effect.

fit: five-odor training including cinnamon and postinfectious olfaction
assessment: Group-by-time TDI comparison favored odor training (p=.018). Multiple combined odors, no oral exposure or Parkinson cohort, and unresolved item-level reporting discrepancy.

fit: cinnamon used as a diagnostic smell-test stimulus
assessment: Participants identified scents including cinnamon and orange. The comparison measures existing olfactory impairment and cognition, with no cinnamon consumption measurement.

fit: confirmed cinnamon odor in a post-traumatic rotating regimen
assessment: The 2024 companion Methods identify cinnamon in month three together with other odors. The same-cohort 2021 report measures general smell outcomes across a combined regimen. No isolated cinnamon effect was estimated.

fit: cinnamon odor response in the precursor PREDICT-PD model
assessment: Correct cinnamon odor identification was associated with lower Parkinson case odds in the 16-odor model (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21–0.45) and the six-odor model (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.15–0.30). These are diagnostic responses, with no cinnamon intake measure.

fit: diagnostic cinnamon smell cue in the community protocol
assessment: The protocol names cinnamon as an odor for identification and provides no odor-specific result or consumed spice contrast. A later presentation gives prevalence. The related PROBE registry has no posted results, and exact cohort overlap is unresolved.

fit: dried cinnamon sniffing and a synthetic cinnamon pen
assessment: The author workbook gives 4/34 Parkinson versus 26/53 control correct responses to sniffing dried cinnamon (p < .001), and 24/80 versus 45/105 for the synthetic pen (nonsignificant). The 2021 dissertation and workbook and the 2022 article are the same study. No cinnamon consumption was measured.

fit: cinnamon odor recognition across causes of hyposmia
assessment: Supplementary Table 1 reports 48% correct in Parkinson hyposmia versus 29% in non-Parkinson hyposmia, n=194 per group, adjusted p=.0087. No intake or symptom change after eating cinnamon was measured.

fit: cinnamon in an abbreviated diagnostic smell battery
assessment: The analysis assesses diagnostic performance across cohorts. It did not test whether ground cinnamon changes smell impairment.

fit: six inhaled odors and olfaction during diabetes-related cognitive impairment
assessment: Abstract reports overall olfaction difference without numeric item effects. Probable registry NCT06327633. No oral intervention or individual cinnamon contrast.

fit: cinnamon diagnostic odor in the 2018 to 2021 cohort
assessment: Cinnamon is one stimulus in the smell test of 1,472 adults without Parkinson disease. No cinnamon ingestion or change in smell impairment was tested.

fit: cinnamon diagnostic smell cue in the 40-item UPSIT
assessment: Original Figure 4 explicitly lists cinnamon. The smell identification comparison establishes diagnostic context. Food intake was outside the study design.

fit: oral ground cinnamon and rated meal-smell pleasantness
assessment: In 19 men with diabetes, ground cinnamon and control sessions yielded inconclusive breakfast-smell pleasantness contrasts. Clinical olfaction and Parkinson disease were outside the study design.

fit: cinnamon odor identification in the 2024 to 2025 cohort
assessment: The two meeting versions describe the same 1,519 participants and time variation in correctly identifying the cinnamon stimulus. People with diagnosed Parkinson disease were excluded.

fit: fresh basil and a separate vial of unspecified culinary basil in a Parkinson diet pilot
assessment: The ingredient form in the vial and participant use cannot be confirmed. The Part I composite supplies no dried-basil result on apathy severity.

fit: basil listed with other spices in a Parkinson hospital diet
assessment: The report gives a baseline Part I total and clinical motor follow-up. Basil preparation, individual consumption and apathy severity results are unavailable.

fit: inhaled basil oil and stress-model mouse immobility
assessment: Inhaled oil reduced forced-swim immobility vs untreated stressed mice. The behavioral measure and route cannot isolate dried-basil intake or clinical apathy.

fit: combined cinnamon bark and ginger Kampo formula
assessment: Dream enactment reportedly stopped in one Parkinson case after a seven-ingredient formula. The contribution of cinnamon was not separated.

fit: rotating versus stable mouse odors including tarragon
assessment: At 60 minutes the rotating odor group preferred a new odor by time and visits, while stable mixture and empty-cage groups lacked clear preference. The assay used limonene and carvone. Tarragon was one enrichment odor.

fit: tarragon versus thyme odor pair in mice
assessment: Author spreadsheets give mean pair 7 acquisition/reversal errors of 7.40/7.47 in 15 Alzheimer-model mice and 7.83/15.22 in 18 controls. Both scents were present, paired exposure was olfactory, and genotype and task order limit interpretation.

fit: odor rotation including tarragon and mouse olfactory deficit
assessment: Discrimination index after reopened naris was lower than intact controls without enrichment, with no clear difference from intact controls in the enriched group. Rotating odors and food ingestion are distinct.

fit: odor rotation including tarragon and mouse odor recognition
assessment: Enriched mice retained odor recognition through 240 minutes while controls showed it only at 30 minutes. Both conditions lacked clear recognition at 480 minutes. No tarragon arm or dietary exposure.

fit: odor rotation including tarragon and impaired mouse odor discrimination
assessment: Double knockouts discriminated two esters after enrichment p < .001, with p = .72 in empty-container animals. The study did not isolate tarragon odor or measure eating dried herb.

fit: raw and dry-fried huajiao volatile oils and evoked mouse pain
assessment: Bian and colleagues compared orally administered volatile fractions from raw and dry-fried huajiao in groups of ten mice. Mean counts of acetic-acid-evoked writhes over 20 minutes were 19.50 and 27.20 for the raw fractions, 18.40 and 21.10 for dry-fried fractions, and 49.60 for vehicle. The abstract reports differences from vehicle but supplies no verified fried-versus-raw contrast or species voucher. It identifies a processed aromatic fraction and an evoked animal outcome, rather than measuring pain after consumption of whole toasted pepper.

fit: isolated compound and mouse mechanical pain
assessment: Local sanshool reduced mechanical hypersensitivity without a comparable heat result. The preparation and route differ from toasted pepper.

fit: formula and gastrointestinal pain in controlled IBS trial
assessment: The double-blind trial detected no significant abdominal pain or rectal sensation effect.

fit: formula and constipation-associated abdominal pain
assessment: Within-group abdominal pain scores fell in the higher-dose arm of a two-dose study without placebo.

fit: species-identified oil and oral discomfort in xerostomia
assessment: Interview ratings for oral pain and discomfort improved after a capsule containing several ingredients in nine women. There was no placebo group.

fit: formula and constipation-associated abdominal pain
assessment: A placebo-controlled constipation trial reported improved abdominal pain within the formula group. This was a secondary endpoint in a different population.

fit: PD saffron capsule; Part III composite motor exam; no fall frequency estimate
assessment: Part III includes gait and postural stability but does not report fall frequency; ground preparation remains unverified.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-15-013 assays hydromethanolic Crocus sativus tepal extracts and performs molecular docking. The floral waste preparation differs from ground stigma, and no symptom was measured.

fit: PD Sargol powder tablet; composite mobility; no fall-count outcome accessible
assessment: Part II walking and balance and III gait or stability do not count falls; reported mobility composite cannot determine fall-frequency direction.

fit: occasional stiffness after whole macadamia kernels in dogs
assessment: Stiffness was among the less frequent field signs after kernel ingestion. The experimental dogs had marked weakness, and Parkinson rigidity and orally administered cold-pressed oil were not tested.

fit: macadamia oil and cerebellar tissue markers in rats
assessment: Author abstract describes changes in biochemical markers and cerebellar pathology after chemical injury. Oil grade, motor outcomes and Parkinson rigidity are not established.

fit: Intentional powdered nutmeg with coexposures at author excerpt depth
assessment: The corrected proof excerpt reports confusion and hallucinations with alcohol and medications. The full case and any resting-tremor examination remain open. A later abstract reports the same presentation.

fit: Ground nutmeg overdose and original neurological examination
assessment: The original case describes slightly unsteady gait without focal deficit and does not document tremor. No Parkinson diagnosis or ordinary culinary exposure.

fit: Distinct Italian poison-center nutmeg abstract
assessment: The abstract records digestive symptoms and headache after intentional excess intake. It does not record a neurological exam, a rest-tremor assessment or a Parkinson diagnosis.

fit: Acute powdered nutmeg intoxication and seizure in original report
assessment: Status epilepticus during a severe overdose. Original clinical account gives no tremor phenotype or Parkinson diagnosis. Distinct from the later Axarquía reports.

fit: Accidental excess nutmeg and neurological examination in one case
assessment: The original reports an unremarkable subsequent neurological examination. Tremor is discussed in the background literature and was not documented as a finding in this case with alcohol coexposure.

fit: Nutmeg overdose case at abstract and original snippet depth
assessment: The publisher snippet identifies an adolescent with no relevant history or regular medication. A conference listing repeats the author abstract. Complete case and any rest-tremor observation remain unverified.

fit: Swiss poison-center cases and grouped acute neurological signs
assessment: Moderate signs include myoclonus in an aggregate series with incomplete medical follow-up. No separate Parkinson rest-tremor outcome or ordinary culinary comparison.

fit: Illinois poison-center reports and unclassified tremor
assessment: The Discussion states that a recorder judged a recorded tremor unrelated to exposure and describes a severely affected patient with tremor and several coexposures. The authors did not report tremor posture or an independent rest-tremor comparison.

fit: acute accidental nutmeg overdose and upper-limb tremor
assessment: Upper-limb tremor followed accidental excess ingestion. Clinical rest tremor, Parkinson disease and usual culinary exposure were not established.

fit: injected nutmeg extract and mouse locomotion from original abstract
assessment: The 1984 author abstract reports moderate reduction in spontaneous activity and separate effects on ethanol and amphetamine activity comparisons. The accessible endpoint is locomotion, with no separate rest-tremor measure and no oral culinary or Parkinson comparison. Original methods and figures remain open.

fit: ground nutmeg poisoning and intention tremor with uncertain report overlap
assessment: Both original accounts describe intention tremor after excess powdered nutmeg. Shared authors, setting, age and time course make the same case plausible. Ingestion details and medication history conflict. The 2017 report includes diazepam co-ingestion and a positive benzodiazepine test, leaving causal attribution and Parkinson rest-tremor effects unresolved.

fit: thyme-containing topical oil blend and registered facial anxiety
assessment: The protocol registers a facial expression scale for anxiety in an intensive-care population, with no posted results, fresh thyme intake or Parkinson reduced expressiveness endpoint.

fit: thyme-containing mixed diet; aggregate motor examination score
assessment: The Part III total includes facial expression, but the paper gives no separate facial item or fresh thyme effect.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes speech, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: low
assessment: Two uncontrolled blepharospasm cases reported symptom or treatment-frequency changes with topical frankincense. Almond oil was one of three possible diluents with no patient-level assignment. No isolated oral almond oil, processing grade or Parkinson-related dystonia measure was verified.

fit: fresh whole blackberries and measured baseline gait speed in older adults
assessment: The mean baseline eight-foot gait speed subscore was 2.6 ± 1.3 out of four in 28 older adults. Plain fresh blackberries were eaten in a separate plate-waste exercise. Attrition of 82% prevented a before-and-after estimate. The registry, thesis and program reports are one study family.

fit: blackberry diet and plank walking in aged rats
assessment: The small-plank task improved after blackberry feeding. The experiment assessed motor coordination in aged rats and gives no human walking speed or raw fruit contrast.

fit: ground sumac as an aroma stimulus
assessment: Ground sumac is the tested smell stimulus. The study did not evaluate impairment after consumption.

fit: sumac volatile profile across fruit preparations
assessment: Volatile analysis describes products and food preparations without clinical smell testing.

fit: aroma compounds across Sicilian sumac preparations
assessment: Headspace chemistry compared sumac sources and processing without exposing Parkinson participants.

fit: sumac descriptor familiarity in an olfactory test adaptation
assessment: Kamrava and colleagues surveyed familiarity with candidate odor descriptors for the Iranian Sniffin’ Sticks identification test. Table 1 gives sumac a 57% familiarity rating in the 200-person survey, below the study’s selection threshold. It was excluded from the final identification odors. No participant consumed sumac as a test exposure, and the result does not measure a change in smell.

fit: COVID-19 trial of commercial sumac plus pomegranate juice
assessment: Men reported less combined smell-and-taste dysfunction within the intervention arm, but the post-treatment comparison was null in both sexes. Sumac was combined with pomegranate and olfaction was not measured separately.

fit: healthy adult sensory crossover of culinary brown sumac
assessment: Aroma liking did not clearly differ between butternut squash soup with versus without brown sumac. The trial excluded factors affecting sensory perception and did not test participants for olfactory impairment.

fit: oral ground botanical as a strained infusion and general tolerability
assessment: The trial asked about tolerability on day 11 and reports no event that substantially affected the protocol. It gives no fatigue scale or arm-specific adverse-event counts.

fit: reduced responsiveness and lethargy after oral infusions
assessment: Poison-center cases describe acute infant hyporeactivity or lethargy after oral laurel preparations, which differs from chronic Parkinson fatigue.

fit: healthy adult randomized safety study of standardized leaf extract
assessment: The abstract reports zero adverse events in 12 extract recipients and 10 placebo recipients after four weeks. It gives no fatigue-specific measure and used an extract in healthy adults.

fit: inhaled leaf and an attention task susceptible to vigilance decline
assessment: Low-exposure inhalation preserved task vigilance. A fatigue severity outcome was not measured.

fit: fatigue during probable injury associated with leaf infusion
assessment: Fatigue accompanied probable herb-induced liver injury after prolonged crushed-leaf infusion exposure. The report describes no standardized fatigue result or Parkinson population.

fit: canola vehicle and stepping tests in a Parkinson model
assessment: The 6-OHDA experiment assessed stepping and bridge performance with canola as the vehicle. It did not estimate independent oil effects or track freezing episodes.

fit: canola menu and freezing-of-gait domains in Parkinson disease
assessment: The Parkinson trial scored the Parts II and III domains containing freezing items. It reports no item-specific change, frequency or independent canola contrast.

fit: canola comparator and six-minute walk in older adults
assessment: The ketone-ester comparison reports inconclusive post-treatment walking distance and composite lower-extremity function. The cohort excluded active neurologic conditions, with no freezing episodes logged and no isolated oil effect.

fit: canola comparator and instrumented walking outcomes in older adults
assessment: Walking speed and step-length differences between arms were inconclusive. The study enrolled healthy elders and did not log freezing events.

fit: canola comparator and timed mobility in adults
assessment: Timed up and go improved in all arms and differed inconclusively between arms. The test did not report freezing frequency.

fit: rectal sesame oil in a multimodal regimen and gait item
assessment: Gait scores improved from baseline in the uncontrolled series. Neither walking speed nor an isolated cold-pressed sesame oil effect was reported.

fit: injected sesame oil comparator in a planned mobility assessment
assessment: The registered critical-care study uses intramuscular oil as the testosterone comparator and plans Timed Up and Go. No posted outcome or oral cold-pressed oil.

fit: same Parkinson rectal sesame-oil cohort across two publications
assessment: The congress item republishes the 15-person rectal formulation comparison. Combined botanical and sesame oil exposures and MDS-UPDRS components provide no separate walking estimate.

fit: oral sesame seeds and Timed Up and Go in knee osteoarthritis
assessment: Timed Up and Go improved in each group, with post-treatment difference p=.002. The abstract gives no group-specific times. Exposure was seed with standard care.

fit: topical sesame oil and eight-meter walk in knee osteoarthritis
assessment: Noninferiority to diclofenac was reported for walk time. The abstract lacks the walk means, interval and margin. Topical treatment of knee osteoarthritis leaves effects of cold-pressed dietary oil on Parkinson gait open.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: Sesame oil acts as an injected vehicle in rat corticosteroid or AF64A experiments, with no oral oil comparison.

fit: isolated sesamol and catalepsy in a manganese rat model
assessment: Bar and grid catalepsy improved with the constituent. The study gives no dystonic posture assessment or toasted sesame oil effect.

fit: open cannabidiol series and sesame vehicle provenance
assessment: The original abstract gives five dystonia cases, two with parkinsonian features. Unofficial Methods transcription names sesame as drug carrier. No verified toasted grade or separate oil effect.

fit: mustard listed on a multi-item Parkinson intervention menu
assessment: The published motor composite includes postural stability. Appendix A names mustard without preparation. No separate postural-stability estimate or effect of the mustard was reported.

fit: anethole and rotarod fall latency in toxin-exposed rats
assessment: The PLoS report describes longer rotarod fall latency and longer stride. Fall frequency in ordinary activity and ground seed were unmeasured.

fit: low
assessment: Aqueous seed extract lowered arterial pressure and heart rate in rats. A likely precursor explicitly used daily oral extract in salt-fed rats. The reports give no measured orthostatic symptoms, everyday falls, or ground-seed clinical exposure.

fit: aniseed ether placebo excipient and a secondary falls outcome
assessment: Vitamin D doses were assigned against placebo in kidney disease. Falls are registered at six months, with no posted results or isolated ground anise exposure.

fit: ground anise mixture and open adverse-event ascertainment
assessment: The acute-COVID trial reports general symptoms including throat itching or thirst in the anise group. No prespecified fall endpoint or fall-frequency result.

fit: topical sweet almond oil massage and knee joint stiffness
assessment: In 60 women with knee osteoarthritis receiving physical therapy, joint stiffness improved within the topical almond-oil massage group (reported change interval −1.04 to −0.36), but between-group stiffness differences were nonsignificant (p=.707). Joint stiffness, topical massage, and Parkinson muscle rigidity are different.

fit: topical sweet almond oil placebo and knee joint stiffness
assessment: The topical sweet almond placebo arm had WOMAC joint stiffness means 6.30, 6.50, 5.10, 4.90 at baseline, immediate postintervention, one week and three weeks versus 6.40, 6.93, 5.53, 5.26 in routine care. Reported three-arm p=.924/.001/.22/.195 with post hoc emphasis on tarragon comparisons. It does not test oral cold-pressed oil or Parkinson muscle rigidity.

fit: banana-flavored grain reward in a macaque drug comparison
assessment: Four rhesus monkeys received a banana-flavored reinforcer. The later papers confirm flavored grain pellets. Drug assignment, uncertain fruit content and reinforcement outcomes leave eating raw banana for the named Parkinson symptom open.

fit: plain levodopa granules mixed directly with banana
assessment: At one hour, 40.0% of starting levodopa remained in the banana-water mixture and 47.0% in the banana-milk mixture. This is chemical compatibility without a dyskinesia outcome.

fit: pediatric case and levodopa compatibility assay
assessment: The poster describes dark vomiting in a child with dystonia and drug loss after direct mixing with banana and milk. No Parkinson dyskinesia result was measured.

fit: banana and milk mixture with dissolved levodopa tablet
assessment: The manufacturer reported a decline in measurable levodopa in a bench mixture. There was no patient exposure or dyskinesia assessment.

fit: fresh banana juice and levodopa exposure in rats
assessment: Drug exposure was lower with fresh juice in a three-rat group. The rat study gives no dyskinesia result.

fit: suspected interaction and secondary report of dyskinesia worsening
assessment: A secondary summary of the same case describes worsening dyskinesia during wearing off, opposite to the frozen claim. The primary text, banana preparation and severity measurements remain unavailable.

fit: banana with levodopa and dark vomiting
assessment: The letter describes a patient observation and separate fruit and levodopa mixture darkening. No dyskinesia or drug exposure estimate is given.

fit: broccoli seed tea and self-rated motor symptoms
assessment: The selected volunteers used broccoli seed tea with mustard. The report gives no fall frequency result or steamed broccoli comparison.

fit: isolated compound and composite motor outcomes
assessment: Study registration with no posted result. Steamed broccoli and fall frequency were not isolated.

fit: bioactivated compound and broader symptoms
assessment: The register lists actual primary completion on October 14, 2026, with no posted results at the November 17 check and no dedicated fall-frequency endpoint. The formulation uses a compound from kale seed bioactivated with mustard seed myrosinase.

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking
assessment: Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

fit: steamed broccoli compared with a control diet in smokers
assessment: The crossover observed blood-cell DNA endpoints. The preparation fits while the falls outcome and diagnosed Parkinson population are absent.

fit: cruciferous vegetable recalls and estimated indole intake
assessment: The study includes broccoli, cauliflower and kale within a food inventory. Neither constituent exposure nor a symptom effect is established for a particular preparation.

fit: carotenoid food recalls and macular pigment measurements
assessment: The participant records name several food sources and the authors report no detected association with optical pigment density. No assigned food preparation or relevant Parkinson symptom was measured.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: The review cites actual broccoli interventions, including a steamed broccoli crossover. The linked studies measure DNA markers, not separately observed Parkinson falls.

fit: isolated broccoli-associated sulforaphane and motor coordination in mice
assessment: The original abstract reports improvements in rotation and motor coordination in lesioned mice. There was no steamed broccoli exposure or clinical fall count.

fit: broccoli as a survey-reported gastrointestinal symptom trigger
assessment: The gastroparesis survey gives no Parkinson falls estimate.

fit: cooked broccoli in a calcium questionnaire and falls in an education trial
assessment: The education arm had fewer reported falls by rank, with a median of zero in both arms. The study did not estimate steamed broccoli intake or effects.

fit: separate gastrointestinal conference member and ingredient context
assessment: P0032 tests isolated sulforaphane in liver fibrosis. Broccoli supplies botanical context, and the constituent study has no broccoli food arm or matched symptom.
